en_text: I pull the car into the driveway. Sit back. Try to relax. The day, I swear to God, has to be at least ninety-ﬁve degrees. Christchurch heat. Schizophrenic weather. Sweat is dripping from my body. My ﬁngers are wet-rubber damp. I lean forward and twist the keys in the ignition, grab my briefcase, and climb out of the car. Out here, the air-conditioning actually works. I reach the front door and fumble with the lock. I breathe a sigh of relief when I step inside.
zh_text: 我把車駛入私人車道。靠著椅背。試圖放鬆心情。我敢對天發誓，今天氣溫起碼有三十五度。基督城式的炎熱。精神分裂症般的天氣。我汗流浹背。手指濕得像是戴著濕塑膠手套。我湊向前去，轉動啟動器上的車鑰匙，拿起我的公事包，開門下車。到了外面，空調終於開始作用了。我來到正門口，打開門鎖。進門之後我才終於鬆了口氣。

en_text: I stroll through to the kitchen. Angela, I can hear, is in the shower upstairs. I’ll disturb her later. For now, I need a drink. I walk to the fridge. It has a stainless-steel door in which my reﬂection looks like a ghost. I open the door and squat down in front of it for close to a minute, making friends with the cool air. The fridge offers me both beer and Coke. I take a beer, twist off the cap, and sit down at the table. I’m no heavy drinker, but I knock this bottle back in maybe twenty seconds. The fridge offers up another bottle. Who am I to say no? I lean back in the chair. Put my feet up on the table. Consider taking off my shoes. You know that feeling? A hot day at work. Stress for eight hours. Then sitting down, feet in the air, beer in hand, and you take your shoes off.
zh_text: 我慢慢晃入廚房。聽得出來安琪拉正在樓上洗澡，我晚點再去煩她。現在，我需要喝點東西。我走到冰箱前。不鏽鋼冰箱門上反射出我的倒影，看來就跟幽靈一樣。我打開冰箱，在前面蹲了將近一分鐘，跟冰涼空氣交朋友。冰箱裡有啤酒和可樂。我拿出一瓶啤酒，扭下瓶蓋，在餐桌旁坐下。我酒量並不好，不過卻在二十秒內就把一瓶啤酒喝光。冰箱問我要不要再來一瓶。我有什麼理由拒絕呢？我背靠椅背，雙腳翹在桌上，考慮要不要把鞋脫了。你知道那種感覺：辛苦工作一整天。經歷八小時的緊張壓力。然後坐下來，雙腳翹在桌上，手上拎著啤酒，接著你就把鞋子脫掉。

en_text: Pure bliss.
zh_text: 單純的幸福。

en_text: Listening to the shower upstairs, I casually sip at my second beer of the year. Takes me ﬁve minutes to ﬁnish this one, and now I’m hungry. Back at the fridge and to the slice of cold pizza I spied on my ﬁrst trip. I shrug. Why not? It isn’t as though I need to watch my weight.
zh_text: 聽著樓上沖澡的聲音，我輕鬆啜飲第二瓶年度最佳啤酒。喝完這瓶酒花了我兩分鐘的時間，接著我又餓了。剛剛在冰箱裡看到一片冰披薩。我聳了聳肩。有何不可？我又不需要注意體重。

en_text: I sit back at the table. Feet in the air. The same thing works for pizza as it does for beer once you get those shoes off. Right now, though, I don’t have the time. I wolf down the pizza, pick up my briefcase, and make my way upstairs. The stereo in the bedroom is pumping out a song I recognize, but can’t name. Same goes for the artist. Nevertheless, I ﬁnd myself humming along as I lay my briefcase on the bed, knowing the tune will be stuck in my mind for hours. I sit down next to the briefcase. Open it. Take the newspaper out. The ﬁrst page offers up the sort of news that makes newspapers sell. Often I wonder if the media makes half this stuff up, just to inﬂate sales. There’s deﬁnitely a market for it.
zh_text: 我坐回桌旁。雙腳翹回桌上。只要脫掉鞋子，吃披薩跟喝啤酒一樣紓壓。不過此時此刻，我沒那個時間。我狼吞虎嚥吃光披薩，拿起我的公事包，朝向二樓走去。臥室的音響正在播放一首曾經聽過但卻不知道歌名的歌。我也不知道是誰唱的。總而言之，我一邊將公事包放在桌上，一邊開始跟著哼歌，心知這個曲調將會在我腦中縈繞數小時。我在公事包旁坐下。打開上蓋。拿出裡面的報紙。第一頁裡印著那種會讓報紙大賣的新聞，我常常懷疑其中有半數新聞是媒體捏造出來的，只爲了提高銷售量；這種新聞保證有市場。

en_text: I hear the shower turn off but ignore it, preferring to read the paper. It’s an article about some guy who’s been terrorizing the city. Killing women. Torture. Rape. Homicide. The stuff movies are made of. A couple of minutes go by and I’m still sitting here reading when Angela, wiping her hair with a towel, steps out of the bathroom surrounded by white steam and the smell of skin lotion. I lower the newspaper and smile. She looks over at me.
zh_text: 我聽見關水的聲音，不過不加理會，繼續閱讀報紙。那是一篇關於某個震驚全市的男子的報導：殺害女人、折磨、強暴、謀殺……完全是那種可以用來拍電影的題材。兩分鐘後，我依然坐在床上看報紙，安琪拉一邊拿著毛巾擦頭髮，一邊走出充滿蒸汽和乳液味道的浴室。我壓低報紙，面露微笑。她看向我。

en_text: “Who the fuck are you?” she asks.
zh_text: 「你他媽的是誰？」她問。

en_text: The sun is heading toward the horizon with only a few hours of life left today, it’s blinding her, making beads of sweat run down the inside of her dress and dampening the material. It glints off the polished granite gravestone, making her squint, but she refuses to look away from the letters that have been scripted across it for the last ﬁve years. The bright light is making her eyes water—not that it matters; her eyes always water when she comes here. She should have worn sunglasses. She should have worn a lighter dress. She should have done more to prevent him from dying.
zh_text: 太陽高掛天際，令她感到十分刺眼，汗珠在連身裙下滴落，浸濕布料。陽光照亮光滑的花崗岩墓碑，迫使她眯起雙眼，不過她拒絕將目光自刻在墓碑上已五年的碑文上移開。耀眼的陽光讓她眼眶潮濕——不過不重要；她每次來此都會眼眶濕潤。她應該要戴太陽眼鏡，她應該穿比較輕便的服裝，最重要的是，她應該做更多事情預防他死亡。

en_text: Sally clutches the cruciﬁx hanging around her neck, the four ends of it digging hard into her palm. She can’t remember the last time she took it off, and she fears that if she did she would roll up into a small ball and just cry forever, spending the rest of her days unable to function. She had it when the doctors at the hospital gave her family the news. She held it tightly as they sat her down, and with their somber faces told her what they had told countless other families who knew their loved ones were dying but who still held out hope. It was hanging over her heart when she drove her parents to the funeral home, sat down with the funeral director, and, over tea and coffee that nobody touched, shopped through cofﬁn brochures, turning the glossy pages and trying to pick out something her dead brother would look good in. They had to do the same for the suit. Even death was fashion conscious. The suits in the catalogs were photographed hanging on mannequins; it would have been in bad taste to have had them on happy-go-lucky people smiling and trying to look sexy. She has had the cruciﬁx every day since, using it for guidance, using it to remind herself that Martin is in a better place now, that life isn’t as bad as it seems.
zh_text: 莎莉緊握掛在脖子上的十字架，四個頂端深深陷入她的掌心。她想不起來上次取下十字架是什麼時候，因為她深怕一旦取下，她就會縮成一團，不停哭泣，一輩子都站不起來。醫生在醫院裡告知家人噩耗的時候，她身上就戴著這枚十字架。她在他們扶她坐下時緊握著它，看著那些陰鬱的面孔說著那些曾經用來告訴過無數明知心愛之人即將死去卻依然抱持希望的家人的話。當她開車載父母前赴殯儀館，跟殯儀館館長在沒人去碰的茶和咖啡之前來討論葬禮事宜，研究棺材型錄，翻著光鮮亮麗的頁面，試圖挑出一副能讓死去的弟弟風光沉睡的棺材時，它就掛在她的心口。他們還得以同樣的方式挑選西裝，就連死亡也要講究品味。型錄中的西裝通通穿在假人身上；如果是找神情輕鬆、笑容滿面的性感男女來拍，看起來就不大對勁了。那天之後，她就一直戴著那只十字架，引導她的人生，提醒自己馬丁如今身處更美好的世界，生活並不像表面看來那麼糟糕。

en_text: She has been staring at the grave for the last forty minutes, unable to move. Fifty feet away a set of oak trees form a partial barrier between her and a small lake which she guesses must almost be right in the middle of the cemetery. A few months ago some bodies were found in that lake. Every now and then the nor’wester will snap one of the growing acorns from the branches and throw it onto a gravestone, the clicking sound like that of a breaking ﬁnger. The cemetery is an expanse of lush lawn broken up with cement markers and, at the moment, mostly deserted, except for a handful of people standing in front of gravestones, all of them with tragedies of their own. She wonders whether more show up during the day, whether the graveyard has peak-hour trafﬁc. She hopes it does. She doesn’t like the idea of people dying and other people forgetting. The grass is longer than usual, and messy around the gravestones and trees. Even the gardens are overgrown. There used to be a caretaker out here who would regularly steer his riding lawn mower like a racing car through the rows of graves, but then he retired or died, she can’t quite remember which, and in the following months nature has been reclaiming the land.
zh_text: 她已經盯著墓碑看了四十分鐘，完全無法移動。附近橡樹的影子逐漸拉長。三不五時會有陣陣強烈的西北風將樹枝上的橡實吹落在墓碑上，發出類似手指折斷的聲音。墓園是一大片蒼翠茂盛的草坪，由許多水泥墓碑分隔開來，此時空蕩蕩地，只有幾個人站在墓碑前面，每個人心中都有屬於自己的悲劇。她在想今天會不會有更多人來，墓園是否也有尖峰時段。她希望有。她不喜歡人們死後就會被遺忘的想法。不遠處有個男人駕駛除草機，像開賽車般地四下除草，大概是想要趕快收工，離開這個地方。除草機的聲音隨風飄入她的耳中。有一天那個男的，墓園管理員，可能也會被埋在這裡，到時候又會換誰除草呢？

en_text: She doesn’t even know why she’s thinking such things. Caretakers dying, peak-hour trafﬁc, people forgetting the dead. She’s always like this when she comes here. Morbid, all messed up, as if somebody has put her thoughts into a cocktail shaker and shaken the hell out of it. She likes to come here at least once a month, if likes is an appropriate word. She always, absolutely always, makes it here on the anniversary of Martin’s death, which is what today is. Tomorrow would have been his birthday. Or still is. She isn’t sure whether it counts once you’re in the ground. For some reason she can’t explain, she never comes here on his birthday. She’s sure it would induce the same result as if she were to take off her cruciﬁx. Her parents made it out here earlier in the afternoon, she can tell by the fresh ﬂowers next to her own. She never comes here with them. That is something else she can’t explain, not even to herself.
zh_text: 她甚至不知道爲什麼會想到這些事情。墓園管理員死亡、探望死者的尖峰時段、人們遺忘逝去之人。每當來到這裡，她就會變成這個樣子。心情沮喪、思緒混亂，彷彿有人將她腦中的想法放入雞尾酒雪克杯裡用力搖晃。她喜歡一個月至少來這裡一次——如果可以用「喜歡」來形容的話。她從未錯過馬丁的忌日，從未，而今天正是馬丁的忌日。明天曾是他的生日，或者現在依然是。她不確定人死之後生日還能不能算是生日。基於某種難以解釋的理由，她從來不曾在他生日當天前來墓園。她很肯定那樣做將會導致跟拿下十字架一樣的後果。她父母今天下午稍早的時候來過；她可以從擺在自己的花旁的鮮花看出這點。她從不跟他們一起來。又是一件她無法解釋的事情，即使對自己也不行。

en_text: She brieﬂy closes her eyes. Whenever she comes here, she always ends up dwelling on what she can’t ﬁgure out. The moment she leaves, things will be better again. She crouches down, caresses the ﬂowers sitting in front of the gravestone, then runs her ﬁngers over the lettering. Her brother was ﬁfteen when he died. One day away from sixteen. One day’s difference between a birthday and a death-day. Probably not even that. Probably only a matter of half a day. How can it make sense that he should die at ﬁfteen, almost sixteen? The other people planted in this location average sixty-two years old. She knows that because she added them all up. She walked from grave to grave, plotting in the numbers on a calculator and then dividing them up. She was curious. Curious as to how many years Martin was cheated of. His ﬁfteen—sixteen years on this earth were special, and the fact he was mentally handicapped actually was a blessing. He enriched her life, and her parents’ lives. He knew he was different, he knew he was challenged, but he never understood what the problem was. For him, life was all about having fun. What could possibly be wrong with that? She has never found any answers to her questions, not here, not even once she has walked away. In that, nothing will ever change. After an hour, she turns away from the grave. She wants to tell her dead brother about the man she works with, who in many ways reminds her of Martin. He has a pure heart and a childlike innocence that is identical to Martin’s. She wants to tell her brother about this, but leaves without saying a word.
zh_text: 她短暫閉上雙眼。每次來此，她最後總會在一些想不透的事情上打轉。只要離開，一切就會開始好轉。她蹲下身去，撫摸放在墓碑前的花束，接著手指輕觸碑文。她弟弟死時十五歲，差一天就十六，或許還不到一天，或許才差半天，六或七小時，或許。他有什麼理由該在十五歲、將近十六歲的時候去世？其他葬在這裡的人平均年齡是六十二歲。她知道這一點是因為她親自算過。她走過一座又一座墳墓，將年齡輸入計算機中，然後計算平均值。她好奇，好奇馬丁究竟被剝奪了多久的壽命。他在世的十五、六年歲月是很特別的，而他的智力障礙其實可以算是好事。他豐富了她的人生，以及她父母的。他知道自己異於常人，他知道自己面臨挑戰，但他從不了解問題出在哪裡。對他而言，人生就是爲了快樂。這樣的人生怎麼可能痛苦？她從未找出這些問題的答案，這裡找不到，離開這裡之後也找不到，這是一個永遠不會改變的事實。一小時後，她離開墳前。她想跟死去的弟弟提起那個在許多方面都讓她聯想到馬丁的同事。他有著與馬丁同樣純潔的心靈以及孩童般的純真。她想要告訴弟弟這件事情，結果卻在沉默中離開。

en_text: She heads out of the graveyard thinking of Martin. Even before she reaches her car, the cruciﬁx starts to take away her pain.
zh_text: 走出墓園的路上，她一直想著馬丁。不過在抵達車旁之前，十字架已經開始消除她的悲痛。

en_text: The newspaper no longer holds any interest for me. Why read the news, when I’m the one making it? So I fold it in half and lay it on the bed next to me. I have newspaper ink on my ﬁngers. I wipe them on the bedspread as I study Angela. She has this look on her face as if she’s trying to digest some really bad news, like her father has just been hit by a car or she’s all out of perfume. I’m watching her towel. It’s sagging down her body. She looks pretty damn good standing there almost naked.
zh_text: 我對報紙已經失去興趣。爲什麼要閱讀我自己製造出來的新聞？我將報紙對摺，放在身旁的床上。我的手指沾上了報紙油墨，我一邊在床單上擦手，一邊打量著安琪拉。她臉上有種試圖消化超級壞消息的神情，像是她父親剛剛被車撞了，或是她的香水通通用光了之類的。我看著她的浴巾。它沿著她的身體下滑，近乎裸體的她看起來真他媽美。

en_text: “Name’s Joe,” I say, reaching toward my briefcase. I select the second-tobiggest knife I have clipped in there. A blade with a ﬁne Swiss design. I hold it up. We can both see it. It looks bigger to her, even though I’m closer. It’s a perspective thing.
zh_text: 「我是喬。」我說著伸手到公事包內，挑出了夾在裡面第二大把的刀。一把瑞士設計的好刀。我舉起刀。拿到我們都看得見的地方。儘管我離刀較近，不過刀在她眼中比較大把。大小這種東西是很主觀的。

en_text: “Maybe you’ve read about me. I’m front-page news.”
zh_text: 「或許妳聽說過我。我是頭條新聞。」

en_text: Angela is a tall woman with legs that go all the way up. Blond hair, obviously natural, that comes down to meet them. She has a good ﬁgure with all the right shapes and curves that have brought me here. An attractive face that could be in magazines marketing contact lenses or lipstick. Blue eyes full of life and, at the moment, full of fear. The fear in her eyes excites me. The fear in her eyes suggests that yes, she has read about me, probably even heard about me on the radio and seen the stories about me on TV.
zh_text: 安琪拉是名雙腳十分修長的高個女子。一頭顯然天生的金髮一路垂到大腿。她身材姣好，擁有將我吸引來此的玲瓏曲線。相貌迷人到足以爲隱形眼鏡或唇膏拍攝雜誌廣告。一雙藍眼充滿生命的氣息，不過同時也充滿恐懼。她眼中的恐懼令我興奮。她眼中的恐懼表示她聽說過我，可能在電台廣播中聽過，或是在電視上看過我的報導。

en_text: She begins shaking her head, as if answering no to a whole lot of questions I haven’t even got to yet. Drops of water ﬂy left and right, like it’s raining inside and horizontally. Her hair swishes behind her, the wet ends striking the walls and the doorframe. It ﬂicks around onto the front of her face and sticks there. She’s walking backward too, like she’s got somewhere better to be.
zh_text: 她開始搖頭，彷彿搶先對我還沒開始問的一大堆問題說不。水滴左右飛濺，好像室內下了一場水平的雨。她的頭髮在身後甩動，潮濕的髮梢打在牆壁和門框上。有些髮絲彈到前面，黏在她的臉上。她開始後退，好像她有別的地方可去。

en_text: “What, w . . . what do you want?” she asks. All the conﬁdent anger from her ﬁrst question of who I was left around the same time she saw the knife.
zh_text: 「你，你想要什麼？」她問，之前喝問第一個問題時的怒意都在看見那把刀的同時蕩然無存。

en_text: I shrug. I can think of several things I want. A nice house. A nice car. Her stereo is still playing that same song—our song now. Yeah. A nice stereo I wouldn’t say no to. But she can’t provide me with any of that. I wish she could, but life isn’t that simple. I decide to keep this to myself for now. There will be time for conversation later.
zh_text: 我聳肩，我可以想到幾樣我想要的東西，一棟好房子、一輛好車；她的音響還在播放同一首歌——如今已經變成我們的歌了。是啊，我不會對一台好音響說不。但是那些東西都不是她能提供給我的。我希望她可以，不過人生沒有那麼簡單。我決定暫時將這些話放在心裡，晚點會有時間溝通。

en_text: “Please, please. Just. Leave.”
zh_text: 「拜託，拜託，請你離開！」

en_text: I’ve heard this so many times I almost yawn, but I don’t, because I’m a polite guy. “You’re being a poor host,” I say, politely.
zh_text: 這話我聽過太多次，聽到我都快打呵欠了，但是我沒有，因為我是個有禮貌的紳士。「你是個很糟糕的主人。」我客氣地說道。

en_text: “You lunatic. I’m calling the . . . umm . . . the police.”
zh_text: 「你這個瘋子。我要，呃，叫警察了。」

en_text: Is she really this stupid? Does she think I’m going to stand here while she picks up the phone and dials for help? Maybe I’ll sit back on the bed, do the crossword in my newspaper while they arrive to arrest me. I start shaking my head, like she was before, only with dry hair. “You could go ahead and try,” I say, “if the phone was on the hook.” Which it isn’t. I took it off while I was eating my pizza. Her pizza.
zh_text: 她真的蠢到這個地步嗎？她以爲我會站在這裡眼睜睜地看著她拿起電話求救嗎？或許我該坐在床上，玩玩報紙上的塡字遊戲，等待警方趕來逮捕我。我開始搖頭，就像她剛剛一樣，不過我的頭髮是乾的。「妳可以試試看。」我說。「如果電話還通的話。」電話不通。我趁吃披薩的時候把電話線拔了，她的披薩。

en_text: She turns and makes a run for the bathroom at the same time I move toward her. She’s quick. I’m quick. I throw the knife. Blade over hilt, hilt over blade. The trick to throwing a knife is all in the balance . . . if you’re a professional. If you’re not, it all comes down to luck. We’re both hoping for a bit of that at the moment. The blade brushes off the side of her arm and clatters off the wall onto the ground as she rounds the bathroom door. She slams it shut and locks it, but I don’t slow down, I just barge sideways into it. It barely rattles in its frame.
zh_text: 她在我向她走去的同時轉身逃向浴室。她動作很快。我動作也很快。我擲出手裡的刀。刀身不斷旋轉，不斷旋轉。丟飛刀的要訣在於平衡——如果你夠專業的話。如果不夠專業，一切就看運氣了。當時我們兩個都在碰運氣，刀身在她閃到浴室門後時掠過她的手臂，撞上牆壁，彈回地面。她用力關門上鎖，但是我沒有放慢動作，順勢側身撞了上去。門只有輕微搖晃。

en_text: I take a few paces back. I can always go home. Pack up my gear. Close the briefcase. Take off my latex gloves. And leave. But I can’t. I have an attachment to both my knife and my anonymity. That means I have to stay. Plus I’m an optimist at heart—I’m not one to give up on myself.
zh_text: 我後退幾步。我可以選擇回家。收拾工具、關上公事包、脫掉乳膠手套，然後離開。但是我不能。我喜歡我的小刀，也不喜歡暴露身分，這表示我必須留下。

en_text: She starts screaming for help. But the neighbors aren’t going to hear her. I know this because I did my homework before arriving. The house is far back on the lot and backs onto a ﬁeld, we’re on the top story, and none of her nearby neighbors is home. It’s all about homework. To be successful, with anything in life, you need to do your homework. It just can’t be stressed enough.
zh_text: 她開始大聲求救。但是鄰居不會聽見她的叫聲。我知道這點是因為我來之前有做好功課。房子位於這一區的邊緣，後方臨接一片牧地，我們又在頂樓，而且她的鄰居都不在家。一切都跟做功課有關，任何事情想要成功都必須做好功課，這個道理再明確不過了。

en_text: I stroll across the bedroom and select another knife. This one is the biggest. I’m about to head back to the bathroom when a cat walks into the room. Damn thing is friendly too. I bend down and pat it. It nudges my hand and starts purring. I pick it up.
zh_text: 我走過臥房，挑出另外一把刀，這把是最大的一把。正當我打算走回浴室時，一隻貓闖入了房內。這可惡的傢伙也很友善。我彎下腰去摸了摸牠，牠頂了頂我的手，然後發出慵懶的叫聲。我抱起貓。

en_text: Back at the bathroom door I call out to her. “Come out or I’ll break your cat’s neck.”
zh_text: 我回到浴室門口，對她叫道：「出來，不然我就折斷貓脖子。」

en_text: “Please, please don’t hurt her.”
zh_text: 「求求你，求求你不要傷害牠。」

en_text: “The choice is yours.”
zh_text: 「看妳怎麼選擇。」

en_text: So now I’m waiting. Like all men do when women are in the bathroom. At least she’s not screaming. I scratch Fluffy beneath her ﬂoppy neck. She isn’t purring anymore.
zh_text: 接著我開始等待。就像所有男人在女人去浴室的時候一樣。至少她沒有大叫了。我抓抓小毛鬆軟的頸部下方。牠不再發出慵懶的叫聲了。

en_text: “Please, what do you want?”
zh_text: 「拜託，你想怎樣？」

en_text: My mother, God rest her soul, always told me to be honest. Sometimes it simply isn’t the right approach. “Just to talk,” I lie.
zh_text: 我母親——願她安息——總是教我要誠實。不過有時候誠實並非正確的作法。「只想跟你聊聊。」我撒謊道。

en_text: “Are you going to kill me?”
zh_text: 你會殺我嗎？

en_text: I shake my head in disbelief. Women, huh? “No.”
zh_text: 我難以置信地搖頭。女人，呃？「不會。」

en_text: The lock makes a deﬁnite twang as it disengages on the bathroom door. She’s actually going to take her chances with me rather than have her cat killed. Maybe it’s expensive. Slowly the door begins to open. I’m motionless, too amazed at her stupidity, which is increasing by the second, to actually move. When the door opens enough, I dump Fluffy on the ground. She lands in a pile of clumped fur, her head twisted sideways and her legs sticking out in every direction, trying to point to the reason why. Angela sees the cat but doesn’t get the chance to scream. I shove my body against the door, and she isn’t strong enough to hold me out. The door goes slack as she loses balance.
zh_text: 門鎖開啓，發出一下聲響。她竟然寧願跟我賭命也不願看到貓咪被殺。或許是隻很貴的貓。浴室門緩緩打開。我無法相信她能蠢到這個地步，而且還能越來越蠢，這讓我吃驚到僵在原地。當門開到夠大時，我把小毛丟向地板。牠墜地時身體捲成一團毛球，腦袋扭向身側，四肢直挺挺地伸向四面八方，試圖找出自己遭此變故的原因。她看見貓的下場，但是沒有機會尖叫。我用力撞上浴室門，她沒有足夠的力氣阻擋我。她重心失衡，房門被我撞開，之後她摔倒在淋浴間裡，雙手放開浴巾。

en_text: She falls against the shower, and her towel falls from her hands. I step into the bathroom. The mirror is still fogged over with steam. The shower curtain has pictures of a few dozen rubber ducks all smiling at me. They point in the same direction and are uniform, as if they’re swimming off to war. Angela starts back with the screaming routine, which hasn’t done her any good so far and doesn’t do her any good this time. I drag her back into the bedroom, and I have to hit her a couple of times to get her to go along with the plan. She tries to stop me, but I have more experience at subduing women than she has at self-defense. Her eyes roll upward and she has the audacity to pass out on me.
zh_text: 我步入浴室。鏡子上還是一片霧氣，浴簾上的十幾隻塑膠鴨全部都對我微笑。它們面朝同一個方向，身上穿著制服，彷彿正要游向戰場。安琪拉又開始發出例行公事般的尖叫，這種叫法之前沒有幫到她，現在也不會有任何幫助。我將她拖回浴室，還得打她幾下才能讓她合作。她試圖阻止我，但是我制伏女人的經驗比她自我防衛的經驗要豐富多了。她雙眼向上一翻，竟然膽子大到昏了過去。

en_text: The stereo is still going. Maybe when all this is over I’ll take it home with me. I pick her up and dump her on the bed, then roll her onto her back. I move around the bedroom, taking down the photographs of her family from the walls, and turning down the others that rest on windowsills and shelves. The last one I look at is a picture of her husband and two kids. I guess he’s about to be granted full custody.
zh_text: 音響還在放歌。或許等一切結束之後，我會把它帶回家。我扛起她，丟到床上，然後將她翻身躺平。我在臥室四處走動，拿下牆壁上的家庭相片，然後將窗台和櫃子上的其他相片放倒。我看到的最後一張照片是她丈夫和兩個孩子的。我想他將會獲得完全監護權。

en_text: The next step I take toward romance is placing my Glock automatic nine-millimeter pistol on the bedside table so it’s within easy reach. Nice piece. Bought it four years ago when I started work. Three thousand dollars it cost me. Black-market guns are always more expensive, but anonymous. I stole the money from my mother, who blamed neighborhood kids. She’s one of those crazy women who are afraid of using banks because she’s suspicious of bank managers. The gun is in case the husband comes home early. Or if a neighbor comes over. Maybe she’s having an affair. Maybe her lover is pulling into the street right now.
zh_text: 我的下一步浪漫舉動就是將我的葛拉克自動九釐米手槍放在伸手可得的床頭桌上。好槍。四年前開始工作時買的。花了三千塊錢。黑市槍械總是比較貴，但不會留下紀錄。我從我媽那裡偷錢來買，她則將丟錢的事情怪到鄰居小鬼頭上。她是那種害怕銀行的瘋狂老太婆，只因為她懷疑銀行經理手腳不乾淨。之所以帶槍是爲了防止丈夫提早回家、或是有鄰居跑來串門子、或許她有搞外遇、或許此時此刻她的愛人正在馬路上停車。

en_text: My Glock is like a magic pill—it will cure all possibilities.
zh_text: 而我的葛拉克手槍就像魔法藥丸——它可以治好所有可能的狀況。

en_text: I pull the phone from the wall. Tear the cord from the end of it. Use it to secure her hands. I don’t want her thrashing about too much. I tie her hands to the headboard.
zh_text: 我扯下牆上的電話。拔下末段的電話線。用電話線綁緊她的雙手。我不希望她掙扎得太過火。我將她的手綁在床頭上。

en_text: I’m just ﬁnishing tying her feet with her underwear when she wakes up. She notices three things at once. The ﬁrst is I’m still here and this is no dream. The second is she’s naked. The third is she’s tied to the bed spreadeagled. I can see her checking these things off in her mind on this big mental list she has. One. Two. Three.
zh_text: 我剛用她的內褲綁好她的腳，她就醒來了。她立刻注意到三件事情。第一就是我還在這裡，而這不是一場夢。第二就是她赤身裸體。第三就是她被四肢張開綁在床上。我看得出來她將這三個事實勾選在她的心靈清單上。一個勾。兩個勾。三個勾。

en_text: From there she’s noticing things that haven’t happened yet. Four. Five. And six. I can see her imagination running wild. The muscles are pulling in her face as she considers asking me a question. Her eyes are darting back and forth as she struggles to work out which part of me to focus on. Her forehead is shiny with sweat. I can see her gripping at levers in her mind, searching for the one to pull that will show her options. I watch her pull all of them, but the levers are just coming off in her hands.
zh_text: 這時她開始注意到一些尚未發生的事情。第四個勾。第五個勾。第六個勾。我可以看出她的想像力無限奔馳。她臉上的肌肉緊繃，考慮該不該開口問我問題。她目光左右閃爍，試圖決定要將目光集中在我身體的哪一部分。她的額頭滲出亮晶晶的汗水。我可以看出她在心中握著一支一支的操縱桿，試圖找出一支拉開就能看見出路的選項。我看著她拉開所有操縱桿，但那些桿子全都被她折斷。

en_text: I show her my knife again. Her eyes come to a stop on the blade. “See this?” She nods. Yeah, she sees it. She’s crying too.
zh_text: 我又拿刀在她面前晃了晃。她的目光停留在刀面上。「看見這玩意兒了嗎？」她點頭。沒錯，她看見了。同時也開始哭了。

en_text: I place the tip of the blade on her cheek and ask her to open her mouth. She becomes eager to help out when the blade starts to scratch her. Then, reaching over to my briefcase, I pull out an egg and slip it into her mouth. Cooperation comes easy once they ﬁnd acceptance. The egg is nothing abnormal, just a standard unboiled egg. The thing about eggs is they’re high in protein. They also make great gags. “If you’ve got a problem with this,” I say, “just let me know.”
zh_text: 我將刀尖頂在她的臉頰上，請她張開嘴巴。當刀尖刺痛她時，她變得非常樂意合作。然後，我伸手到公事包裡，拿出一顆蛋，塞到她的嘴裡。一旦起了頭，對方就會非常合作。這顆蛋沒什麼特別的，只是一顆標準的生蛋。蛋的好處在於蛋白質高，它們同時也適合塞在嘴裡讓人閉嘴。

en_text: I head into the bathroom, ﬁnd her towel, bring it back out, and cover her face with it. I take my clothes off and climb onto the bed. She hardly moves, doesn’t complain, just keeps on crying until she can cry no more. When we’re done and I climb off, I ﬁnd that at some point the egg has slipped to the back of her mouth, at which point it proceeded to choke her, successfully. This explains the gagging I heard and, at the time, mistook for something else. Oops.
zh_text: 我走入浴室，拿起她的浴巾，帶回臥室，蓋在她的臉上。我脫光衣服，爬到床上。她幾乎沒有任何動作，也不抱怨，只是一直在哭，直到哭不出來爲止。完事之後，我爬下床，隨即發現剛剛辦事過程中那顆蛋滑入她的喉嚨裡，成功導致她窒息身亡。這解釋了我聽見的那陣窒息聲，不過當時我以爲是別的聲音。哎呀。

en_text: I shower, dress, and pack my gear together. The faces on the photographs lining the staircase watch me as I walk downstairs. I keep expecting them to say something to me or, at the very least, complain about something I’ve done here. When I get outside and away from them, I’m washed over by a warm ﬂood of relief.
zh_text: 我淋浴，穿衣，然後收拾工具。樓梯間旁的照片中人看著我走下樓梯。我一直期待他們開口對我說話，或至少，抱怨我在這裡的所作所爲。出了屋子，遠離他們後，我全身徜徉在一股如釋重負的感覺中。

en_text: The relief is short-lived, and within a few seconds I start to feel rotten. I cast my eyes down and watch my feet as I walk. Yep. Feeling bad. Feeling blue. Things didn’t go as they should have, and I ended up taking a life. I pause on the lawn and pluck a ﬂower from a rosebush. I hold it to my nose and smell the petals, but it can’t bring a smile to my face. A thorn pricks my ﬁnger and I put the wound into my mouth. The taste of blood begins to replace the taste of Angela.
zh_text: 那感覺稍縱即逝，幾秒之後，我的心情就變得非常糟糕。我壓低目光，低頭盯著我的雙腳走路。是啊。感覺很糟，很憂鬱，事情不如預期中順遂，我竟然奪走了一條性命。我在花園裡停步，於玫瑰叢中摘下一朵花。我將花拿到鼻子前，聞聞花香，但卻無法令我面露微笑。玫瑰刺傷了我的手指，我將手指放入口中。安琪拉的氣味開始被血腥味取代。

en_text: I put the ﬂower in my pocket and make my way to her car. The sun is still out, but lower now, shining directly into my eyes. The day has cooled so maybe the heat I feel isn’t from the sun, but is inside me. I want to smile. I want to enjoy the remaining day, but I can’t.
zh_text: 我將花放入口袋，朝向她的車走去。太陽還沒下山，不過快了，陽光直接照入我的雙眼。氣溫已經下降了，所以或許我感到的熱氣並非發自太陽，而是發自內心。我很想微笑。我很想享受天剩下的時光，但是辦不到。

en_text: I have taken a life. Poor Fluffy. Poor pussycat.
zh_text: 我奪走了一條性命——可憐的小貓咪。

en_text: Sometimes animals have to be used as tools. It’s not my place in this crazy, mixed-up universe to question that. Still, I can’t help but feel sick for breaking the little cat’s neck.
zh_text: 有時候動物必須被當作工具。我沒有資格在這個瘋狂混亂的宇宙中質疑這一點。儘管如此，我還是對於扭斷貓咪的脖子感到非常厭惡。

en_text: I climb into Angela’s car and have to drive over the front lawn to avoid the stolen car in the driveway. It’s a nice ride—a couple of years old at the most. I wish I could keep it. The picture-perfect home that represents a picture-perfect family life grows smaller in my rearview mirror. The manicured lawn I can no longer smell looks like a miniature-golf course as I glance back at it. The rose from that lawn is warm in my pocket. I pass three or four parked cars. People are walking up driveways and arriving home. Two old women talk over a low fence about whatever it is old women face in life. Another old woman on her knees painting her mailbox. A young boy delivering the community paper. People are at home here, and they are at peace. They don’t know me and pay no attention as I drive past their windows and out of their lives. Technically we’re approaching the middle stages of autumn, but nobody has told Mother Nature, so we’re all still experiencing the heat of summer.
zh_text: 我上了安琪拉的車，必須開上前院才能避開停在車道上的贓車。代表完美家庭生活的完滿房屋在我的後照鏡中越來越小。已經聞不到花香的整齊花園在我回頭去看時像是一座迷你高爾夫球場。來自那座花園的玫瑰在口袋中傳來暖意。我駛過三、四輛停好的車。人們沿著車道走回家。兩個老女人在矮籬兩側聊著老女人必須面對的生活問題。另外一名老女人蹲在地上漆郵箱。一個年輕小夥子在送報紙。這裡的人生活安定，怡然自得。他們不認識我，絲毫沒有注意到我駛過他們的窗口，遠離他們的生活。

en_text: It hasn’t rained in over a month. None of the trees are getting ready for the winter and losing their leaves. Some of those leaves right now are rustling above me in a light breeze, attached to a line of birch trees that grow from the sides of the road and make an arch overhead where ﬁngerlike branches interlock. Birds are at play up there. In the distance, I can hear lawn mowers closing out the afternoon and starting the evening. This is going to be a beautiful night. It’s going to be the type of night that makes me glad to be alive. The type of night New Zealand summers are famous for. Just not normally in April.
zh_text: 慢慢地，一陣清風取代了一月的煩熱。路旁兩排樹枝如同手指在道路上方交握的樺樹樹葉沙沙作響。鳥兒在天上玩耍。遠方，我能聽見除草機爲午後畫下句點，揭開傍晚的序幕。今晚將會是個美麗的夜晚。今晚將會是個讓我感覺活著眞好的那種夜晚，令紐西蘭的夏季舉世聞名的那種夜晚。

en_text: Finally I begin to relax. I turn on the car stereo and hear the same damn song that was playing in Angela’s house. What are the chances? I hum along, singing my way into the evening. My thoughts turn from Fluffy to Angela, and only then does the smile come back to my face.
zh_text: 我終於開始放鬆心情。我打開車用音響，聽到安琪拉家那首天殺的歌曲。怎麼會這麼巧？我跟著哼，在歌聲中駛入黑夜。我的思緒自小毛轉往安琪拉身上，直到那時，微笑才再度回到我的臉上。

en_text: I live in an apartment complex that would be worth more if sold as scrap. Because of its location, it will never be torn down and replaced because a new apartment complex isn’t going to fetch any more rent. It isn’t exactly the worst part of town, according to those who live here, but it is according to everybody else. It’s barely habitable, but it’s cheap, so that’s the trade-off. The complex is four stories high, covers the best part of a block, and I live on the top, giving me the best part of a very poor view. In total I think there are maybe thirty apartments.
zh_text: 我住在一間當垃圾賣說不定還比較值錢的公寓裡。由於地段的關係，這棟公寓永遠沒有機會拆掉重建，因為全新公寓也不可能收到更多房租。根據住在這裡的居民所說，這裡並非城裡最糟糕的地區，不過對所有不住在這裡的人而言，這裡就是。環境簡直不能住人，但是因為便宜，所以還是有人住。這棟公寓四層樓高，位於街區最好的位置，而我住在頂樓，能夠享受絕佳的超爛景觀。據我估計這棟公寓裡總共約有三十間房。

en_text: I see none of my neighbors as I make my way upstairs, but this is neither bad nor uncommon. I ﬁnd myself dwelling on poor Fluffy as I unlock the door and walk inside. My apartment has two rooms. One of these is a bathroom, and the other a combined everything else. The fridge and stove look so old I doubt carbon dating would identify an age. The ﬂoors are bare and I have to wear shoes all the time to avoid splinters. The walls have cheap, dark gray wallpaper so dry that it crumbles a little bit more every time I open my door and create a draft. Several edges of it have peeled away and hang like ﬂat tongues. A set of windows runs along one wall where my view consists of power lines and burned-out cars. I have an old washing machine with a noisy spin cycle, and hanging on the wall above it is a dryer that’s just as loud. Along the window is a line where I hang my washing during the summer. Currently nothing is hanging on it. I own a single bed, a small TV, a DVD player, and some basic furniture that’s sold in a box with assembly instructions in six different languages. None of it sits straight, but I don’t know anybody who would visit to complain. Select romance paperbacks that I’ve read are dumped on my sofa. The covers are full of strong-looking men and weak-looking women. I throw my briefcase on top of them before checking my answering machine. The light is blinking, so I push play. It’s my mother. She’s left a message telling me about her powers of deduction. She believes that since I’m not home, and not at her place, it means I have to be on the way to her place. I said earlier, “God rest her soul.” I didn’t mean she’s dead. She soon will be, though. Don’t misunderstand me. I’m not a bad guy or anything, I would never do anything to harm her, and I’m disgusted at anyone who would think otherwise. It’s just that she’s old. Old people die. Some sooner than others. Thank God.
zh_text: 上樓途中，我一個鄰居也沒遇到，不過這並非什麼不尋常的壞現象。開門進屋時，我心裡還想著可憐的小貓。我家有兩個房間。其中一間是浴室，其他的東西全部集中在另外一間。冰箱和火爐老舊到就連用碳十四測年法都未必能測出年代。地板是光禿禿的木板，我在家都得穿鞋，不然會被木頭碎片扎到。牆上貼有廉價的深灰色壁紙，乾到我每次開門激起氣流的時候都會導致更多壁紙脫落。好幾處邊緣已經剝離，如同扁平的舌頭般垂在牆上。一面牆上有窗戶，窗外可以看見電線和焦黑汽車組成的景觀。我有一台洗衣機，脫水的時候非常吵，而掛在上方牆上的吹風機則跟它一樣吵。沿著窗戶上掛著一條夏天用來曬衣服的線。此刻上面空空如也。我有張單人床，一台小電視，一部錄影機，還有一些裝在附有六國語言組裝說明紙箱裡買來的基本家具。沒有一件家具不會搖晃，不過我不認識任何會來拜訪我並且抱怨家具的人。幾本看完的精選平裝版言情小說被丟在沙發上。封面上盡是一些強壯的男人和嬌弱的女人。我將公事包丢在小說上面，然後查看答錄機。指示燈在閃，所以我按下播放。媽打來的。她在留言中展現她的消去法能力。她認爲既然我不在家，也不在她家，就表示我一定在前往她家途中。我稍早的時候說過：「願她安息。」我的意思並不是說她已經死了。不過她很快就會死的。不要誤會。我不是個壞人或什麼的，我絕對不會做任何傷害她的事情，而我厭惡任何以為我會傷害她的人。她只是年紀大了，老人都會死的，有些死得比較早。感謝上帝。

en_text: I glance at my watch. It’s already six thirty. It’s starting to get dark. I make room on the sofa, stretch my arms out behind me, and try to relax. Think about what’s best for me. If I don’t go to my mother’s for dinner the results will be disastrous. She will ring me every day. Nag me for hours on end. She is unaware I have a life. I have responsibilities, hobbies, places I want to go, people I want to do, but she doesn’t see it. She thinks I live just to sit around my apartment waiting for her to call.
zh_text: 我瞄一眼手錶。已經六點半了。我在沙發上清出一塊空位，往後伸展手，試圖放鬆全身。想想怎樣才是最好的作法。如果不去我媽家吃晚飯，絕對不會有好結果的。她會每天打電話來。連續騷擾我數個小時。她沒有意識到我有自己的生活。我有職責、興趣、想去的地方、想殺的人，她通通視而不見，是吧？她認爲我的人生就是坐在公寓裡等她電話。

en_text: I change into some more respectable clothes. Nothing too ﬂashy, but slightly better than casual. Don’t want Mom insisting on buying my clothes for me like she used to. She went through a stage, a year ago, of buying my shirts, my underwear, my socks. Sometimes I remind her I’m more than thirty years old and can do this myself, but sometimes she does it anyway. On the small coffee table in my small living room, in front of the small sofa that looks like it belongs in some hippie recording studio, sits a large goldﬁsh bowl with my two best friends inside: Pickle and Jehovah. My goldﬁsh don’t complain. Goldﬁsh have memories of ﬁve seconds, so you can really piss them off and they won’t remember. You can forget to feed them, and they’ll forget they’re hungry. You can pull them from the water and throw them on the ﬂoor, and they’ll ﬂap around and forget they’re suffocating. Pickle is my favorite; I got him ﬁrst—two years ago. He is an albino goldﬁsh from China, with a white body and red ﬁns, and is slightly bigger than the width of my palm. Jehovah is a little smaller, but she’s gold. Goldﬁsh can live up to forty years, and I hope to get at least that out of mine. I don’t know what they get up to when I’m not watching them, but so far no little goldﬁsh have appeared.
zh_text: 我換了一套比較體面的衣服。不算太隆重，只是比隨便穿穿好一點。我不希望老媽像以前一樣堅持幫我買衣服。一年前，她經歷過一定要幫我買襯衫、內褲、襪子的階段。我提醒她我已經年過三十，可以自己做這些事情了，但有時她就是非做不可。小客廳有張嬉皮風的小咖啡桌，上方擺著一口大金魚缸，裡面住了我兩個最好的朋友：泡菜和耶和華。我的金魚不會抱怨。金魚只有五秒鐘的記憶，所以不管你怎麼激怒他們，他們都不會記得。你可以忘記餵食他們，他們就會忘記飢餓。你可以把他們拿出魚缸，丟在地上，他們就會拍擊尾巴，忘記自己難以呼吸。我最喜歡泡菜；我先開始養他的——兩年前。他是條來自中國的白化金魚，擁有白色的身體和紅色的魚鰭，比我的手掌還要大上一點。耶和華體型較小，但他是金色的。金魚的壽命長達四十年，我希望我的金魚起碼要活那麼久。我知道我沒在看的時候他們有多要好，但是截至目前爲止，還沒有小金魚冒出來。

en_text: I sprinkle in some food, watch them rise to the surface of the bowl, and watch them eat. I love them dearly, yet at the same time I feel like God. No matter who I am, no matter what I do, my goldﬁsh look up to me. The way they live, the conditions they live in, when they get dinner—these things are all up to me. I like having that responsibility.
zh_text: 我撒了點飼料進去，看著他們游到水面上來，然後吃東西。我非常喜愛他們，不過在餵魚的時候，我會有種扮演上帝的感覺。不管我是什麼人，不管我做過什麼事，我的金魚都會尊敬我。他們生活的方式、生活的環境、什麼時候有飯吃——這些通通掌握在我的手中。

en_text: I talk to them while they eat. A few minutes go by. I have talked enough. The pain of killing Fluffy is nearly gone now.
zh_text: 我趁他們吃飯的時候跟他們聊天。幾分鐘過去了。我聊夠了。殺害小毛的痛苦幾乎完全消失了。

en_text: Mom lives in South Brighton near the beach. No green lawn out here. Like the plants, it matches the shade of rust that visits every metal surface exposed to the salt air. Grow a rosebush and the entire block goes up in value. Most of the homes are sixty-year-old bungalows that are struggling to hold on to their character as the paint ﬂakes away and the weatherboards slowly rot. All the windows are clouded over with salt. Wooden joinery is stained with dead pine needles and sand. Patches of sealant and plaster block up holes and keep the insides dry. Even crime out here has its downside— when you weigh in the cost of gas it takes to get here against the value of anything you might ﬁnd in any of these dumps, it’s hardly worth breaking into somebody’s house.
zh_text: 我媽住在南布萊頓，靠近海灘。那裡沒有綠草。就像樹木般，那裡的草跟所有暴露在海風下的金屬一樣呈現腐鏽的顏色。只要能夠種出玫瑰叢，整塊街區就會房價飄漲。大部分的房舍都是六十年以上的老平房，在斑剝的油漆與緩緩腐爛的護牆板中努力維持自我的個性。所有窗戶都蒙了一層鹽。木質部分積滿松針和沙。破洞上塗了密封劑和泥灰，藉以保持室內乾燥。這裡就連犯罪都很麻煩——如果把油錢考慮進去，闖空門的成本通常大於收益。

en_text: It takes thirty minutes for the bus to get to Mom’s house. When I get out, I can hear the waves crashing against the shore. The sound is relaxing. This is the only beneﬁt to South Brighton. It is a minute’s walk to the beach from here, and if I still lived in this suburb, I would walk that extra minute and just keep on swimming. At the moment it feels like I’m standing in a ghost town. Few houses have their lights on. Every fourth or ﬁfth streetlight is busted. Nobody around.
zh_text: 公車開到我媽家花了三十分鐘。下車時，我能聽見海浪拍擊海灘的聲響。這個聲音十分紓壓。這是南布萊頓唯一的好處。從這裡到海灘步行只要一分鐘，如果我還住在這附近，我就會走過這一分鐘的路程，然後下海游泳。此時此刻，我覺得自己彷彿站在鬼城之中。只有幾間房舍亮著燈火。每隔四或五盞路燈就有一盞壞掉。附近空無一人。

en_text: I suck in a deep breath of salty air while standing at the gate. My clothes already stink of rotten seaweed. Mom’s house is in as much disrepair as any other house in this neighborhood. If I came around here and painted it, her neighbors would probably kick her out. If I mowed the dry lawns, I’d have to mow everybody’s. Her house is a single-story weatherboard dwelling. White paint, now the color of smog, falls from the warped boards and settles in the yard alongside the dusting of rust from the iron roof. The windows are held in place with both cracking joint compound and luck. A real-estate agent would call Mum’s house a great investment for the handyman.
zh_text: 我站在門口，深吸一口鹹鹹的空氣。我的衣服已經沾上腐敗海草的臭味。媽家就跟這附近所有房舍一樣年久失修。如果我跑來幫她重新粉刷，她的鄰居可能會把她趕走。如果我除了她的乾草皮，我就必須幫所有人通通除草。她家是間單層護板牆的房舍。原本的白漆如今已經變成灰煙色，自變形的牆板上脫落，與鐵皮屋頂落下的塵封鐵鏽一同躺在地下。窗戶靠油灰和運氣固定在原位。

en_text: I walk up to the door. Knock. And wait. A minute goes by before she ﬁnally ambles to it. It sticks in the frame and she has to pull it hard. It shudders open and the hinges squeak.
zh_text: 我走到門口。敲門。然後等候。一分鐘過去，她終於慢慢來到門後。門卡在門框裡，所以她必須用力拉門。鉸鏈吱吱作響，門在晃動中開啓。

en_text: “Joe, do you know what time it is?”
zh_text: 「喬，你知道現在幾點了嗎？」

en_text: I nod. It’s nearly seven thirty. “Yeah, Mom, I know.”
zh_text: 我點頭。快要七點半了。「是，媽，我知道。

en_text: She closes the door, I hear the rattle of a chain guard, and then the door swings back open. I step inside.
zh_text: 她關上門。我聽見一陣拉開鎖鏈的聲響，接著門整個向後打開。我步入屋內。

en_text: Mom will be sixty-four this year, but looks a good ten years older. Or a bad ﬁve. She’s only ﬁve feet two, and has curves in all the wrong places. Some of those curves stretch out over others, some are heavy enough to tighten the wrinkles in her neck. Her gray hair, she keeps pulled back into a tight bun, but at the moment she’s wearing something over it—one of those old hairnets with curlers tied into it that for some reason makes me think of black-and-white movies and women smoking cigarettes. She has blue eyes so pale they are nearly gray, covered by a pair of thick-rimmed glasses that may, with a lot of luck, one day come into style. On her face are three moles, each of them with a dark hair that she won’t cut. Her upper lip is cultivating a soft line of fuzz. She looks like she belongs in a nursing home as the head matron.
zh_text: 媽今年即將六十四歲，不過看起來起碼有七十了。她身高只有五呎二吋，不該有曲線的地方都有曲線，有些曲線還跟其他曲線交疊在一起，有些則嚴重到足以扯緊頸部皺紋的地步。她將滿頭灰髮在腦後盤成髮髻，不過此刻頭上戴了樣東西罩住它——用來夾髮卷的老式髮網。她的藍眼珠淡到像是灰色的，戴著一副永遠不入流行的厚框眼鏡。臉上有三顆痣，每顆痣上都長有她說什麼也不肯剪的毛。她的上唇長了一片細毛，看起來像是安養院裡的護士長。

en_text: “You’re late,” she says, blocking the doorway while adjusting one of the curlers in her hair. “I got worried. I nearly called the police. Nearly called the hospitals.”
zh_text: 「你遲到了。」她說，一面擋住門廊，一面調整髮網中的髮卷。「我很擔心。我差點就報警了。差點打電話去醫院了。」

en_text: “I was busy, Mom, with work and everything,” I say, relieved she didn’t ﬁle a missing person report. “Too busy to call your mother? Too busy to worry yourself about my breaking heart?”
zh_text: 「我很忙，媽，有工作還有其他事情。」我說，心想幸好她沒有通報失蹤人口「忙到沒時間打電話給你媽？忙到沒時間擔心這個心碎的老媽？」

en_text: I’m all she has left. My dad died a few years ago, and I’ve always considered him to be the lucky one. It seems the only thing Mom has to live for is talking. And complaining. Luckily the two go hand in hand for her.
zh_text: 我是她僅存的一切。難怪我爸要死。幸運的混蛋。我媽活著唯一的樂趣似乎就是說話。還有抱怨。幸運的是，這兩樣事情可以一塊兒來。

en_text: “I said I’m sorry, Mom.”
zh_text: 「我說我很抱歉，媽。」

en_text: She clips me around the ear. Not hard, but enough to show me her disappointment. Then she hugs me. “I made meatloaf, Joe. Meatloaf. Your favorite.”
zh_text: 她擰了擰我的耳朵。不是很用力，不過足以表達她的失望。接著她擁抱我。「我做了烤肉餅，喬。烤肉餅。你的最愛。」

en_text: I hand her the rose I picked from Angela’s garden. It’s slightly crushed, but Mom’s expression is priceless when I hand over the red ﬂower.
zh_text: 我把在安琪拉家花園裡摘的玫瑰交給她。有點壓壞了，但是看著我媽接過紅玫瑰時的表情，切就都值得了。「喔，你實在太窩心了，喬。」她說著將花拿到鼻子前面聞。

en_text: “Oh, you’re so thoughtful, Joe,” she says, taking it to her nose to smell. I shrug. “Just wanted to make you happy,” I say, and even for an optimist like me that’s always been a pretty ambitious goal. Her smile is making me smile.
zh_text: 我聳肩。「只想看到妳開心。」我說，她的微笑勾起我的微笑。

en_text: “Ow,” she says, pricking her ﬁnger on one of the thorns. “You give me a rose with thorns? What sort of son are you, Joe?” Obviously a bad one. “I’m sorry. I didn’t mean for that to happen.”
zh_text: 「噢，」她輕呼一聲，手指被刺了一下。「你給我一朵帶刺的玫瑰？這算什麼兒子，喬？」顯然是個壞兒子。「很抱歉。我沒想到會這樣。」

en_text: “You don’t think enough, Joe. That’s always been your problem. Along with always being late. I’ll put it in water,” she says, and steps aside. “You might as well come in.”
zh_text: 你想得不夠周到，喬。我去把花放水裡。」她說著讓到一旁。「你最好進來吧。」

en_text: She closes the door behind me and I follow her down the hallway to the kitchen, passing photographs of my dead dad, a cactus that has looked dead from the day she got it, and a seascape painting of a place my mother would maybe like to visit. The Formica-top table has been set for two.
zh_text: 她在我進屋後關上房門，我跟著她穿越走廊，來到廚房，路過我死去父親的相片、一株打從來到她家那天起看起來就像枯死的仙人掌，以及一幅我媽可能想去旅遊的地方的海景畫，塑膠桌上擺了兩人份的餐具。

en_text: “Do you want a drink?” she asks, putting the rose into a glass. “I’m ﬁne,” I say, tightening my jacket. It’s always cold in this house. “The supermarket has Coke on special.”
zh_text: 「要喝東西嗎？」她問，將玫瑰放入一只玻璃瓶裡。「我不渴。」我說，抓了抓夾克。這間房子裡總是很冷「超商的可樂在特價。」「我不渴。」

en_text: “I’m ﬁne.” “Three dollars for a six pack,” she says. “Here, I’ll ﬁnd you the receipt.” “Don’t worry, Mom. I said I’m ﬁne.”
zh_text: 「三塊錢可以買六罐。來吧，我拿收據給你看。「別麻煩了，媽。我說我不渴。」

en_text: “It’s no hassle.”
zh_text: 「不麻煩。」

en_text: She wanders off, leaving me alone. There’s no way to say it nicely, but my mother is getting crazier by the day. I believe her that Coke is on special, yet she still feels the need to show me the receipt. A few minutes go by where all I can do is look at the oven and microwave, so I spend the time ﬁguring just how awkward it would be to ﬁt an entire person into either one of them. When she comes back, she has also found the supermarket ﬂyer advertising the Coke.
zh_text: 她晃了出去，把我留在廚房。我想不出比較溫和的說法，只能說我媽瘋得一天比一天嚴重。我相信可樂在特價，但她依然覺得有必要拿收據給我看。幾分鐘過去了，而我只能盯著烤箱和微波爐，於是我開始想像把一整個人塞到這兩樣東西裡面去會是什麼景象。她回來時還順便帶了超商可樂特價的傳單。

en_text: I nod. “Three dollars, huh? Amazing.”
zh_text: 我點頭。「三塊錢，呃，太驚人了。」

en_text: “So you’ll have one then?”
zh_text: 「所以你要來一罐嗎？」

en_text: “Sure.” It’s the easiest option.
zh_text: 當然。這是最輕鬆的答案。

en_text: She serves dinner. We sit down and begin eating. The dining room connects to the kitchen, and the only view I have is either of my mother or the wall behind her, so I watch the wall. Some of these appliances here went out of date when electricity was invented, and the rest not long after. The linoleum ﬂoor looks like it was made from Kermit the Frog after he was hunted down and skinned. The dining table is the color of bananas. The legs are cold metal. The chairs are padded and wobble slightly when I move. Mom’s has been reinforced.
zh_text: 她將晚餐端上桌。我們坐下來吃飯。餐廳跟廚房相連，我唯一看得到的東西就是我媽或是她身後的牆壁，於是我看著牆壁。這裡的用品早在電力發明的年代就已經過時了。油布地毯看起來像是青蛙可米特被剝皮後製成的。餐桌是香蕉色，桌腳是冰冷的金屬。椅子用東西墊著椅腳，我一移動就會搖晃。媽的椅子有補強過。

en_text: “How was your day?” she asks. A tiny piece of carrot is stuck on her chin. One of the moles there looks as though it’s trying to skewer it.
zh_text: 「今天過得如何？」她問。一小塊胡蘿蔔黏在她的下巴上。長在附近的痣一副要用毛把它串起來的樣子。

en_text: “Good.”
zh_text: 「過得很好。」

en_text: “I haven’t heard from you all week.”
zh_text: 「你一個禮拜沒跟我聯絡了。」

en_text: “The job?”
zh_text: 「工作上的事？」

en_text: “The job.”
zh_text: 工作上的事。

en_text: “Your cousin Gregory is getting married. Did you know?”
zh_text: 「你表哥葛雷葛利要結婚了。你知道嗎？」

en_text: I do now. “Really?”
zh_text: 我现在知道了。「眞的？」

en_text: “When are you going to ﬁnd yourself a wife, Joe?”
zh_text: 「你什麼時候才要找個老婆，喬？」

en_text: I’ve noticed that old people always chew with their mouths open, so you get to hear the food slopping against the roof of their mouth. It’s because they’re always about to say something.
zh_text: 我注意到老人總是會在張嘴的時候咀嚼食物，這會讓你聽見食物在嘴裡撞來撞去的聲音，因為他們總是在說話。

en_text: “I don’t know, Mom.”
zh_text: 「我不知道，媽。」

en_text: “You’re not gay, are you, son?”
zh_text: 你不是同性戀，對吧，兒子？

en_text: She says this while still chewing. Like it’s no big deal. Like she just said, “That shirt looks good on you,” or “Nice weather we’re having.”
zh_text: 她一邊咀嚼食物一邊說這句話。好像這不是什麼大不了的事情一樣。好像她說的是：「你穿這件襯衫很好看。」或是「今天天氣不錯。」之類的話。

en_text: “I’m not gay, Mom.”
zh_text: 「我不是同性戀，媽。」

en_text: In fact, it isn’t that big a deal. I have nothing against gay people. Nothing at all. They are, after all, just people. Like anybody else. Now it’s people I have something against.
zh_text: 事實上，同性戀沒什麼大不了的。我不會排斥同性戀。一點也不。畢竟，他們只是人。就像其他人一樣。我排斥的是人。

en_text: “Huh,” she huffs.
zh_text: 「嗯。」她吐氣說道。

en_text: “Nothing.”
zh_text: 「沒事。」

en_text: “I’m just wondering why you don’t ever bring a girl around.”
zh_text: 我只是在想你爲什麼還沒交女朋友。

en_text: I shrug.
zh_text: 我聳肩。

en_text: “Men shouldn’t be gay, Joe. It’s not . . .” she searches for the word, “fair.” “I don’t follow.”
zh_text: 男人不該是同性戀，喬。這種事情就是，」她考慮該怎麼接，「不應該。」「我不懂妳的意思。」

en_text: “It doesn’t matter.”
zh_text: 「無所謂。」

en_text: She seems happy to let the subject go, and I’m happy to let her. We eat in silence for a minute, which is all my mother can handle before talking again. “I started a jigsaw puzzle today.” I’m not brave enough to tell her I’ll alert the media. Instead I go with,
zh_text: 我們一言不發地吃了一會兒，我媽只能保持沉默這麼點時間。「我今天開始玩拼圖。」「嗯哼。」

en_text: “Uh huh.” “It was on special. Down from thirty dollars to twelve.”
zh_text: 「特價品。三十塊錢降到十二塊。」

en_text: “Bargain.”
zh_text: 「很划算。」

en_text: “Here, I’ll ﬁnd you the receipt.”
zh_text: 「等等，我去拿收據給你看。」

en_text: I add more gravy to my dinner and try to eat quicker while she’s gone, knowing that eating quickly doesn’t necessarily mean a quick escape, but also knowing it’s worth a shot. I watch the clocks on the microwave and the oven, and I race them against the clock hanging on the wall, but they all drag along at the same pace. It doesn’t take Mom long to ﬁnd the receipt so I ﬁgure she must have kept it aside to show me. She waddles over with the advertising ﬂyer as well. I do my best to calm my excitement.
zh_text: 我趁她去忙的時候繼續吃飯，心裡清楚早點吃完並不表示我能早點逃離現場。我看著微波爐跟烤箱上的時鐘，讓它們跟牆壁上的時鐘賽跑，但是它們移動的步調一模一樣。媽沒花多久時間就找到收據了，所以我想她一定是放在順手的地方準備給我看。她搖搖晃晃地走過來，手裡還拿著宣傳單。我竭盡所能壓抑激動的情緒。

en_text: “See? Twelve dollars.”
zh_text: 「看到沒？十二塊。」

en_text: “Yeah, I see.” The ﬂyer has Chockablock with Entertainment written across it. I wonder what the person was thinking when they wrote that. Or what they were on.
zh_text: 「是，我看到了。」宣傳單上寫著「樂趣十足」幾個大字。我不知道寫這幾個字的人當時腦子裡在想什麼或是嗑了什麼藥。

en_text: “That’s eighteen dollars. Well, actually it was twenty-nine ninety-ﬁve down to twelve dollars, so that’s eighteen dollars and ninety-ﬁve cents.” I do the arithmetic as she talks to me, and quickly see she’s off by a dollar. Best not to say anything. I’m ﬁguring if she realizes she saved eighteen dollars and not nineteen, she’s going to take it back. Even after she’s done the puzzle.
zh_text: 「省了十八塊。好吧，事實上這玩意兒是二十九塊九毛五降到十二塊，所以我一共省了十八塊九毛五。」我在腦中心算了一下，隨即發現她多算了一塊錢。不過此時最好什麼都別說。我想如果讓她知道她只省了十七塊而不是十八塊，她很可能拿回去退貨，就算拼圖已經玩過了也一樣。大船。「你知道那艘船？」

en_text: “It’s of the Titanic, Joe,” she says, even though the picture in the ﬂyer is of a large boat with the word Titanic stenciled across its helm. “You know, the boat?”
zh_text: 的拼圖，喬。」她說，雖然傳單上已經明白印了一艘舵上印有鐵達尼號字樣的

en_text: “Oh, that Titanic.”
zh_text: 「喔，那艘鐵達尼。」

en_text: “A real tragedy.”
zh_text: 「人間慘劇。」

en_text: “The movie?”
zh_text: 「妳說那部電影？」

en_text: “The boat.” “I hear it sank.”
zh_text: 「我說那艘船。」「聽說它沉了。」

en_text: “Are you sure you’re not gay, Joe?”
zh_text: 「你確定你不是同性戀嗎，喬？」

en_text: “I’d know, wouldn’t I?”
zh_text: 「是的話我會知道，不是嗎？」

en_text: After dinner, I offer to clean up, even though I know what she’s going to say.
zh_text: 晚餐過後，我說要清理餐桌，雖然我很清楚她會怎麼說。

en_text: “You think I want you around here to be my maid? Sit down, Joe. I’ll clean up. What sort of mother won’t take care of her son? I’ll tell you what sort—a bad mother, that’s who.”
zh_text: 「你以爲我要你來是想把你當佣人嗎？坐下，喬。我來清。不懂得照顧兒子算是什麼母親？我告訴你什麼母親——壞母親，就是那種。

en_text: “I’ll do it.”
zh_text: 「我來清。」

en_text: I sit down in the living room and stare at the TV. There’s a news bulletin on. Something about a dead body. Home invasion. I change channels. Finally Mom comes through to the living room carrying a cup of tea for herself and nothing for me.
zh_text: 我去客廳坐下，盯著電視看。螢幕上播著新聞快報。跟一具屍體有關。私闖民宅。我轉台。媽終於來到客廳。

en_text: “It seems my whole life was spent cleaning up after your father, and now I’m spending the rest of it cleaning up after you.” “I offered to help, Mom,” I say, standing up.
zh_text: 「我這輩子都在幫你爸清理餐桌，現在好像又得用餘生去幫你清理餐桌。」「我有說要幫忙，媽。」我說著起身。

en_text: “Well, it’s too late now. It’s done,” she snaps. “You should learn to appreciate your mother, Joe. I’m all you have.”
zh_text: 「好了，太晚了。清完了。」她大聲道，「你應該要珍惜你媽，喬。我是你僅有的一切。」這段話我聽過很多次了，每聽一次就道歉一次。我又向她道歉一次，感覺好像我跟母親的對話中有一半是我在道歉。她坐下來，我們一起看電視——一齣演員會把「沒事」說成「沒素」的英文影集，而我甚至不知道「混怒」到底是他媽什麼意思。

en_text: I know this speech, and have apologized as many times as I’ve heard it. I say I’m sorry once again, and it seems offering apologies to my mother makes up ﬁfty percent of my conversations with her. She sits down and we watch some TV—some English drama about people who say nufﬁnk instead of nothing, and I don’t even know what in the hell bollocks really means. Mom watches it as if she can’t already predict that Fay is sleeping with Edgar for his inheritance, and Karen is pregnant from Stewart—the town drunk and her long-lost brother. When the commercials come on, she ﬁlls me in on what the characters have been up to, as if they’re part of the family. At least she isn’t offering to cook them meatloaf. I listen and nod and forget what she says within seconds. Like a goldﬁsh. When it comes back on, I end up watching the carpet, ﬁnding more entertainment in the brown, symmetrical patterns that were all the rage back in the ﬁfties— proving that everybody was completely mad back then.
zh_text: 媽看影集的樣子好像她猜不出來菲是爲了遺產才跟愛德嘉上床、而凱倫的孩子是史都華的（鎭上的酒鬼兼她失聯許久的哥哥）一樣。廣告時，她就會告訴我這些角色最近在做些什麼，彷彿他們都是我們家人。我聽她說，然後點頭，接著在數秒之內忘記她說了什麼，就像金魚一樣。廣告結束後，我開始盯著地毯看，覺得來自憤怒五〇年代的棕色對稱花紋比電視更有看頭——證明了當年每個人都是徹頭徹尾的瘋子。

en_text: The drama ends and the highly depressing theme music starts to play. As sad as the tune is, I’m feeling in high spirits because that music means it’s time for me to go. Before I leave, Mom tells me more about my cousin Gregory. He has a car. A BMW. “Why don’t you have a BMW, Joe?”
zh_text: 影集結束，非常令人沮喪的主題音樂響起。儘管曲調悲傷，我還是覺得十分亢奮，因為這表示我回家的時候到了。離開前，我媽跟我提起葛雷葛利表哥的事情。他有一輛車，BMW。「你為什麼沒有BMW，喬？

en_text: I’ve never stolen a BMW. “Because I’m not gay.”
zh_text: 因為我從來沒偷過BMW。「因為我不是同性戀。」

en_text: I’m the only person on the bus. The driver is old, and his hands shake as I give him the exact change. As we drive along, I start to wonder what would happen if he sneezed. Would his heart explode? Would we career into other trafﬁc? I feel like giving him a dollar tip when he gets me safely to my stop, but I ﬁgure the excitement will ﬁnish off what the Grim Reaper started years ago. He wishes me a good night as I leave the bus, but I don’t know if he really means it. I don’t wish him anything back. I’m not looking to make any friends. Especially old ones.
zh_text: 我是公車上唯一的乘客。司機很老，當我多給小費的時候，他的手在發抖。行車途中，我開始想像萬一他打噴嚏會怎麼樣。他會不會心臟病發？我們會不會撞上其他車輛？當我安然抵達車站之時，我很想多給他一塊錢小費，不過我怕這種刺激會害死他。他在我下車時跟我道再見，我不知道他是不是誠心的。我沒有跟他道再見。我不打算交朋友，尤其是跟老人。

en_text: When I get home I step into the shower and spend an hour washing away my mother. When I climb out, I spend some time with Pickle and Jehovah. They look happy to see me. A few minutes later and it’s lights out. I slip into bed. I don’t ever dream, and tonight is going to be no exception.
zh_text: 回家後，我跑去浴室花了一整個小時洗淨我媽的味道。出來之後，我跟泡菜和耶和華混了一曾兒。他們看到我似乎很開心。數分鐘後，熄燈。爬上床。我從不做夢，今晚也不會例外。我想到安琪立和小毛，接著我終於完全放空。

en_text: I think of Angela and Fluffy, and ﬁnally I think of nothing.
zh_text: 我想到安琪拉和小毛，接著我終於完全放空。

en_text: Right on seven thirty, I wake up. I don’t need an alarm clock to pull me from sleep. My clock is internal. Never needs winding. Never breaks down. Keeps on ticking.
zh_text: 我準時七點半起床。我不需要鬧鐘叫我。我的時鐘是內建的。從不需要上發條。從來不會壞。一直滴答滴答。

en_text: Another Christchurch morning and I’m already bored. I look at the clothes in my wardrobe, but it’s pointless. I get dressed, then start breakfast. Toast. Coffee. Doesn’t get more sophisticated than that. I talk to my ﬁsh and tell them about Karen and Stewart and the rest of the nufﬁnk squad, and they listen intently to what I have to say, and then they forget it. I feed them as a reward for their loyalty.
zh_text: 又是另一個基督城的早晨，而我已經開始感到無聊了。我看著衣櫥中的衣服，不過沒什麼好挑的。我換裝好，開始吃早餐。吐司、咖啡，最精緻的早餐不過如此。我跟我的魚說起凱倫和史都華以及其他那些「沒素」的傢伙，而他們十分專心地聽我說話。爲了獎勵他們的忠誠，我餵他們吃了點飼料。

en_text: I head outside. It’s another summer day in autumn. There aren’t many people around. Unfortunately I don’t have a car. Angela’s I left parked on the other side of town. I left the keys in the ignition in case somebody else wanted to take it for a spin. Stealing keys is a lot easier than hot-wiring the thing, though I’ve got plenty of experience when it comes to both.
zh_text: 我開門出去。附近還是沒人。不幸的是，我沒車。我把安琪拉的車丟在鎭上另外一邊，將鑰匙插在啓動器上，說不定還有其他人想要開去兜風。偷鑰匙比接線啓動要容易多了，雖然這兩種手法我都很熟。昨晚我花了一個小時的時間走路回家，所以我才會遲到那麼久。

en_text: I am at the bus stop with my ticket in my hand when the bus pulls up. The side of it is covered in advertisements for vitamin pills and contraceptives. The doors open with a swish. I climb on board.
zh_text: 公車停下來時，我已經拿著車票等在車站。車身側面貼滿了維他命和避孕藥的廣告。車門咻地一聲打開。我上車。

en_text: “Hey ya doin’, Joe?”
zh_text: 「今天好嗎，喬？」

en_text: “Joe’s ﬁne, Mr. Stanley.”
zh_text: 「喬很好，史丹利先生。」

en_text: I hand Mr. Stanley my bus ticket. He takes it from me and, without clicking it, hands it back. Winks at me like old bus drivers do. The whole side of his face crushes down like he’s having a stroke. Mr. Stanley is probably in his sixties, and looks like he gets a kick out of life. On mornings like these, he always likes to say, “Hot, ain’t it?” He wears the uniform all bus drivers wear: dark blue shorts, a light-blue short-sleeved shirt, and black shoes.
zh_text: 我將公車票交給史丹利先生。他接過票，看也不看就又還了回來。接著像個老公車司機一樣跟我眨眼。他半邊臉好似中風般整個皺成一團。史丹利先生約莫五十來歲，看起來十分享受生活。在這樣的早晨，他總是喜歡說：「熱啊，是不是？」他身穿和所有公車司機相同的制服：深藍色的短褲，淺藍色的短袖上衣以及黑色的鞋子。

en_text: “This one’s on the city this morning, Joe,” he says, still winking, just in case I hadn’t noticed. “Sure is a hot one today, Joe, ain’t it?”
zh_text: 「今天早上市政府請客，喬。」他說，又眨了眨眼，以免我沒看見。「今天可真熱啊，喬，是不是？」

en_text: I ﬁgure if I smile back, I’ll get more free bus rides. “Gee. Joe’s thankful, Mr. Stanley.”
zh_text: 我想如果他微笑的話，我就能多免費乘車幾次。「是啊，喬很感激，史丹利先生。」

en_text: Mr. Stanley smiles at me and I wonder how he would look if I opened my briefcase and showed him what’s inside. Putting the bus ticket into my pocket, I walk down the aisle. The bus is fairly empty—a handful of school kids scattered randomly, a nun in one of those stifﬂy starched black-andwhite outﬁts, a businessman with an umbrella even though it has to be ninety degrees outside.
zh_text: 史丹利先生對我微笑，我在想如果讓他看到我公事包裡的東西會是什麼表情。我將公車票放回口袋，沿著走道走去。車上很空——零星坐了幾個學生、一名身穿僵硬刻板黑白修女服的修女、一個帶著雨傘的生意人，雖然外面一定超過三十度。

en_text: Regular people. Like me.
zh_text: 都是普通人。像我一樣。

en_text: I sit near the back behind two sixteen- or seventeen-year-old schoolgirls. I prop my briefcase up on the empty seat next to me. Nobody is sitting behind or opposite me. I thumb the combination on each side of the case. Slide the latches. Open the case. I have my knives stored away carefully inside—three in the lid, and three in the base. They’re held in place by strands of material that loop over them and snap into place with metal domes. The gun is the only thing that ﬂoats around free, but it’s in a black leather pouch to protect it, and the knives. The gun has three internal safeties, so I’d have to be three times unlucky—or stupid—to have any sort of accident. Ahead of me, the schoolgirls are giggling.
zh_text: 我坐在車尾兩名十六或十七歲的女學生後方，將公事包放在旁邊的空位上。我身後及走道對面的座位上都沒人。我以拇指撥動公事包兩側的密碼。滑開彈簧鎖。打開上蓋。我將刀子小心地收藏在裡面上蓋上有三把，底層也有三把。它們以布料綑起，然後用金屬環固定。槍是裡面唯一沒固定住的東西，不過放在黑皮套裡藉以保護它，也保護刀子。這把槍有三道內建保險，所以我得要有三倍不幸——或是愚蠢——才會發生槍枝走火的意外。此時前方傳來女學生的嬌笑聲。

en_text: I take out a knife with a blade only two inches long, which cost twentyﬁve dollars. It takes a lot of stabbing to kill somebody with a knife that short. Once, about eighteen months ago, it took me a good forty or ﬁfty goes. Small cuts. Lots of blood. I was sweating like a pig afterward. My shirt was pasted to me. He deserved it, though.
zh_text: 我拿出一把刀身只有五公分長的小刀，價值二十五塊錢。這麼短的刀要刺很多下才能刺死人。有一回，大概十八個月前，我足足刺了一百多下才幹掉一個混蛋。傷口很小，血很多。完事之後我像豬一樣汗流浹背。我的上衣都黏在身上。不過他倒是罪有應得。

en_text: Mr. Stanley is a much nicer bus driver.
zh_text: 史丹利先生比那個公車司機要和善多了。

en_text: I’m absentmindedly running the blade up and down the back of the seat of the girl on the left. I’m thinking about women in general when her friend, the blond girl, turns around at the sound. I hide the knife behind my leg. Smile innocently as if I have no idea where I even am, as if all I’m doing is singing mentally to myself: The wheels on the bus go round and round, round and round. She glares at me. Watching her, I can feel the beginnings of a relationship. She looks away without comment, and they return to their giggling. I tuck the knife away in my briefcase. I’m not even sure why I got it out. I stare out the window and watch as the bus approaches the central city. More trafﬁc, more smog, more aggravation as people get caught up at trafﬁc lights. We pass a guy sitting on the side of the road next to a mountain bike, the front wheel all buckled up, both of his knees are bleeding. He catches me staring at him and gives me the ﬁnger.
zh_text: 我用那把刀在左邊女孩的椅背後方劃來劃去。正當我把椅背幻想成女人之時，她的朋友，金髮女孩，應聲回頭。我將小刀藏在腳後。面露天眞的微笑，彷彿我甚至不知道自己身在何處，只是在心裡哼著：公車車輪轉呀轉，轉呀轉（一首兒歌的歌詞）。她瞪了我一眼。看著她，我彷彿感覺到一段戀情即將展開。

en_text: I have the briefcase closed up by the time my stop appears. Mr. Stanley makes a special exception for me, stopping the bus directly outside my work. I give him a smile from the end of the bus. We exchange waves as I step off from the back exit.
zh_text: 她一言不發地偏過目光，又回去笑她們的。我將小刀塞回公事包。我甚至不確定爲什麼要拿出來。快到站的時候，我關上公事包。史丹利先生特別照顧我，將公車直接停在我工作場所外。我站在車尾對他微笑。自後門下車時，我們互相揮手道別。

en_text:
Christchurch. City of Angels this isn’t. New Zealand is known for its tranquility, its sheep, and its hobbits. Christchurch is known for its parks and violence. Throw a bag of glue in the air and a hundred welfare recipients will knock each other over in an effort to sniff from it. Despite the blue skies, Christchurch City is still mostly gray. Many of the buildings date back a hundred years, some even more, gothic architecture imported from England along with the population back then. Gray buildings, gray roads, lots of ofﬁce and shop windows reﬂecting it all. However there is the occasional splash of greenery: trees, shrubs, ﬂowers. You can’t take twenty paces without passing something out of nature. Walk ten minutes to the west, and you’ll ﬁnd the Botanic Gardens; more than twenty hectares of land dedicated to showing the rest of the world how clever we are at turning seeds into plants. In these gardens are thousands of ﬂowers and hundreds of trees, but you can’t go there at night without getting stabbed or shot, becoming fertilizer.
I take a few paces forward, and my boredom does nothing to let up. It’s this city. Nobody can feel excited surrounded by buildings that date back a hundred years. Between the buildings is a warren of alleyways that any selfrespecting drug addict can walk with their eyes closed. Christchurch patients live down these alleyways. If a businessman or businesswoman were to venture down one, they would have more of a chance of ﬁnding Jesus than getting out of there without being molested or urinated on. As for the shopping, well, shopping here is going out of style, and that’s reﬂected in the empty stores with signs hanging in the windows saying For Lease or For Sale. Even so, you can never ﬁnd a damn parking space anywhere.
zh_text:
基督城。不是什麼天使之城。紐西蘭是以寧靜、綿羊以及哈比人聞名於世的。基督城最著名的則是花園和暴行。往天上丟一袋強力膠，立刻就有上百個人爭先恐後地衝上去吸。這裡沒有什麼值得一看的東西。很多建築物，不過全部灰濛濛、陰森森。很多條路，一樣都是灰色的——就像大部分日子的天空。
這裡就跟其他城市一樣是座水泥叢林，不過這裡的水泥偶爾還能看見綠地的空間：樹木、灌木、花朵。每隔二十步，你一定能夠路過天然景觀。城內大片的綠地，像是植物園，則是用來向全世界展示我們多有辦法將種子變成植物。這些花園裡種植了數千種花朵和數百種樹木，但是如果晚上跑去，你一定會受到刀槍攻擊，然後用你的屍體幫助植物成長。

en_text: Christchurch is voted one of the friendliest places in the world. By who, I have no idea. Certainly not anybody I’ve ever met. But despite all of this, Christchurch is my home.
zh_text: 我向前走出幾步，不過無聊的感覺一點也沒有好轉。這是城市的問題。沒有人能在一堆百年建築中興奮雀躍。建築物之間有許許多多陰暗曲折的小巷道。基督城的毒蟲就住在這些巷道之花點時間來個三百六十度迴轉，你就會看見南邊的波特山，至於東邊、西邊和北邊，除了一大片平地之外什麼也看不到。基督城被票選爲全世界最友善的城市之一。誰選的，我不知道。一定不是任何我認識的人。不過儘管有以上種種缺點，基督城還是我的家鄉。

en_text: The air shimmers with heat, and in the distance it makes the roads look wet. Cars have their windows down and drivers’ arms are hanging in the breeze, cigarette ash dropping onto the sidewalk. Plenty of trafﬁc is racing by, too much for me to run through, so I push the button for the crossing signal and wait. When it ﬂashes and beeps for me to walk, I wait a few more seconds for the red-light runners to speed by, then cross the road. I roll my sleeves up. The air feels good on my forearms. I can feel beads of sweat running down the sides of my body.
zh_text: 空氣熱得發亮，讓遠方的道路看起來有點潮濕。車輛都放低車窗，司機將手垂在車外吹風，菸灰撒落一地。許多車輛呼嘯而過，多到我沒辦法穿越馬路，於是我按下紅綠燈按鈕，耐心等候。當紅綠燈轉換燈號和聲響，通知我通行時，我又等了幾秒鐘讓闖紅燈的車輛先行，然後才過馬路。我捲起衣袖。手臂吹吹風感覺很舒服。我感到汗水沿著身側滴落。

en_text: Two minutes later I’m at work.
zh_text: 兩分鐘後，我抵達工作場所。

en_text: I walk directly to the fourth ﬂoor, taking the stairs since stealing cars doesn’t provide any real exercise. The stairwell smells of urine at the bottom, and more like disinfectant the higher I get. On the fourth ﬂoor I enter the conference room and place my briefcase, locked, down on the table, and move over to the photographs pinned to the wall.
zh_text: 我直接走上三樓，由於偷車不算真的運動，所以我選擇走樓梯。樓梯間底部聞起來有股尿騷味，越往上走消毒水的味道就越重。到三樓後，我走入會議室，將上鎖的公事包放在桌上，走過去看著釘在牆上的照片。

en_text: “Morning, Joe. How are you this morning?”
zh_text: 早安，喬。今早過得如何？

en_text: I look at the man I’ve positioned myself next to. Schroder is a big guy with more muscle than brain. He has those rugged good looks of an actionmovie hero, but I doubt he has any heroism left. He hates this city as much as anybody else. He has buzz-cut graying hair that would look better on a sixty-year-old drill sergeant than on him, an almost forty-year-old homicide detective. His forehead and face are covered in stress lines, which I no doubt put there. He has bags under his eyes, no doubt put there by the new baby he has at home. At the moment he’s going for the hard-workeddetective look, and with his cheap shirtsleeves rolled up and his thrift-store tie loosened, he has certainly achieved it. He has a pencil jammed up behind his ear, and another one in his hand, which he was chewing on before he spoke. He is standing with one foot forward, slightly ahead of the other, as if ready to pounce at the wall and start pounding on it.
zh_text: 我看著站在我身旁的男人。施羅德是個肌肉比腦袋發達的大個子。他擁有動作電影明星般的英挺外表，不過我懷疑他是否還保有任何英雄氣概。他跟所有人一樣痛恨這座城市。他留著一頭比較適合六十歲訓練官的灰髮平頭，但他其實是一名四十歲的重案組警探。他的額頭和臉上布滿被我逼出來的壓力皺紋。此時他正裝出一副認真辦案的警探模樣，捲起昂貴的衣袖，拉鬆名牌領帶，可謂扮演得十分成功。他耳朵後方插了一支鉛筆，手裡也拿著一支，不過手裡那支在他開口說話前都是放在嘴巴裡咬的。他一腳微微向前，站在衆人之前，一副打算衝上前開始毆打牆壁的模樣。

en_text: “Morning, Detective Schroder.” I nod slowly toward the photographs like I’m agreeing with what I just said. “Any new leads?”
zh_text: 「早安，施羅德警探。」我緩緩朝向牆上的照片點頭，彷彿在認同我剛剛說的話一樣。「有新的線索嗎？」

en_text: Detective Inspector Schroder is the lead detective on this case, has been since the second murder. He shakes his head like he’s disagreeing with himself, straightens his back and massages out a crick by pushing his palms against it, then gets back to looking at the photographs. “Nothing yet, Joe. Only new victims.”
zh_text: 施羅德倶維督察乃是這個案子的首席警探，自從第二宗謀殺案發生開始就是了。他搖了搖頭，彷彿不同意自己的說法般，挺直背脊，在掌心按摩下發出骨頭移位的聲響，然後又回頭去看照片。「沒有新線索，喬。只有兩名新的被害人。」

en_text: I let his statement hang in the air. Pretend I’m thinking about what he’s saying. Thinking and processing. Has to take me longer when I’m standing in front of a cop. “Oh? Did this happen last night, Detective Schroder?”
zh_text: 我一言不發。假裝我在思考他說的話。思考並且消化。在警察面前我必須假裝久一點。「喔？昨晚發生的嗎，施羅德警探？」

en_text: He nods. “Sick bastard broke into her house.”
zh_text: 他點頭。「那個變態闖入她家。」

en_text: His ﬁsts are shaking. The pencil he’s holding breaks. He tosses it onto the table, where a small graveyard of other broken pencils lies, and then grabs hold of the one from behind his ear. He must keep a supply just for these occasions. He chews on it for a few seconds before turning toward me and snapping it in half.
zh_text: 他的大拳頭在顫抖。手中的鉛筆折成兩段。他將斷筆丟在桌上那片小斷筆墳場裡，然後取下插在耳朵後方的那一支。他必定專門爲了這種情況準備了不少鉛筆。他咬了那支筆幾秒鐘，然後轉向我，將筆折成兩半。

en_text: “I’m sorry, Joe. You’ll have to excuse my language.”
zh_text: 「對不起，喬，很抱歉我口出惡言。」

en_text: “That’s okay. You said victims. Does that mean there was more than one?”
zh_text: 沒事。你說兩名受害者。不只一個？

en_text: “Another woman was found in the trunk of her car, parked up the victim’s driveway.”
zh_text: 「還有一名女子陳屍在她的後車廂裡，停在被害人的車道上。」

en_text: I exhale loudly. “Gosh, Detective Schroder, I guess that’s why you’re the detective and I’m not. I would never have looked in the trunk. Even now, she’d still be in there, alone and everything.” Like the detective, I’m shaking my ﬁsts now too, but unlike the detective I don’t have a supply of pencils to start breaking. “Gee, I would have let everybody down,” I add under my breath but loud enough for him to hear.
zh_text: 我長吁一口氣。「天啊，施羅德警探，我猜這就是你是警探而我不是的原因。我絕對不會去查後車廂。要是我的話，現在她還孤零零地躺在裡面呢。」就跟警探一樣，我的拳頭也在顫抖。「唉，是我的話一定會讓所有人失望的。」我低聲補充，不過聲音大到足夠讓他聽見。

en_text: “Hey, Joe, don’t beat yourself up. Even I didn’t look in the car. We didn’t even notice the second victim until this morning.”
zh_text: 「嘿，喬，不要太苛責自己了。我也沒去查車子。我們直到今天早上才發現第一名被害人。」

en_text: He’s lying. His rugged face is looking at me with pity.
zh_text: 他在說謊。他嚴峻的臉上露出同情的表情。

en_text: “Really?”
zh_text: 「眞的？」

en_text: He nods. “Sure.”
zh_text: 他點頭。「當然。」

en_text: “Can I get you some coffee, Detective Schroder?”
zh_text: 「我可以幫你拿杯咖啡嗎，施羅德警探？

en_text: “Well, okay, Joe, but only if it isn’t any hassle.”
zh_text: 「這個，好啊，喬，如果不麻煩的話。」

en_text: “No hassle. Black, one sugar, right?” “Two sugars, Joe.”
zh_text: 「不麻煩。純咖啡，一顆糖，是吧？」

en_text: “Right.” I make him remind me every time I offer. “Can I leave my briefcase on the table here, Detective Schroder?”
zh_text: 「對。」我每次幫他倒咖啡都讓他提醒我一次。「我可以把公事包放在這裡一下嗎，施羅德警探？」

en_text: “Go ahead. What do you carry in that thing anyway?”
zh_text: 放著吧。你那裡面都放些什麼啊？

en_text: I shrug and look away. “You know, Detective Schroder, documents and stuff.”
zh_text: 我聳肩，轉開頭去。「你知道的，施羅德警探，只是文件之類的東西。「我想也是。」

en_text: “Thought so.” Bullshit. The bastard ﬁgures I have lunch in there, and maybe a comic book. Nonetheless, I walk from the room and into the corridor, where I move among dozens of ofﬁces and ofﬁcers and detectives. I head past several cubicles, and straight to the coffee machine. It’s easy to use, but I make it look more complicated than it is. I’m thirsty, so I make myself one ﬁrst and quickly drink it since it’s not that hot and because it tastes like dirt. Most of the other cops nod at me. It’s that dumb silent greeting that’s in fashion at the moment—the one where you nod abruptly and raise your eyebrows—and starts to get uncomfortable when you keep passing the same people. Then you have to make idle chitchat. Mondays are okay, because they ask how your weekend was. Fridays are okay too, because they ask what you have planned for the weekend. But the days in between really are a bastard.
zh_text: 狗屁。那混蛋以爲我在裡面放了午餐，或許還有漫畫。不管怎樣，我離開房間，步入走廊，行走在幾十名警官、警員和警探之間。我路過數間辦公隔間，直接來到咖啡機前。咖啡機很容易使用，不過我裝作一副對我來說很複雜的樣子。我很渴，所以先幫自己弄了一杯，然後迅速喝掉，因為咖啡不是很燙，而且由於喝起來像泥巴的關係，這裡的咖啡一定要很快喝掉才行。大部分的警察都向我點頭。最近流行這種愚蠢的沉默招呼方式——就是突然點頭，然後揚起眉毛的那種——跟著又在遇上同批人時開始變得尷尬。然後你就必須開始閒聊。禮拜一還好，因為他們會問你週末過得怎麼樣，禮拜五也還好，因為他們會問你週末要幹什麼，不過週二到週四真的很煩人。

en_text: I pour Schroder his coffee. Black. Two sugars.
zh_text: 我倒了施羅德的咖啡。純咖啡，兩顆糖。

en_text: For the last few months, the police station has been alive with the hustle and bustle of stressed and anxious detectives. The immediate day of a homicide and the day after are when that hustling and bustling are at their greatest. Meetings are held every hour of the day. Statements are pored over by eager eyes, looking for vital clues or discrepancies from anybody who knew one of the victims. Information is gathered only to become forgotten evidence the moment another killing takes place. After all these killings, they still have nothing. I actually feel bad for them in some ways—all this never-ending work that produces nothing. During the day, reporters keep showing up every time they hear a new piece of evidence has been uncovered, a new witness spoken to, or—their personal favorite—when a new victim has been found. The latter ensures them more sales of newspapers and of revenue from ads as the bulletins go to air. Reporters armed with microphones ﬁre questions at anybody who looks like a policeman as they come and go. Cameras are rolling. All this and they ignore the one man who can give them the inside scoop.
zh_text: 過去幾個月來，警局裡的警探個個忙碌奔走、緊張焦慮。最忙碌的時刻就是謀殺案發生當天以及隔天。每個小時就要開一次會。他們迫切地四下蒐集證詞，在所有認識被害人的人身上找尋重要線索或是矛盾說詞。每當下一件謀殺案發生時，之前收集的證據通通就變得無關緊要。在發生這麼多起案件之後，他們依然一無所獲。就某些方面而言，我真的很同情他們——做得要死要活，卻沒有半點成果。白天的時候，記者一聽說風吹草動立刻就會跑來，不管是找到新證據、發現新證人，或是他們最愛的情況——出現新的被害人。最後一種情況可以保證報紙大賣，並且在播放新聞的時候收取大筆廣告費。記者會對所有出入警局看起來像是警察的人提問。攝影機不停拍，麥克風沒關過。如此大張旗鼓，偏偏沒人注意到唯一能夠提供內幕消息的人。

en_text: I carry the coffee back into the conference room. By now, a few other detectives are milling around inside. I can feel the anguish in the air—the desperation to catch the man doing this to them and their city. The room smells like sweat and cheap aftershave. I hand Schroder his coffee with a smile. He thanks me. I pick up my briefcase to leave and the knives don’t jingle.
zh_text: 我帶著咖啡回到會議室。這時裡面又多擠了幾名警探。我可以感覺到充斥空氣中的苦惱氣息——迫切地想要抓到如此折磨他們和這座城市的男人。會議室內瀰漫著汗臭和廉價鬍後水的味道。我笑著將咖啡交給施羅德。他向我道謝。我拿起我的公事包離開，刀子沒有發出任何聲響。

en_text: My ofﬁce is on the same ﬂoor. Unlike the cubicles, mine is actually an ofﬁce. It’s at the end of the corridor, just past the toilets. The door has my name on it. It’s one of those little gold plaques with black lettering. Joe. No second name. No other initial. Just Joe. Like an everyday average Joe. Well, that’s me. Everyday and average.
zh_text: 我的辦公室也在同一層樓。跟那些小隔間不同，我的是眞的辦公室。它位於走廊底端，廁所旁邊。門上掛有我的名字。就是那種印著黑字的金色小名牌。喬。沒有姓，沒有其他縮寫，只有「喬」。一個普通通的名字。好吧，這就是我，一個普通通平凡人。

en_text: I have my hand on the handle and am about to turn it when she comes up behind me and taps me on the shoulder.
zh_text: 我伸手握住門把，正要轉動的時候，她來到我的身後，輕拍我的肩膀。「你今天過得如何，喬？」

en_text: “How are you doing today, Joe?” Her voice is a little loud and a little slow, as if she’s trying to break through a language barrier with somebody from Mars.
zh_text: 她說話有點大聲、有點緩慢，彷彿正試圖突破一道火星人的語言藩籬。

en_text: I force the smile onto my face, the one that Detective Schroder sees every time he shares a pleasantry with me. I give her a big-kid smile, the type with all teeth, spreading my lips as far apart as possible in every direction.
zh_text: 我強擠出笑容，每當施羅德警探向我示好時就會看到的那種。一個大孩子的微笑，露出所有牙齒，嘴角朝向四面八方開到最大的笑容。

en_text: “Good morning, Sally. I’m ﬁne, thank you for asking.”
zh_text: 早安，莎莉。我很好，謝謝妳。

en_text: Sally grins back at me. She is dressed in a pair of black overalls that are slightly too big for her, but don’t hide the fact that she is slightly too big herself. Not fat, but somewhere between solid and chubby. She has a pretty face when she smiles, but it isn’t pretty enough for somebody to ignore the few extra pounds and slip a ring on her ﬁnger. At the age of twenty-ﬁve, it’s her chances that are getting slimmer, not her weight. Smudges of dust on her forehead look like the remnants of a fading bruise. Her blond hair is tied into a ponytail, but it doesn’t look like it’s been washed in weeks. She doesn’t look slow—it isn’t until she speaks that you know you’re talking to somebody whose parents kept dropping her on her head for fun.
zh_text: 莎莉回應我的笑容。她身穿一件有點大的工作服，不過無法掩飾有點壯的身材。算不上胖，只是介於壯和胖之間。她笑的時候還算漂亮，但是沒有漂亮到會讓人忽視她的微胖，願意在她手上套上一枚戒指的境界。以二十五歲來講，逐漸變少的是她嫁人的機會，而不是她的體重。她額頭上的污垢看起來像是快好的瘀傷。她將一頭金髮綁成馬尾，不過似乎幾個禮拜沒有洗過了。她看起來手腳不慢——除非開口說話，不然你不會發現她是一個沒有大腦的女人。

en_text: “Can I get you a coffee, Joe? Or an orange juice?”
zh_text: 「我可以幫你倒杯咖啡嗎，喬？還是柳橙汁？」

en_text: “I’m ﬁne, Sally. That was nice of you to ask, though.”
zh_text: 「不用了，莎莉，妳眞好心。」

en_text: I open my door and get half a step inside before she taps me on the shoulder again.
zh_text: 我打開門，跨出半步，她又在我肩膀上拍了一下。

en_text: “Are you sure? It really wouldn’t be a problem. Not really.”
zh_text: 「你確定嗎？真的不麻煩。一點也不。」

en_text: “I’m not thirsty right now,” I say, and she looks sad. “Maybe later.”
zh_text: 「我現在不渴。或許待會兒吧。」

en_text: Sure, whatever. I slowly nod “Okay,” and a moment later I get the rest of the way into my ofﬁce and close the door.
zh_text: 當然，隨便啦。我緩緩點頭。「好的。」片刻過後，我步入辦公室，關上房

en_text: Sally says hello to everybody she knows on her way to the elevator, and to those not in earshot she offers a small wave. She pushes the button and waits patiently. She never feels the temptation to keep pushing the button like others do. The elevator is empty, which is a shame, because she would have liked the company on the way to her ﬂoor.
zh_text: 莎莉在前往電梯的途中跟所有認識的人打招呼，若是對方站得遠就揮揮手。她按下按鈕，耐心等候。她從來不會像其他人一樣不停按按鈕。電梯是空的，太可惜了，因為她希望有人陪她一同前往她的樓層。

en_text: She thinks about Joe, and what a nice young man he is. She’s always had the ability to see people for what they really are, and she can tell Joe is a wonderful human being. Though most people are, she thinks, since they’re all made in God’s image. She wishes there were more like Joe, though. Wishes there was more she could do for him.
zh_text: 她想著喬，想著他是多好的一個年輕人。她總是有辦法看出一個人的本性，她看得出來他是个大好人。雖然大部分的人都是大好人，她認爲，因為大家都是以上帝的形象創造出來的。不過她希望世界上有更多像喬這種人。希望自己可以幫他更多忙。

en_text: When the elevator comes to a stop, she steps out, ready to smile, but the corridor is empty. She makes her way to the end of the hallway and walks through the door marked Maintenance. Inside, the room is full of neatly kept shelves on which are several varieties of hand and power tools, different types and sizes of wooden beams, metal beams, spare panels of suspended ceiling, spare ﬂoor and wall tiles, pottles of adhesive and grease, jars full of screws and nails, clamps, a spirit level, various saws, different types of everything.
zh_text: 電梯停了，她走出去，準備微笑，但是走廊空無一人。她朝向走廊底端走去，穿越一扇標示「維修室的門。進門之後，裡面擺滿整整齊齊的架子，上面有各式各樣手動與電動工具，不同形式與尺寸的天花板木樑、鐵樑，與鑲板備料、地板與牆壁磁磚備料、黏膠與潤滑劑、裝滿螺絲和釘子的瓶子、螺絲鉗、一個水平儀、各式鋸子、各式各樣的其他工具。

en_text: She moves over to the window and picks up the glass of orange juice she set there twenty minutes earlier, just before rushing downstairs to say good morning to Joe. She isn’t sure why she made the effort. Probably because of Martin. She thinks about Martin more than ever over these two days of the year, and that has somehow led her to start thinking of Joe. People outside her family did very little to help Martin. Some, and she thinks about the kids at school, went out of their way to make life hard for him. It was the same for all the kids who were different. It will always be the same, she thinks, as she sips from her orange juice. It’s warmer than she would have liked, but the taste still makes her smile.
zh_text: 她走到窗旁，拿起二十分鐘前急急忙忙衝下樓去跟喬說早安前放在那裡的柳橙汁。她不確定自己幹嘛要這樣做。或許是因為馬丁的關係，每年這兩天，她都會特別想念馬丁，而這股思念又讓她開始聯想到喬。家族以外的人沒幫馬丁做過什麼。有些人——她想起學校的那些小鬼——甚至還刻意捉弄他。所有與衆不同的孩子都會遭到這種待遇。這情況永遠不會改變，她邊喝柳橙汁邊想。柳橙汁不冰了，但那味道依然足以讓她微笑。

en_text: She ﬁnishes her drink, then moves over to a large box full of cardboardwrapped ﬂuorescent tubes jammed tightly. She takes two out, one for this ﬂoor, the other for the ground ﬂoor. While she replaces the ﬁrst blown tube, she remembers how Martin’s disability changed her own life. Growing up with him, she had the idea that she wanted to become a nurse. She wanted to be able to help people.
zh_text: 她喝完飲料，然後走到一只裝滿日光燈管的大箱子前。她取出兩根燈管，一根是這層樓要換的，另外一根是給底層用的。換第一根壞燈管時，她想起了馬丁的智力障礙如何改變她的人生。與他一同長大讓她萌生當名護士的念頭。她想要幫助他人。

en_text: She had spent the last three years of her life, until six months ago, at nursing school. It was difﬁcult to decide exactly which path she wanted to follow, whether to work in a hospital, in a retirement home, or whether to help those who were mentally challenged like Martin and Joe. There were plenty of options, but she never got the chance. Martin died, and that made wanting to help people harder to do. There were too many diseases out there, too many viruses. You could live life the best you could, do the right things, make the right decisions, and still be struck down by something you were born with that had been biding its time. There were simply too many ways to die, and she didn’t want to see that happen to people she knew she would become attached to.
zh_text: 過去三年，一直到六個月前，她都在念護校。她很難決定想走哪一條路，是該去醫院工作、養老院，還是去幫助類似馬丁和喬那種有智力障礙的人。選擇很多，但是她一直沒機會選。馬丁死了，這個事實打擊了她幫助他人的信心。世界上有太多疾病、太多病毒了。你可以仔細照顧你的身體、做所有該做的事、下達各式正確的決定，結果還是死在某種與生俱來卻一直潛伏在體內的疾病之下。世界上死法實在太多了。然而每當想起馬丁對她的期待，她就會覺得輟學是種很可恥的行爲。她沒有機會幫助他了，這明確到了極點、也痛苦到了極點，不過還不至於阻止她去幫助他人。

en_text: The other factor was her father. Two years ago he was diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease, which quickly led to him losing his job. Since then the disease has advanced. He can’t work, and his weekly beneﬁt payments aren’t enough to cover the medical bills. She didn’t have the luxury of completing her studies. Her family needed her, not only to help look after her father, but to help them survive. She had to earn money. She had to help them get through this. She couldn’t afford to keep studying.
zh_text: 阻止她這麼做的是她父親。兩年前他被診斷出罹患帕金森氏症，沒多久就讓他丟了工作。那之後病情開始惡化。他無法工作，週領的救濟金不夠支付醫療費；醫療保險也應付不來家裡的新夢魘。她沒有辦法完成學業。她的家人需要她，不光只是要她看顧父親，還要幫助他們生存下去。她必須出來賺錢，她必須幫助家人度過難關。

en_text: Her father had a friend who was a full-time maintenance worker at the police station, a friend who was getting older and needed an assistant who would one day replace him. Sally took that job, and now, six months later, she even has his desk and view.
zh_text: 她父親有個朋友在警局擔任全職維修工，他年事漸長、需要訓練一名將來可以取代他的助手。莎莉接下了這份工作，如今，她甚至接收了他的辦公桌和窗外景觀。

en_text: She catches the elevator down to the ground ﬂoor; the entire trip down she thinks about Joe, and she thinks about what she can do to make his life better.
zh_text: 她搭乘電梯，路過喬的樓層，前往底層，沒有屈服在想看看他過得如何的誘惑下。

en_text: The police station is ten stories of nothing-going-on, made from concrete block and bad taste. My ofﬁce is small, perhaps the smallest in the whole damn building. Still, it’s mine, I share it with nobody, and that’s the most important thing.
zh_text: 警局是一棟毫無特色的十層樓建築，由水泥磚和低級品味搭建而成。我的辦公室很小，或許是整棟建築內最小的辦公室。儘管如此，它屬於我，不用和任何人分享，這才是重點。

en_text: I dump my briefcase on the bench, walk to the window and look out to the city beyond. Hot out there. Warm in here. Warm and stuffy. This is great weather not to be working in. Women walk the streets wearing skirts and tops made from nearly nothing. On a good day, from up here, you can see right down their tops. On a really good day, you can see nipple. By the end of the day, all these women are hidden away. They’re scared they might be the next victim plastered across the news. The nighttime air has a charged feeling of fear, and it isn’t going to change anytime soon. They do what they can to pretend nothing bad can ever happen to them.
zh_text: 我將公事包丟在工作台上，走到窗口，看著窗外的城市。外面很熱。裡面很暖。暖暖悶悶的。這是個不用上班的好天氣。女人會穿裙子和幾乎沒有什麼布料的上衣上街。天氣好的時候，從這個角度，你可以直接看穿她們的上衣。天氣超好的時候，還可以看見她們的奶頭。白天結束時，這些女人就全部躲起來了。她們深怕自己會淪爲新聞中的最新被害人。夜間的空氣裡瀰漫著一股額外的恐懼，而這種情況短期內不會改變。她們竭盡所能地假裝壞事不會發生在自己身上。

en_text: I turn from the window and undo the top button of my overalls. My ofﬁce consists of a bench that stretches the length of the room—about thirteen feet—along the same wall as the window. The other half of the furniture is a chair. Stacked around the ofﬁce are paint tins and plenty of rags, brooms, and cleaning solvents, which sometimes give me a headache. There are buckets and mops, tools, cables, spare shelving, spare parts, spare lots of things. The ofﬁce is well lit because it gets the sun most of the day, which is just as well, because fewer than half of the four ﬂuorescent lights in the ceiling actually work.
