I keep forgetting to get Sally to replace them, and when I do remember, I’m afraid to ask her. I’m sure she has a crush on me, which is normal for most women, but creepy when it comes to someone like Sally.
zh_text: 我轉離窗戶，解開工作服最上面的釦子。我的辦公室裡有張跟房間一樣長的工作台，大約四公尺，擺在有窗戶的牆下。另外一樣家具是把椅子。辦公室中放滿了油漆罐和許多抹布、掃把，以及有時會導致我頭痛的清潔劑。水桶和拖把、工具、線材、多餘的棚架、備用零件、很多東西的備料。辦公室的光線充足，因為白天大部分的時間都照得到太陽，這樣也好，因為天花板上的日光燈有半數的時間根本不會亮。我老是忘記請莎莉來換燈管，而想到的時候，我又不敢找她。我很肯定她喜歡我，這對大部分的女人而言都很正常，但是讓莎莉那種女人喜歡就有點詭異了。

en_text: Because my ofﬁce has faulty air-conditioning and a window that doesn’t open, I have an electric fan that sits on the desk and whirs noisily when turned on. Next to it is a coffee mug with my name stenciled on it. A wellthought-out gift from my mother. On the end of my bench is a framed photograph of Pickle and Jehovah that I gave to myself last Father’s Day.
zh_text: 由於我辦公室的空調故障，又有一扇窗戶打不開，所以我在辦公桌上放了一台電風扇，只要一開就會發出很大的噪音。電風扇旁邊擺著一個印有我名字的咖啡杯。我媽送的貼心禮物。工作台末端擺了一張泡菜和耶和華的裱框相片

en_text: I grab the bucket from the corner of my room, pick up the mop from next to it, and head for the air-conditioned third ﬂoor. Then I walk into the even cooler men’s bathroom. The smell of disinfectant forces me to breathe through my mouth for fear of passing out.
zh_text: 我抓起屋角的水桶，拿起旁邊的拖把，前往有空調的三樓。接著我步入更涼快的男廁。消毒水的味道迫使我必須用嘴巴呼吸，不然我可能會當場昏倒。

en_text: “Hi there, Joe.”
I turn to see a man who is trying to hide his geekiness with a handful of hair gel and a half-grown mustache. “Morning, Ofﬁcer Clyde,” I say, setting the bucket on the ﬂoor.
zh_text: 我轉過身去看見一個試圖用一堆髮膠和稀疏的小鬍子隱藏滿身宅男氣息的男人。「早安，克萊德警員。」我說著將水桶放在地板上。

en_text: “Beautiful morning, Joe, ain’t it?”
zh_text: 「美麗的早晨，喬，是不是？」

en_text: “Sure is, Ofﬁcer Clyde,” I answer, agreeing with his outstanding perception and thinking he’d get on well with Bus Driver Stanley. I stare at the wall, trying not to glimpse his small dick as he ﬁnishes taking his long leak. He bends his knees as he zips up, as if he needs all the momentum he can muster to close his ﬂy. He doesn’t wash his hands.
zh_text: 當然，克萊德警員。我回答，認同他驚人的觀察力。事實上，不光只是個美麗的早晨——這一整個禮拜都很美麗。我凝視牆壁，努力不在他尿完長長的一泡尿時瞄到他的小老二。他彎腰拉上拉鍊，彷彿需要全身的力量才拉得起來一樣。他沒有洗手。

en_text: “Have a good day, Joe,” he says, pitying me with a smile.
zh_text: 祝你有個愉快的一天，喬。」他說，面露同情的微笑。

en_text: I start ﬁlling my bucket with water. “I’ll try.”
zh_text: 我開始在水桶中裝水。「我會努力。」

en_text: He winks at me and at the same time uses his ﬁngers to imitate a gun, and then shoots me while clicking his tongue as he leaves. The bucket full, the cleaner added, I throw the mop back and forth across the toilet ﬂoor. The linoleum soon glistens and becomes a health hazard. I set a plastic sign on the ﬂoor that has the word Caution, states that the ﬂoor is wet, and has a picture of a red stick ﬁgure slipping, about to crack open his perfectly round stick-ﬁgure head.
zh_text: 他向我眨眼，離開的同時用手指比成手槍，嘴裡喀地一聲朝我開了一槍。水桶滿了，清潔劑加了，我拿拖把在廁所地板上甩來甩去。地板很快就閃閃發光，變成容易摔跤的危險地帶。我在地上擺了個寫著「小心」的塑膠牌，表示地板是濕的，還外帶一張紅色竹竿人摔倒在地，即將摔破渾圓腦袋的貼紙。

en_text: I’ve been working here more than four years now. Before that, I was unemployed. I remember killing somebody, I can’t remember his name, but he was my ﬁrst. Well, kind of my ﬁrst—there was that one kid back in high school, but I don’t like to think about that one. This guy I do consider to be my ﬁrst was Don or Dan or somebody, I think. What’s in a name? I killed him when I was twenty-eight years old. It was a time in my life when the fantasy of wondering how it would feel blended with a desire that became a need to know. The fantasy wasn’t as good as the reality, and the reality was much messier, but it was an experience, and they say practice makes perfect. Ron or Jim or Don or whoever must have been somebody important because two months after they found his body, a ﬁfty-thousanddollar reward was posted. I’d only found a few hundred dollars in his wallet when I killed him, so I felt cheated. Like God or fate was mocking me.
zh_text: 我已經在這裡工作超過四年了。那之前，我沒有工作。我記得殺過某人，不記得叫什麼名字，只知道他是我殺的第一個人。唐恩還是丹恩還是什麼的，我想。名字代表什麼意義？我是在二十八歲的時候殺死他的。那是我生命中將融入慾望的好奇心轉變爲需求的幻想年代。幻想沒有現實美好，而現實很難收拾殘局，不過那是一段經驗，而有人說熟能生巧。隆恩或吉姆或唐恩還是誰的必定是個重要人物，因為發現屍體兩個月後，警方發佈了五萬元的懸賞。殺他時，我只在他的皮夾裡找到幾百塊錢，所以我覺得自己被唬弄了，好像上帝還是命運在嘲笑我一樣。

en_text: I began getting nervous. Agitated. I needed to know if the police were close to catching me. I couldn’t help it, the desire to see where the investigation was kept me without sleep for those two months. I could feel myself cracking up. Every morning I would wake up and stare out at my shitty view, wondering if this was the last time I’d get to see it. I started drinking. I ate badly. I became such a desperate wreck that I did the boldest thing I’ve ever done: I came down to the police station to “confess.”
zh_text: 我開始緊張，不安。我需要知道警方是不是快要抓到我了。我無法克制，那兩個月裡想要得知調查進度的渴望令我輾轉難眠。我覺得自己快崩潰了。每天早上我都會望著窗外髒亂的街景，懷疑這是否就是我最後一次看它。我開始酗酒，食慾不振。我沮喪絕望到了極點，終於做出了這輩子最勇敢的舉動：我前往警局「自首」。

en_text: Detective Inspector Schroder dealt with me. It was the ﬁrst time I met him, and within seconds I wasn’t scared because I was too smart to be scared, and much smarter than any cop. I had left no evidence—burning the body had destroyed any DNA I had left behind, and dumping the burned carcass into a river washed away whatever was left. I was pretty conﬁdent I knew what I was doing. Would I do it again? Deﬁnitely not.
zh_text: 施羅德督察負責偵訊我。我毫不恐懼，因為我聰明到不會感到恐懼，比任何警察聰明許多。我沒有留下證據，焚燒屍體摧毀了我所有的DNA，將焦屍棄置河中洗淨了其他證據。我深信自己知道自己在做什麼。我會再犯嗎？肯定不會。

en_text: Two of them sat me inside a small interrogation room. The room had four concrete walls and no view and smelled of chewing gum and sweat. In the center were a wooden table and a couple of chairs. There were no potted plants. No paintings. Just a mirror. The legs on the front of my chair were slightly shorter, and I kept sliding forward, which was pretty uncomfortable. A tape recorder sat on top of the table. I clean that room once a week now.
zh_text: 兩名警察叫我坐在一間小偵訊室裡。那個房間有四面石牆，沒有窗戶。房間中央有張木桌以及兩張椅子。沒有盆栽，沒有畫像，只有一面鏡子。我的椅子的前椅腳比較短，導致我一直向前滑動，說實在的不太舒服。桌上擺了一台錄音機。如今我每個禮拜清理那房間一次。

en_text: I started off by saying I’d like to confess to the murder of that woman who was killed a few months back.
zh_text: 我一開口就說我坦承犯下幾個月前的那件女子謀殺案。

en_text: What woman, sir?
zh_text: 「什麼女子，先生？」

en_text: You know. The dead one with the reward.
zh_text: 「你知道。有懸賞的那個。」

en_text: That was a man, sir.
zh_text: 「那是個男人，先生。」

en_text: Yeah, I killed him. Can I have my money now?
zh_text: 「是啊，我殺了他。現在可以給我賞金了嗎？」

en_text: It wasn’t hard for them to doubt my story, and when I pushed for the reward, saying I had earned it by killing him, and then used the word outside to describe where I had stabbed my victim, my Slow Joe act was cemented. As I turned from Hannibal Lecter to Forrest Gump in a matter of seconds, I learned the police had no suspects at all. I didn’t get any reward, but I was given coffee and a sandwich. That night when I got home, I slept like a rock. The following day I felt like a new man. I felt fantastic. When I came back to “confess” again, this time to a murder I knew nothing about, they took pity on me. I was a nice guy—they could see that; I was merely looking for attention in the wrong places. When one of their cleaners “happened” to disappear, I applied for and was given this job. Because of government regulations in a world trying to be as politically correct as possible, departments all over the country have a quota to ﬁll when it comes to hiring people who are fucked either physically or mentally. The police seemed happy to hire me since they ﬁgured a cleaner didn’t need to know much more than how to run a vacuum cleaner and dunk a mop in water. It was either me, or go through the employment lottery where they’d have to choose some other disabled guy.
zh_text: 要讓他們懷疑我的說詞並不困難，而當我要求懸賞，宣稱那是我殺他所應得的獎金，跟著又用「室外」來描述我殺害被害人的地點時，我就已經演活了「智障喬」的角色。當我在轉眼之間從漢尼拔·萊克特轉變成佛勒斯·甘時，我得知警方完全沒有掌握任何嫌犯。我沒有收到任何賞金，不過得到了一杯咖啡和三明治。那天晚上回家後，我睡得跟豬一樣熟。第二天我彷彿重獲新生。我覺得棒透了。當我再度回去自首，坦承犯下一件我一無所知的謀殺案時，他們開始同情我。我是個好人，他們看得出來，我只是試圖在錯誤的地點引人注目。當他們的一名清潔工「剛好」失蹤時，我申請職缺，獲得這個工作。根據這個盡可能達到政治正確的政府規定，全國所有部門都必須雇用一定配額的身心障礙人士。警方似乎很高興能雇用我，因為他們認爲清潔工只需要知道如何使用吸塵器並且將拖把放入水桶中就夠了。要嘛就是用我，不然就是去找就業中心挑選其他殘障人士。

en_text: So now I’m the harmless guy who waltzes up their hallways with brooms and mops, a minimum-wage lackey. But at least the sleepless nights are a thing of the past.
zh_text: 於是我變成了拿著掃把和拖把大搖大擺來去警局的無害人士，以最低薪資雇用的僕少少失眠夜已成過往雲煙。

en_text: It generally takes me an hour to clean the toilets. Today is no different. When I ﬁnish I go through to the women’s toilets and do the same, hanging a sign on the door ﬁrst to say that cleaning is in progress. Women never come in here while I’m cleaning. Maybe they think the red stick ﬁgure they see on the sign is a pervert. When I’m done I empty the contents of the bucket, then store it and the mop back in my ofﬁce. I grab a broom and slide it back and forth down the corridors and around the cubicles, heading toward the conference room. When I get inside I don’t need to make myself invisible because I’m the only one in here. The day’s work has begun. Leads have been found. Evidence to follow. Prayers go unanswered.
zh_text: 我通常要花一個小時清理廁所。今天沒有什麼不同。清理完畢後，我前往女廁，重複同樣的動作，先在門口掛上一個清理中的牌子。女人從來不曾在我打掃的時候進來。或許她們認爲牌子上的紅色竹竿人是個變態。清理好後，我把水桶中的污水倒掉，然後將水桶和拖把回我的辦公室。我拿根掃把，在走廊和小隔間外東掃西掃，朝向會議室前進。掃進去後，我不用刻意降低存在感，因爲裡面空無一人。一天的工作已經開始，線索找到了，證據出現了，可惜祈禱還是沒有獲得回應就是了。

en_text: I lean my broom against the door. The conference room is pretty big. To my right, a window the width of the room overlooks the city. To my left, a matching window looks into the fourth ﬂoor. At the moment the view is only of thin, gray, venetian blinds, which have been pulled closed. In the center sits a long rectangular table with several seats around it. In the past this room has been used to interview suspects because it looks intimidating. What happens is hundreds of photographs are hung up, stacks of paper are piled against the walls, and ofﬁcers walk past the window carrying ﬁles before popping in to whisper something to the detective doing the interview. The murder weapon is nearby so the killer gets a good look at it, and he soon feels they have more than enough information on him. He cracks under the pressure. In the corner, alongside the window, is a huge potted plant. I take special care when watering it.
zh_text: 我將掃把靠在門上。會議室很大。右手邊，一扇跟會議室同長的窗戶可以俯瞰外面的城市。左手邊，同樣的窗戶可以看見三樓的情況。此時薄薄的灰色活動百葉窗是拉下來的，所以看不見外面。會議室中央有張矩形長桌，周圍擺了幾張椅子。過去這個房間是用來偵訊嫌犯的，因為它給人一股壓迫感。他們會在牆上貼個幾百張照片，地上堆著幾疊文件，讓員警拿著檔案路過窗外，然後跑進來在負責偵訊的警探耳邊輕輕說幾句話。兇器就擺在旁邊讓兇手看，要不了多久他就會以為警方已經掌握足夠的證據，於是在壓力下崩潰。房間角落，窗戶旁邊，擺著一盆盆栽。我澆水的時候都會特別照料它。

en_text: I step up to the wall of photographs—pictures of victims and crime scenes have been pinned to a long corkboard. Pictures of the latest victims, Angela Durry and Martha Harris, are up there, making a total of seven bodies over the last thirty weeks. Seven unsolved murders. It only took two for the police to make the connection, even with the different MO. Modus operandi. An MO is what’s similar about the way two or more crimes are committed—the same gun, the method of breaking in, the way he confronts his victim. This is different from a signature. A signature is what a killer needs to do for fulﬁllment—he may need to masturbate over the body, or follow a script, or force his victim to participate. An MO is upgradable. The ﬁrst time I broke into a house I smashed a window. Then I learned if you put duct tape over the glass, it doesn’t shatter and make as much noise. Then I learned how to pick locks.
zh_text: 我走到照片牆前——被害人和犯罪現場的照片被釘在一張軟木板上。最新的被害人，安琪拉·杜利和瑪莎·哈里斯的照片被釘在上面，讓過去三十週內的屍體總數增加到七具。七件尚未偵破的謀殺案。只需要兩件就足以讓警方聯想在一起了，即使MO（Modus Operandi）不同也一樣。MO就是慣用的犯案手法，也就是指不同的案件中類似的部分——同樣的槍、闖入的方式、攻擊受害人的手段。這跟簽名特徵（Signature Aspect）不同。簽名特徵是兇手爲了滿足自我而非做不可的行爲——他可能需要在屍體上自慰、或是按照劇本演出、或是強迫被害人參與演出。犯案手法是可以升級的。第一次闖入民宅時，我打破了一扇窗戶。後來我發現只要在玻璃上貼膠帶，它就不會弄得滿地碎片，也不會發出那麼大的聲響。然後我學會開鎖

en_text: A signature isn’t upgradable. A signature is the whole point of the murder. It’s the gratiﬁcation. I don’t have one because I’m not like those sick perverted bastards who go around killing women out of a sexual need. I do it for fun. And that’s a big difference.
zh_text: 簽名特徵乃是殺人的根本意義，無法升級。它能讓兇手感到滿足。我沒有簽名特徵，因為我跟那些爲了滿足性慾而四處殘殺女人的變態不一樣。我殺人是爲了好玩，這可是很大的不同。

en_text: Of the seven unsolved murders, only six are mine. The seventh has been tacked onto my lot because the police are inept. It’s strange how things in this world have a way of balancing themselves out; one woman I killed has never shown up. And where is she?
zh_text: 這七件尚未偵破的謀殺案裡，只有六件是我幹的。第七件會被賴到我的頭上都是因爲警方無能。有趣的是，這個世界就是有辦法自行取得平衡；有一個死在我手上的女人一直沒有出現。那麼她在哪裡呢？

en_text: Long-term parking. I dumped her body inside the trunk of her car, drove into town, grabbed a ticket for a parking building, and left the car on the top ﬂoor. It’s very rare that the building is so full that cars reach the top ﬂoor. I wrapped her body in plastic, ﬁguring it would stop the smell for maybe a day or two. Three, if I was lucky. If I was really lucky, nobody would go up there for maybe a week.
zh_text: 長期停車場。我將她的屍體丟入她自己汽車的行李廂，開進城裡，拿了一張立體停車場的票卡，把車留在頂樓。那座立體停車場很少有車多到要停到頂樓的狀況。我把她的屍體包在塑膠袋裡，想說這樣可以隔絕屍臭一到兩天。幸運的話，三天。真的非常幸運的話，或許一個禮拜都不會有人上去。

en_text: She was the second of my seven, and she’s still there now, with the wind gusting through the exposed top ﬂoor and dissipating the scent. The chances are high that nobody has even been up there.
zh_text: 她是我七名受害者中的第一名，而她至今依然待在那裡，因爲頂樓開放式的強風吹散了屍臭，而且很有可能根本沒有人跑上去過。

en_text: I would never have thought to look in the trunk, Detective Schroder.
zh_text: 我絕對不會去查後車廂，施羅德警探。

en_text: I still have the ticket as a memento. It’s hidden beneath my mattress at home.
zh_text: 我還保留那張停車票卡作爲紀念，它就收藏在我家的床墊底下。

en_text: When I ﬁrst started out it seemed to me that dumping the body was the way to go. That quickly evolved, though, because in all the other cases somebody ended up ﬁnding them anyway, and the ﬁrst place the cops went after identifying them was to their houses. All I was doing was putting myself to extra work. Well, live and learn, I guess. I decided to start leaving them in their homes.
zh_text: 一開始殺人的時候，我原以爲棄屍才是正確的作法。不過這一點很快就進化了，因爲在所有其他的案例裡，屍體最後總是會被找到的，而警察在辨識出身分後第一個前往的地方就是他們家。所以棄屍對我而言只是在做白工而已。好吧，活到老學到老，我想。我決定把她們留在家裡就好了。

en_text: The woman in long-term parking isn’t among the faces looking at me. Instead a stranger looks out from the lineup. Number four in the allotted seven. I know her name and I know her face, but until her picture was pinned up I’d never seen her before. She has been up there for six weeks now, and every day I pause to look at her features. Daniela Walker. Blond. Pretty. My type of woman—but not this time. Even in death her eyes sparkle out from her corpse like soft emeralds. She has both a pre- and postdeath photograph. At ﬁrst Detective Inspector Schroder didn’t want me coming in here because of these pictures. Either he simply forgot after a while, or he just doesn’t care.
zh_text: 待在長期停車場裡的女人不在此刻盯著我看的這些面孔之中，不過有個陌生人的照片釘在牆上看著我，七名被害人中的第四號。我知道她的名字，也知道她的長相，但是在她的照片被釘上牆壁之前，我從來沒有見過她。她已經待在牆上六個禮拜了，每天我都會停下來看看她的臉。丹妮耶拉·沃克。金髮。美女。我喜歡的類型——但是這個不算。即使已經身亡，她的雙眼在屍體上依然綻放如同綠寶石般的神采。牆上貼有死前和死後的照片。剛開始，施羅德督察因為這些照片的關係不希望我進入會議室。後來不知道他是忘了這件事，還是不在乎了。

en_text: The picture of Daniela Walker in life shows her as a happy thirtysomething, two or maybe three years before her death. Her hair shimmers over her shoulder as she turns toward the camera. Her lips are parting in a smile. Her picture has been on my mind every day since it has been up here. And why?
zh_text: 丹妮耶拉·沃克生前的照片顯示她是名開朗的三十來歲女子，死前兩三年拍的。她身體傾向相機，亮麗的秀髮披在肩上，雙唇敞開，面露微笑。自從出現在牆上後，她的照片就在我腦海中揮之不去。爲什麼？

en_text: Because whoever killed her pinned her murder on me. Whoever killed her was too scared to take the credit, so rather than try and get away with it in his own clever fashion, he gets away with it by using me. All without my permission!
zh_text: 因為殺她的人把案子嫁禍給我。殺他的人沒有膽量居功，不願意憑藉自己的力量逃過法律制裁，而是利用我來置身事外。這樣做竟然也不先問過我一聲！

en_text: I keep looking at her picture. One in life. One in death. Green eyes sparkling in each.
zh_text: 我一直看著她的照片。一張生前，一張死後。兩張裡的綠眼睛都炯炯有神。

en_text:
For the last six weeks I’ve thought of little other than ﬁnding the man who did this to us. Can it be that difﬁcult? I have the resources. I’m smarter than anybody else in this department, and that’s not just my ego talking. I scroll my eyes over the victims. Look at them closely. Fourteen eyes staring at me. Watching. Seven pairs. Familiar faces.
Bar one.
zh_text:
過去六週裡，我一心只想找出對我做出這種事的人。這會很難嗎？我掌握了辦案資源。我比這個部門裡的所有人都來得聰明，而這樣說絕非出於自負。我目光在所有被害人臉上掃視。仔細打量她們。十四隻眼睛盯著我瞧，七雙眼睛，熟悉的面孔。
除了其中之一。

en_text: A ring of deep bruises form a necklace around Daniela Walker’s throat from strangulation. They aren’t consistent—ruling out a scarf or a rope— and look like they were formed by knuckles. More pressure can be applied with knuckles than ﬁngers. It’s also harder to defend against. The problem with strangulation is it takes four to six minutes to complete. Sure, they give up struggling within the ﬁrst, but the pressure needs to be kept on for at least another three to starve the body of oxygen. That’s three minutes I could be using for something better. Using knuckles increases the chances of crushing the victim’s windpipe.
zh_text: 丹妮耶拉·沃克的頸部有一圈如同項鍊般的勒傷瘀痕。瘀痕粗窄不一——排除圍巾或是繩索的可能——看起來像是由指節造成的。指節能夠產生比手指更大的力道。而且更難抵禦。不過勒殺的問題在於需要四到六分鐘才能完事。當然，她們會在一分鐘內停止掙扎，但是必須持續施壓至少三分鐘才能阻隔氣氣供應。我可以拿那三分鐘去做更好玩的事情。用指節還會提高壓碎被害人氣管的機會。

en_text: Beneath the corkboard is a set of shelves, and on top of these are seven piles of folders—one per victim. I head over to them. It’s like looking at a menu and already knowing in advance which item to choose. I walk to the fourth pile and pick up one of the folders from the top. Every detective on the case has one of these folders and the spares are here for anybody who becomes assigned. Like me.
zh_text: 軟木板下有一個架子，最頂層放了七疊檔案夾——一名被害人一疊。我走向它們。那感覺像是看著一份早就知道要點什麼的菜單。我來到第四疊檔案夾前，拿起最上面的檔案。偵查此案的所有警探都有一份這種檔案夾，剩下的則是讓其他參與辦案的人拿去看的。就像我。

en_text: I unzip the front of my overalls, stuff it down my front, then zip them up again. Back to the wall of the dead. I smile at the latest two. This is their ﬁrst morning here in the assembly. No doubt they were pinned up last night. They don’t smile back. Angela Durry. Thirty-nine-year-old legal executive. She suffocated on an egg. Martha Harris. Seventy-two-year-old widow. I’d needed a car. She had caught me taking hers.
zh_text: 我拉下工作服的拉鍊，將檔案夾塞入其中，然後拉回拉鍊。回到死者之牆。我向最後兩名死者微笑。這是她們加入這個聚會的第一個早晨。她們沒有回應我的微笑。安琪拉·杜利。三十九歲的法律行政員。她被雞蛋噎死。瑪莎·哈里斯。七十二歲老寡婦。我需要弄輛車，她抓到我在偷她的車。

en_text: I take my spray bottle and rags and move to the window. I spend ﬁve minutes cleaning it, staring beyond the streaks and my reﬂection at the world outside to the little people walking among the little streets. I spend some quality time with the plant. I replace the microcassette tape from the audio recorder I have hidden in there, careful to touch the recorder only with the rags. I tuck the tape into my pocket. I still have a job to do, and I head back to my ofﬁce to grab the vacuum cleaner, then return and use it to clean up.
zh_text: 我拿出清潔噴霧劑和抹布走到窗戶前，花了五分鐘的時間清理它，同時透過窗葉和我的倒影凝視著外面的世界。我還有工作要做。我清理了大會議桌，然後走回我的辦公室拿吸塵器，跟盆栽相處了一段時間。我更換了藏在這裡的錄音機裡的微型錄音帶，隨時注意只讓抹布碰到錄音機，然後將錄音帶塞入口袋。

en_text: Ten minutes later I leave the conference room as I found it—only tidier and without as many ﬁles. I wheel the vacuum cleaner into the supply room on the other side of the ﬂoor and start vacuuming. Nobody is around so I do the Boy Scout thing and stock up on a few more pairs of gloves— not that I’ll be killing anybody tonight. I don’t suffer from compulsions to kill all the time. I’m no animal. I don’t go running around venting childhood aggressions while looking for excuses to kill. I’m not itching to make a name for myself or gain the notoriety of Ted Bundy or Jeffrey Dahmer. Bundy was a freak who had a following of groupies during and after his trial, and he even got married after he was sentenced to death. He was a loser who killed more than thirty women, but he got caught. I don’t want fame. I don’t want to be married. If I wanted fame, I would kill somebody famous—like that Chapman chap who loved John Lennon so much he shot him. I’m just a regular guy. An average Joe. With a hobby. I’m not a psychopath. I don’t hear voices. I don’t kill for God or Satan or the neighbor’s dog. I’m not even religious. I kill for me. It’s that simple. I like women, and I like to do things to them they won’t let me do. There have to be maybe two or three billion women in this world. Killing one every month or two isn’t a big deal. It’s all about perspective. I grab some other stuff. Nothing major. Gear ofﬁcers are always taking.
zh_text: 離開的時候，會議室就跟我來時一模一樣——不過比較乾淨，也沒有原先那麼多檔案。我將吸塵器推到這層樓另外一端的庫房去，然後開始吸塵。附近沒人，所以我搞起童子軍那一套，偷拿了幾副手套——倒不是說我今晚還要殺人。我沒有隨時都想殺人的衝動。我不是禽獸。我不會一邊編造殺戮的藉口，一邊又四下發洩童年的憤恨。我不渴望建立自己的名聲，變得像泰德·邦迪或是傑弗瑞·達默那樣惡名昭彰。邦迪是個怪物，在審訊期間和之後都有無數少女爲他痴狂，甚至在獲判死刑後還有人要跟他結婚。他是個殺了超過三十個女人的敗類，但是他被抓了。我不想要成名。我不想要結婚。如果想成名，我會找個名人來殺——就像那個查普曼，喜愛約翰·藍儂到一槍斃了他的地步。我只是個普通人。平凡的傢伙。有點小嗜好。我不是反社會份子。我不會聽見腦中的聲音。我不會爲了上帝或撒旦或是鄰居的狗而殺人。我甚至不信教。我殺人完全爲了自己。就是這麼簡單。我喜歡女人，我喜歡對她們做些她們不讓我做的事情。世界上起碼有二、三十億個女人。一個月殺一個並不是什麼大不了的事。一切只是看待事物的觀點不同。

en_text: Nothing anybody will notice gone. Nobody notices anything around here. The supply room is good like that. It supplies. No reason for it not to supply me. I look at my watch. Twelve o’clock—lunchtime. I head back to my ofﬁce. The tools and the cords and the paint—this gear I don’t get to use. All I do is clean. Everybody here thinks I have the IQ of a watermelon. But that’s okay. In fact, it’s perfect.
zh_text: 我拿了些沒什麼重要的、其他警員時常在拿的東西。不會有人注意到不見的東西。這裡沒人注意到任何事情。庫房就是有這個好處。提供東西給大家使用。它沒有理由不提供東西給我用。我看了看手錶。十二點——午餐時間。我走回我的辦公室。那些工具、繩子、油漆——都不是我該用的東西。我在這裡只是打掃而已。這裡的人通通認定我的智商跟顆西瓜一樣。不過沒關係。事實上，這樣太完美了。

en_text: My chair is uncomfortable and my lunch isn’t that great. With several nice sights out the window, I lean over and look at the women out there as prospective lovers. Should I go down there? Find where one works? Where she lives? Then, one night, ﬁnd her in between those two places?
zh_text: 我的椅子不舒服，午餐也不好吃。由於在窗外路過幾個好貨色，我乾脆湊到窗口如同欣賞未來女友般打量那些女人。我應該下樓去嗎？查查看美女在哪兒工作？住在哪裡？然後，某天夜晚，在這兩地之間與她巧遇？

en_text: Men and women are walking back and forth, treating the warm afternoon street like a singles bar. Women dress like whores and take offense when men stare at them. Men dress like pimps and take offense when nobody notices. I use the two-inch knife to cut into my apple, small drops of juice spraying out. I slice it into sections. I’m chewing them while picking a target. My mouth waters before taking each bite.
zh_text: 男男女女來來往往，彷彿把溫暖的午後街道當成單身酒吧一樣。女人打扮得跟妓女一樣，還不爽男人盯著她們看。男人則打扮得像是皮條客，還不爽沒人盯著他們看。我用五公分的小刀來切蘋果。將它切成一塊一塊的。我一邊吃蘋果，一邊挑選目標。蘋果很多汁。我每咬一口嘴裡都會冒出口水。

en_text: Of course, I can’t go down there. I have other things to do now, a new hobby. What sort of guy would I be if I picked up a new hobby and dumped it after only an hour? I’d be a loser. The sort of guy who can’t ﬁnish what he starts. And that’s not me. I didn’t get to where I am by never ﬁnishing anything.
zh_text: 當然，我不能下去。我現在有其他事情要做：一個新嗜好。如果染上了一個新嗜好，又在一個小時後就放棄的話，我還算是什麼男人？我會是個失敗者。就是那種沒辦法完成自己起頭之事的人。而我不是那種人。要是從未做完任何事情，我絕對不能走到今天這個地步。

en_text: My thoughts are interrupted by a knock on my door. Nobody ever comes here while I’m eating lunch, and for the briefest of moments I’m sure the police are going to burst in and arrest me. I start to reach for my briefcase. A moment later the door swings open and Sally is standing there, making me think I need to put a lock on that door.
zh_text: 一陣敲門聲打斷了我的思緒。從來沒人在我吃午飯的時候跑來，一時之間，我幾乎肯定是警方要闖進來逮捕我。我伸手去拿我的公事包。片刻過後，門打開了，莎莉站在門口。

en_text: “Hi, Joe.”
I lean back. “Hi, Sally.”
zh_text: 我向後靠。「嗨，莎莉。」

en_text: “How’s the apple? Is it nice?”
zh_text: 「蘋果如何？好吃嗎？」

en_text: “It’s nice,” I say, though I’m quickly losing my appetite now. I jam a slice of it in my mouth so I don’t have to make more conversation. What in the hell could she want?
zh_text: 好吃。」我說，然後立刻塞一塊到嘴裡，爲了不必繼續廢話。她到底想幹什麼？「我幫你做了鮪魚三明治。」她關上房門，走向我的工作台。

en_text: “I made you a tuna sandwich,” she says, closing the door behind her and heading over to my bench. My ofﬁce has only one seat and I’m in it. I don’t offer it to her because I don’t want her to stay. I take the tuna sandwich from her and smile at her, showing my fake gratitude along with a mouthful of apple. She offers me the kind of smile that suggests she would sleep with me if only, please God, if only he would ask. But I’m not going to ask. Her tuna sandwiches are always pretty good, but not that good. I swallow my piece of apple and take a huge bite of tuna and bread.
zh_text: 我的辦公室裡只有一張椅子，而我正坐在上面。我沒起身讓她坐，因為我不想要她待在這裡。我接下她的鮪魚三明治，然後向她微笑，透過滿嘴蘋果表達感激之情。她露出一種拜託老天只要我開口，她就願意跟我睡覺的微笑。但是我並不打算開口要求。她的鮪魚三明治一向很好吃，但還沒有好吃到那種地步。我嚥下我的蘋果，咬了一大口鮪魚和麵包。

en_text: “Yummy,” I say, making an effort to have crumbs spill from my mouth. Just because Sally is an idiot doesn’t mean I can drop the Slow Joe act around her. I can never, never let anybody—not even Fat Sally—get an idea just how intelligent I really am.
zh_text: 「好吃。」我說，刻意讓麵包屑滑落嘴角。儘管莎莉比胡蘿蔔還蠢（我猜她的午餐都是她媽做的），在她面前我還是得扮演智障喬。我絕對、絕對不能讓任何人，就算是個白痴，發現我到底有多聰明。

en_text: Sally leans against the bench and looks down at me as she takes a bite out of an identical sandwich. I guess that means she’s planning on hanging out here for a bit. She keeps smiling at me as she chews. Crumbs don’t fall out of her mouth, but if they did it might help her lose a bit of weight. I can’t remember ever seeing her without that stupid grin on her face. She talks to me as I eat my lunch. Tells me stuff about her mom and dad, about her brother. She tells me it’s his birthday today, but I don’t bother asking how old he is. She tells me anyway.
zh_text: 莎莉靠在工作台上，一邊吃著同樣的三明治，一邊低頭看我。我猜這表示她打算在這裡多待一會兒。她吃東西的時候一直對我微笑。我不記得曾經見過她臉上沒有那個愚蠢笑容的模樣。她趁我吃飯的時候跟我說話。告訴我她父母的事情，還有她弟弟。她告訴我今天是她生日，我沒費心問她今年幾歲，但她還是告訴我了。

en_text: “Twenty-one.”
zh_text: 二十一歲。

en_text: “You doing anything to celebrate?” I ask, since it’s expected of me.
zh_text: 「你們有慶祝嗎？」我問，因為這時候就該這麼問。

en_text: She starts to say something, then pauses, and I realize she’s going through one of her simple/special people routines where she has to think things through, starting with whether or not she even has a brother, and if he really is twenty-one today. Women may be from Venus, but nobody knows where the hell people like Sally come from.
zh_text: 她張口欲言，但卻沒說出口，我立刻知道她又進入了那種單純／特殊人物的恍神境界，必須把事情從頭到尾想過一遍，從她到底有沒有弟弟，以及今天是不是真的二十一歲開始想起。女人或許來自金星，但是沒人知道莎莉這種人是打哪兒來的。

en_text: “We’re just having a simple thing at home,” she says, sounding sad, and I guess I’d be sounding sad too if I had to have a simple family celebration at home. She reaches for the cruciﬁx hanging from her neck. I’ve always found it ironic that retarded people can not only believe in God, but think He’s a pretty good guy. The cruciﬁx has one of those bulky soldered-on metal ﬁgures of Jesus, and this Jesus looks to be in pain—not because he’s been cruciﬁed, but because his head is permanently cast downward forcing him to look down Sally’s top.
zh_text: 「家裡有個小活動。」她說，聽起來有點悲哀，而我想如果是我要在家裡舉辦個簡單的小活動的話也會有點悲哀。她伸手去摸掛在脖子上的十字架。我總是覺得智障的人不但願意相信上帝，同時還認定祂是個好神是件十分諷刺的事情。十字架上焊著一個大大的金屬耶穌像，而這個耶穌看來十分痛苦，不光只是因為他被釘在十字架上，同時也因為他被迫必須永遠低頭面對莎莉的胸部。

en_text: I can feel the minutes slipping away. The ﬁle is still in my overalls. I want Sally to leave me alone, but I don’t know how to say it. I start on the second sandwich she gave me. She tries to include me in her conversation by asking about my own family. I don’t have anything to offer on that subject, other than my mother is nuts and my dad is dead, and that neither of those things is ever going to change, so I keep it to myself. Then she asks how my day has been going, how yesterday went, how tomorrow is going to be. It’s as bad as talking about the weather—it’s all conversational ﬁller I couldn’t be any less interested in.
zh_text: 我感覺時間一分一秒流逝。檔案夾還在我的褲襠裡。我想要莎莉別來煩我，但是我不知道該怎麼說。我開始吃她給我的第二個三明治。她問起我的家人，試圖讓我加入這段談話。然而除了我媽瘋了，我爸死了，而且這兩點都不可能改變之外，這個話題我沒什麼可說的，於是我什麼也沒說。接著她問起我今天過得好不好，昨天過得怎麼樣，明天又會如何。這感覺就跟聊天氣一樣糟糕——全部都是我完全不感興趣的廢話。

en_text: After twenty minutes of chewing really slowly and nodding at the same pace, of having my stomach itch from the edges of the ﬁle, Sally ﬁnally straightens up and leaves, throwing a Be seeing you soon at me on the way out the door. As soon as she is gone, I pull the ﬁle from my overalls and lay it on the bench. I never used to be nervous with what I brought in here to look through, but now I am. Sally could come back in, but I ﬁgure she wouldn’t understand what she was looking at, so it’s safe for me to carry on.
zh_text: 經歷二十分鐘細嚼慢嚥和以同樣步調的點頭，加上肚子讓檔案夾的角角搔得超癢之後，莎莉終於起身離開，在出門的同時丟了句「晚點見」給我。她前腳剛跨出去，我立刻從褲襠裡取出檔案夾，放在工作台上。我從來不會對拿進來看的東西感到緊張，但是這下我開始緊張了。莎莉有可能回來，不過我認爲她看不懂這是什麼，所以我可以安安穩穩地繼續看下去。

en_text: Carefully, like an archaeologist opening a just-uncovered gospel, I open the cover. The ﬁrst thing I see is Daniela Walker. She looks up at me with eyes open and neck bruised. I pull the photo out and lay it faceup on my bench.
zh_text: 我小心翼翼地開啓檔案夾，如同考古學家翻開一本剛剛出土的福音書般。首先映入眼簾的就是丹妮耶拉·沃克。她帶著瘀青的脖子瞪大雙眼看著我。我拿出照片，正面朝上放在我的工作台上。這是九張照片中的一張。並非所有照片全部是她，不過大部分都是。

en_text: It’s only one in a series of ten. Not all of them are of her, though most are. I lay them side by side in a row like I’m playing some freak game of solitaire with creepy playing cards. She looks at me from four of the photographs, and in the progression it seems her skin gets grayer. Time codes on the pictures suggest they were taken over the course of an hour, so she may well have been changing color. In fact, in the last picture, her twinkling green eyes no longer twinkle. They have taken on the texture of spoiled plums. The other six photographs are of the bedroom from varying angles.
zh_text: 我將照片排成一排，彷彿在拿令人戰慄的撲克牌玩某種奇怪的接龍牌戲般。她自四張照片中看著我，依照時間順序來看，她的皮膚似乎越來越灰。照片上的時間顯示這些照片都是在一個小時內拍攝的，所以她說不定真的在變色。事實上，在最後一張照片裡，她明亮的雙眸已經黯淡無光。它們已經變得像是兩顆熟透的梅子。其他六張照片則是各種角度的臥房照片。

en_text: According to notes in the ﬁle, another one hundred and twenty photographs were taken—quite the portfolio—and these pictures detail many of the items in the house, as well as the rooms. The catalog of those photographs is speciﬁc: door, stairs, bed, furniture, smudges on the handles. Anything and everything.
zh_text: 根據檔案中的筆記，另外還有一百二十張照片——鉅細靡遺——而那些照片記載了屋中的各式物品，還有其他房間的內部與外部照片。這些照片的目錄十分明確：門、樓梯、床、家具、門把上的污點。什麼東西都照。

en_text: I look hard at the pictures, but see nothing. So I look at them harder. I’m trying to imagine myself inside her house. It’s hard, because the pictures I have were all taken in the bedroom. The natural insight I was waiting to experience from my own experience doesn’t come along.
zh_text: 我仔細觀察那些照片，但是什麼都看不出來。於是我更仔細地再看一遍。我試圖想像自己站在她家。這不容易，因為我手頭上的照片都是臥房照。想要倚賴本身經驗靈光一現看出端倪並不是那麼容易的事情。

en_text: I glance through the report. She was found by her husband, her entire body draped by a sheet. Did her killer feel bad at what he’d done? Was covering her an act of decency?
zh_text: 我翻閱報告，發現屍體的是她丈夫，當時她全身都被包在一張床單下。殺手對於自己的作爲感到難過嗎？蓋上屍首是不是一種尊重死者的表現？

en_text: I read the toxicology report. It takes most of my lunch break to decipher that the ten-page report says only that I’ve just wasted my time, that there were no drugs in her system. Or any alcohol. Or any poisons.
zh_text: 我開始讀起驗毒報告。我花了整個午餐時間才搞清楚這份長達十頁的報告只是在浪費我的時間，她的身體裡沒有任何藥物。沒有酒精，也沒有毒素。

en_text: The postmortem is an even longer report, but less complicated. It makes for easy reading, and I know how it’s going to end even before I ﬁnish it. It reveals in an exceptionally unenthusiastic manner what Daniela went through, probably because the pathologist has seen it all before and has got bored with it. The report comes with pre-illustrated diagrams of the female body and its anatomy, and the pathologist has used these to point to where and what was damaged during her ordeal. There were no traces of semen. A condom was used. Her pubic hair had been combed and washed by the killer, removing any hair and skin cells he would have left behind. This isn’t something I’ve been doing, and I won’t do it now—even though it isn’t such a bad idea. It indicates her killer is far from crazy, and has an insight into police forensics.
zh_text: 驗屍報告更長，不過沒有那麼複雜。讀起來十分輕鬆，而且我還沒看完就知道結果。它以冷淡的語調描述丹妮耶拉所經歷的驗屍過程，或許是因為法醫早已見識過一切，所以覺得有點無聊。報告附了一張預先印好的女體解剖圖，法醫利用這張圖來解說她在案發過程中有哪些部位受到傷害。她身上沒有留下精液，對方有用保險套。兇手有梳洗過她的陰毛，清掉所有他所留下來的毛髮和皮膚細胞。我之前沒有做過這種事情，也不打算從現在開始——雖然這並不是個壞主意。這種情況表示殺害她的兇手一點也不瘋狂，而且熟知警方的驗屍程序。

en_text: There were extensive bruises in all the places where there ought to be bruises, and she suffered two cracked ribs. She was punched once in the eye and once in the mouth. There were other, older injuries there—some as recent as two months before she died. Injuries that had not been reported. Injuries, in the opinion of the pathologist, consistent with being beaten. So Daniela was used to what she was getting. Cause of death: strangulation.
zh_text: 所有該有瘀傷的地方都有大片瘀傷，她還被打斷了兩根肋骨。眼睛與嘴巴各挨了一拳，還有其他之前受的傷——比較新的約莫是死前兩個月留下的。根據法醫研判，那些都是被打出來的。所以丹妮耶拉早就被毆打慣了。死因：勒斃。

en_text: The rest of the postmortem is both standard and uninteresting. It’s like reading a mechanic’s report about ﬁxing a car. The body was fully dismantled and tested. The weight of the organs. The size of her brain. Detailed references to photographs taken during the autopsy take up two pages—photos of her hands, of her neck, of her feet. I don’t bother with any of this.
zh_text: 驗屍報告其他部分都是標準說詞，枯燥乏味。感覺像是閱讀技工的修車報告一樣。屍體被完全拆解，徹底檢測：器官的重量。腦袋的大小。驗屍期間照片的詳盡解說就佔了兩頁：雙手的照片、頸部的照片、腳掌的照片。我一張也沒去看。

en_text: DNA was found at the scene. No ﬁngerprints. The killer used latex gloves, like the type I wear. A residue from the gloves was left on the door handles from the tips of his ﬁngers. Also there was plenty of residue all over the victim. The only prints found were latent smears on her eyelids, but these were only partial and too badly damaged to be of any use. That’s the beauty about human skin—it’s one thing ﬁngerprints struggle to stick to. They did ﬁnd hair, though, in other places. And carpet ﬁbers. And shoe prints. So far they have narrowed them down only to the husband who found the body, and the ofﬁcers and detectives who worked the scene. It’s impossible to keep a crime scene free of any contamination. In order to do that, the room would need to be inside a large plastic bubble that nobody would ever be allowed to go inside to collect the pristine evidence.
zh_text: 沒有指紋。兇手使用乳膠手套，就像我用的那種。門把上找到指尖留下的手套殘餘物質。屍體全身上下也都有殘餘物質。兇手必定戴了兩層手套，因為就連一點指紋的輪廓都沒有留下。只有在眼瞼上採集到模糊的指紋，不過殘缺不全，難以辨識。這就是人類皮膚的美妙之處——指紋會努力黏在上面。不過他們倒是在其他地方找到毛髮。還有地毯纖維。還有鞋印。目前爲止，他們將這些證物排除到剩下找到屍體的死者丈夫，以及處理現場的警員和警探。想要犯罪現場完全不被外界污染是不可能的。要達成這個目的，犯罪現場必須被包在大型塑膠泡泡裡面，而且絕不允許任何人進去採證才行。

en_text: The police have their own DNA databases of their people who go to scenes. This way they eliminate evidence left by their own men and women. Next, they take blood from the victim’s family, friends, and neighbors, until they narrow the ﬁeld right down. Last night, I left plenty of evidence behind: saliva on the two bottles of beer, carpet ﬁbers, hair. But I have no criminal record. Nothing to match my name to these samples. So I’m a free man.
zh_text: 警方擁有所有前往犯罪現場人員的DZA資料庫。這樣他們就能排除自己人所留下的證據。接著，他們會找死者的家人、朋友、鄰居抽血，進一步縮小現場蒐證的範圍。昨晚，我留下了大量證據：兩瓶啤酒罐上的口水、地毯纖維、毛髮。但是我沒有犯罪紀錄。沒有東西符合那些樣本。所以我還是自由身。殺害丹妮耶拉的人可能有犯罪紀錄

en_text: Whoever killed Daniela may have a criminal record. The evidence I leave behind ties my killings together. I don’t know whose decision it was to include Walker among those women, but it was a bad one. Lunchtime is nearly over. I’m still hungry. No eggs today. I keep studying the autopsy report. Her ﬁngernails were clipped after death, so it seems she scratched her killer. I’ve been scratched several times, never in the face, though, and I don’t mind because that would be like a chef complaining about getting burned or a crash-test dummy complaining about being dumb—it comes with the job. I just never roll my sleeves up until those scratches are gone. I’ve never even thought about clipping their nails afterward to hide the evidence. Why would I cut the nails from this victim and wash her pubic hair, and not any of the others? How can the police really toss this death into the same mix?
zh_text: 我留在現場的證據將所有兇案串在一起。我不知道是誰決定要把丹妮耶拉算到我頭上的，但那真是個很爛的決定。吃完蘋果，沒有其他東西可吃了。今天沒蛋。午餐時間即將結束，不過我還有時間繼續研究驗屍報告。她的指甲死後讓人修剪過，所以她很可能有抓傷兇手。我被抓傷過好幾次，不過不曾傷到臉過。我不介意，因為這個工作就是如此。只是在傷痕癒合前，我不會捲起衣袖而已。我從沒想過要在完事後剪掉她們的指甲來湮滅證據。我有什麼理由剪掉這名死者的指甲、清理她的陰毛，卻沒有如法炮製其他死者？警方有什麼理由把這名死者賴在我的頭上？

en_text: I put the photographs and ﬁles into my briefcase, along with the microcassette tapes from the conference room, lock it, and leave it on the bench. I head up a ﬂoor, where there are more rooms and fewer people and no conference room. I repeat the same procedure up here with my mop and my vacuum cleaner. Say hello to everybody. Everyone smiles at me as if I’m their best friend.
zh_text: 我將照片和檔案放入公事包，還有從會議室裡拿來的微型錄音帶，鎖起來，然後把它留在工作台上。我前往四樓，這裡房間更多、人更少、沒有會議室。我用抹布和吸塵器重複之前的工作。向所有人打招呼。所有人彷彿都把我當作他們最好的好朋友般對我微笑。

en_text: I do my job and I do it well, and I ﬁnish it at four thirty, earlier than anybody else. This enables me to catch an earlier bus home. I say hello to those I pass on my way out, and they tell me to have a nice night. I tell them I intend to. Sally calls out a good-bye, but I pretend I can’t hear her.
zh_text: 我工作，工作得很勤奮，在四點半的時候完工，比其他人都早一點。這讓我可以搭乘早一點的公車回家。我在離開警局的時候向所有遇上的人招呼，他們都祝我有個愉快的夜晚。我告訴他們我會的。莎莉大聲道再見，不過我假裝沒有聽到。

en_text: Christchurch is buzzing with life. Trafﬁc blocks the roads. Pedestrians block the sidewalks. I walk among them and none of them knows who I am. They look at me and all they see is a man in overalls with a happy-golucky look about him. Their lives are in my hands, but I’m the only one who knows it. It’s both a lonely and a powerful feeling. A little bit of the day’s heat has ebbed away, but not much. There’s still going to be sun for a couple of more hours. I start to think about what I might want to do tonight. I reach the bus stop. I wait for only a few seconds with a bunch of nondescript people I could kill right now if I wanted to before the bus shows up. As usual, my briefcase is in my right hand, my ticket in my left. I hand it over. “Hi there, Joe.” She gives me a big smile.
zh_text: 基督城人潮洶湧。車輛阻塞馬路。行人阻塞人行道。我行走在人群中，沒人知道我是誰。他們看著我，只看到一個身穿工作服的男人。他們的命掌握在我手中，不過我是唯一知道此事之人。那是一種孤獨而又大權在握的感覺。還有幾個人也在等公車，單調乏味的人，喜歡的話我當場就可以殺掉他們。公車抵達時，我最後一個上車的。一如往常，我將公事包提在右手，車票握在左手。我遞出車票。「嗨，喬。」她對我露出燦爛的微笑。

en_text: “Hi, Miss Selena. How are you?”
zh_text: 「嗨，瑟蓮娜小姐。妳好嗎？」

en_text: “Very well, Joe,” she answers, punching my ticket. “Missed you yesterday, Joe.”
zh_text: 「我很好，喬。」她回答，剪了我的票。「你昨天沒搭上我的車，喬。」

en_text: I couldn’t exactly catch the bus to Angela’s house. “I was late, Miss Selena.”
zh_text: 搭這班車到不了安琪拉家。「我晚下班，瑟蓮娜小姐。」

en_text: She hands back my ticket. I study how she moves, how she sounds, the way her eyes look me up and down. She smells like soap and perfume and makes me think of other women I’ve been with. Her shoulder-length black hair is slightly damp, and I can only assume she has showered with seeing me in mind, and since I’m in the process of assuming that, I like to assume she was in pretty good spirits as she soaped herself down. All that assuming makes the front of my overalls go a little tight. Her olive skin gives her a slightly exotic look, and she talks with an accent that’s erotic. She has a nice tight body and ﬁrm skin. Her dark blue eyes look into mine, and they see me differently from how Mr. Stanley sees me. He sees a defunct personality caught inside a healthy body. Miss Selena sees me as a man who can satisfy her. Her ﬁngers deliberately brush against my hand. She wants me. Unfortunately, I like her too much as a bus driver to indulge her. Perhaps I’ll wait until she changes jobs.
zh_text: 她交還我的車票。我研究著她的動作、她的語調、她上下打量我的樣子。她身上有股肥皂和香水的味道，讓我想起其他跟我在一起過的女人。她披肩的黑髮有點潮濕，我只能假設她剛剛曾一邊想著我一邊淋浴。她橄欖色的皮膚憑添些許異國風味，而她說話的口音性感撩人。她身材很好，皮膚緊實。深藍色的眼珠凝望著我的雙眼，看我的目光和史丹利先生大不相同。他看到一個受困於健康肉體中的殘缺人格。瑟蓮娜小姐眼中的我卻是一個能夠滿足她的男人。她的手指刻意撩過我的手。她想要我。不幸的是，我太喜歡這個公車司機了，不能滿足她的需求。或許我該等到她換工作再說。

en_text: I walk down the aisle. The bus isn’t packed, but I’m forced to sit next to some young guy dressed as a punk. He looks like he couldn’t make conversation about the weather unless it included beating the shit out of a weatherman. He’s dressed entirely in black, with a black studded collar around his neck. He has red hair, spikes in his nose, and faucet washers stretching his earlobes. Another regular citizen of this ﬁne city. A chain runs from his lower lip to his throat. I consider pulling on it to see if I can ﬂush his mind. His T-shirt says Don’t worry, I know the hymen maneuver. It’s ﬁve thirty when I get home, by which time the front of my building is in complete shade. Somebody has tipped over some trash bins, so the sidewalk right outside is covered in old food and lawn clippings, and the old food and lawn clippings are themselves covered in ﬂies. I climb the steps to the top ﬂoor and the ﬁrst thing I do when I get into my apartment is open the window, then the second thing I do is close it because something out there smells bad.
zh_text: 我沿著走道走過去。公車上人不多，不過我還是得坐在別人身旁。我旁邊的是個年輕的龐克族。我絕對不會去跟他交談，因為我懷疑他有辦法在不惡言相向的情況下談論天氣。他穿得一身黑，脖子上掛著黑色的飾釘項圈。他一頭紅髮，鼻子裡插了根鋼刺，耳垂上撐了一枚螺絲墊圈。一個這座城市的普通市民。一條鎖鏈鑲在他的下唇到喉嚨之間。我很想拉拉這條鎖鏈，看看能不能把他的腦袋沖乾淨。他的汗衫上印著：別擔心，我懂處女膜修補術。

en_text: I turn on an electric fan that looks just like the one at work and, I must confess, actually came from work. I open my briefcase on the sofa, take out the microcassette tape, and listen to it while I change out of my overalls. The tape contains nothing interesting. Inside the conference room they admit to themselves they have nothing. Outside to the media, they have several leads. I stiﬂe a laugh and toss the tape back into the briefcase. I’ll swap them again tomorrow.
zh_text: 我於五點半時回到家。我打開我的公事包，拿出微型錄音帶，一邊換衣服一邊聽。沒什麼好聽的。他們在會議室裡對自己承認一點線索也沒有。不過在媒體面前，他們倒是有好幾條線索。我忍著笑意，將錄音帶丟回公事包。明天我再換回來。

en_text: I sit on the sofa and watch my goldﬁsh. I give them some food and they swim up and start eating. Five-second memories or not, they always recognize food. They also recognize me. When I put my ﬁnger on the edge of the bowl, they follow it. I sometimes think that society would be great if we all had ﬁve-second memories. I could kill as many people as I wanted. Of course, maybe I wouldn’t remember that I liked killing people, so maybe it wouldn’t be that great after all. I could be right in the middle of tying somebody up when I’d forget why I was there. A ﬁve-second-memory society would just be full of awkward moments like that. When Pickle and Jehovah have eaten and are back into their happy routine of swimming around and around, I lock up and head downstairs, keeping a tight grip on my briefcase.
zh_text: 我坐在沙發上看金魚。丟了一點飼料，他們游上來吃。不管記憶力是不是只有五秒鐘，他們總是認得食物。他們也認得我。當我將手指放在魚缸邊緣時，他們會跟著我的手指移動。有時候我覺得如果大家都只有五秒鐘的記憶，世界一定十分美好。我想殺多少人就殺多少人。當然，或許我不會記得我喜歡殺人，所以或許沒有那麼美好。我可能會在把人綁起來的時候突然忘記自己在幹什麼。

en_text: I walk a few blocks, studying all the cars parked along the side of the road. Fifteen minutes later I’m driving to the address on page two of the folder I picked up earlier. I’m in a Honda that’s ten years old and has the aroma of cigarette smoke stained into the seats and carpet, but despite that it’s a pretty nice ride. I ﬁnd them easier to steer without the weight of a body in the trunk. I drive slowly past Daniela Walker’s house. It is a twostory town house that looks like it was built only yesterday—bright red brick, dark brown steel roof, aluminum window framing. I’m surprised there’s no price tag hanging off one of the corners. The garden is looking scruffy, not that it’s very extensive: a few shrubs, a couple of baby trees, clumps of ﬂowers that have wilted in the sun. No price tags on those either. The driveway is paved with paving stones. A pathway to the front door is cobbled with cobblestones. The lawn is dry and long. The mailbox is full of circulars. A garden gnome with painted red pants and a painted blue shirt is lying on its side in the garden. It looks like it’s been shot.
zh_text: 當泡菜和耶和華吃完晚飯，繼續不停地游來游去之後，我鎖上房門，朝樓下走去，緊緊握著我的公事包。我走出幾條街口，打量著所有停在馬路邊的車輛。十五分鐘後，我駕車前往稍早取得的檔案夾裡第二頁上的地址。我駕駛的是一輛本田Integra汽車，座位和地毯上沾有一股菸味。九四年或九五年的車款，酒紅色、五段變速、燃油噴射系統。好車。我發現這種車在後車廂裡沒有屍體的情況下比較好駕馭。我放慢車速駛過丹妮耶拉·沃克家。那是一棟兩層樓高的宅邸，看起來像是昨天才落成的一樣——亮紅色的磚塊、深棕色的鋼頂、鋁製窗框。我很訝異竟然沒有在哪個角落裡掛出售價。院子看起來很髒亂，倒不是說它有多大：幾株灌木、兩棵小樹、一些花草。那些東西上面也沒有標價。車道鋪有鋪路石板。通往前門的小徑鋪著大圓石。草皮又乾又長。信箱塞滿傳單。一座藍衣紅褲的花園地精像側躺在花園裡。它看起來像中槍身亡的樣子。

en_text: I circle the block and come back, then, satisﬁed nobody is watching, I pull up outside. I hop out of the car, straighten my tie, adjust my jacket, then realize the back of my pants have been tucked into my socks on the left side. I ﬂick it out. I take my briefcase to the front door with me. I seldom leave it behind.
zh_text: 我沿著街區繞一圈，然後又繞回來，接著確認沒人在看之後，我將車停在屋外。我跳下車，整整領帶，理理外套，扯扯褲管，確保它們沒塞在襪子裡，讓自己看起來像個宅男。我帶著公事包來到前門。我很少沒帶它就出門。

en_text: Knock.
zh_text: 敲門。

en_text: Wait.
zh_text: 等待。

en_text: Knock again.
zh_text: 再敲門。

en_text: Wait. Again.
zh_text: 再等待。

en_text: Nobody home. Just as the report conﬁrmed. Since the murder, the husband—who I have already chalked up as suspect number one—hasn’t been back in the house. His mail has been redirected to his parents’ house, where he’s now staying with the kids.
zh_text: 沒人在家。就跟報告裡寫的一樣。打從兇案發生後，死者丈夫——那個已經被我當作一號嫌犯的傢伙——就不曾回家過。他的郵件都被轉寄到他父母家中，如今他和孩子住在那裡。

en_text: The police tape crisscrossing the front door was taken down two days after the murder. That’s the sort of thing that invites trouble. Invites vandalism. It’s like putting up a large button with a sign saying Don’t Push.
zh_text: 門上拉的警方封條在兇案發生過後兩天就已經拆掉。那種東西會招惹麻煩。會引人跑來破壞房舍。那就像是架設一個標示「不要按」的大按鈕一樣。

en_text: I ﬁgure it’ll be a miracle if I walk inside and don’t ﬁnd giant penises painted all over the walls and the furniture not nailed down missing. I ﬁsh into my pocket and ﬁnd my keys hiding beneath my handkerchief. Fumble with the lock for maybe ten seconds. I’m good at this. I take a quick glance over my shoulder into the street. I’m all alone.
zh_text: 我伸手在口袋中摸索，拿出藏在手帕旁邊的鑰匙，在鎖孔裡搞了十秒。我很會開鎖。我迅速瞄了身後的街道一眼。附近沒人。

en_text: I open the door and walk inside.
zh_text: 我打開房門，走了進去。

en_text: Sally leaves work the same time Joe does, and though she tries to catch up to him, even calls out to him more than once, he doesn’t hear her. He reaches the bus stop, and a moment later the bus pulls away, spitting out a cloud of diesel fumes, some of which stick to the back of the bus, the rest disappearing into the air. She’s curious about where Joe goes. Sometimes he walks, sometimes he catches the bus. Does he live with his parents? Does he live with others like him? One of the things she likes the most about Joe is that he appears independent, and it wouldn’t surprise her if he lived in a ﬂat or an apartment somewhere, fending for himself. Does he even have family? He’s never spoken of them. She hopes he does. The idea of Joe being all alone in this world is unsettling. She must make more of an effort to involve herself in his life, the same way she would want people to involve themselves in Martin’s life. If he were still alive.
zh_text: 莎莉跟喬同時離開警局，儘管她想要追上他，甚至不止一次出聲叫他，他卻始終沒有聽見她的聲音。他抵達公車站，片刻過後，他的車就開走了，噴出一大堆柴油黑煙，車身劇烈抖動。她很好奇他到底要去哪裡。有時候他會走路，有時候他會坐車。他跟父母同住嗎？還是跟和他一樣的人住在一起？她最喜歡喬的一點就在於他看起來十分獨立，如果他自給自足地住在某間套房或公寓裡的話，她也不會感到驚訝。他到底有沒有家人？他從不提起他的家人。她希望他有。想到喬獨自一人活在世界上就令她感到不安。她努力想要走入他的生活，就像她希望人們能夠走入馬丁的生活一樣。如果他還活著的話。

en_text: He would be twenty-one today. What would they have been doing to celebrate? They would have thrown a party, invited family and friends, strung up a bunch of balloons and stabbed twenty-one candles into a chocolate cake shaped like a racing car.
zh_text: 今天他滿二十一歲了。他們本來會如何慶祝？他們會開個派對，邀請家人和朋友，吹幾顆氣球，在賽車形狀的巧克力蛋糕上插滿二十一根蠟燭。

en_text: She walks toward the parking building where she keeps her car. She ought to offer Joe rides home—he might like that. And she’d get to know him better too. Tomorrow she’ll ask him.
zh_text: 她走向每天上班停車的立體停車場。她應該說要載喬回家的：他或許會想讓她載。然後她就可以更加了解他。明天她要問他。

en_text: Christchurch is beautiful, she thinks, and she especially loves walking alongside the Avon River with its dark waters and lush, green banks—a strip of nature running through the city. Though the banks aren’t quite as lush as normal because of the lasting summer, but they’re still pretty green close to the waterline. Sometimes she eats her lunch out here, sitting on the grass, watching the ducks, throwing them pieces of bread as they play and feed in the water. She ought to ask Joe to join her. She’s sure he would like it. More and more he reminds her of her brother, and since she can no longer help Martin, perhaps she can help Joe. Is that such a crazy idea? There is a homeless man sitting a few yards from the doorway into the parking building. He’s wearing a dark-blue tracksuit jacket that you only see in TV shows that came out of the ’80s. He’s got on a pair of plastic sunglasses with green arms, and a baseball cap with so much paint splashed on it she can’t read the team. He has a few days worth of stubble, which means somehow he’s still ﬁnding a way to shave. It makes Sally happy to know he still thinks appearances are important. She smiles at him and he smiles back, and she hands him a small plastic bag jammed full with sandwiches.
zh_text: 基督城很美，她心想，她特別喜歡漫步在雅芳河畔，欣賞著深色的河水與翠綠的河岸——一條貫穿城市的自然美景。有時候她會在河畔午餐，坐在草地上，看著河面上戲水覓食的鴨子，丟點麵包給牠們吃。她應該找喬共進午餐的。她可以確定他會樂意前來。他越來越讓她想起弟弟，而既然她已經無法幫助馬丁，或許她能夠幫助喬。這個想法真的會很瘋狂嗎？

en_text: “Better now, Sally,” he says, standing up and tucking his T-shirt into too large, too worn jeans. “Better now. How’s your dad doing?”
zh_text: 「現在好多了，莎莉。」他說著站起身來，雙手插入那條太大也太破的牛仔褲口袋裡。「現在好多了。妳爸還好嗎？」

en_text: “He’s doing okay,” she answers, but of course he isn’t. He’s doing badly. That’s what happens with Parkinson’s disease. You never get any better. It gets into your body and sets up a home and has no intention of ever leaving. Doing okay is the best anybody can hope for. “It’s his birthday this week. We’re going to take him out to dinner,” she says, but it won’t be fun. His birthday never is, not since Martin died. Maybe it would be if it had been a month before or a month after, but having it the same week . . .
zh_text: 「他還不錯。」她回答，不過當然他不好。他的情況很糟。帕金森氏症就是這個樣子。病情絕對不會好轉。它主動跑到你的身體裡。把你的身體當成自己的家。永遠住在裡面。沒有惡化就是最好的情況。「他這個禮拜生日。我們要帶他出門吃晚餐。」她說，但那絕對不好玩。自從馬丁去世之後，他的生日就不好玩了。如果他的生日在馬丁忌日的前一個月或後一個月，情況或許不會這麼糟，但是在同一個禮拜……

en_text: “Well, you have a good time,” Henry says, interrupting her thoughts. “And say hi to him for me. And remember, Sally, that Jesus loves you.”
zh_text: 「好吧，妳們好好去玩。」亨利說，打斷她的思緒。「幫我向他問好。還有記得，莎莉，耶穌愛妳。」

en_text: She smiles at Henry. She knows that Jesus loves her, and that Jesus loves Henry too, and at the end of the day that makes everything okay. When she ﬁrst started to make Henry sandwiches (she would never give him money, which would surely go toward substances that would make him sin) she used to be the one telling him that Jesus loved him, and his reply was never positive. He used to tell her that God and Jesus hated him. God had made him unemployed. God had made him homeless. She pointed out it was more likely that Henry himself had been the cause of that. He had replied by telling her that God had given him his gambling habit—or at the very least hadn’t taken it away. She asked if Henry still gambled now, to which Henry said no, to which Sally pointed out that God had indeed helped him. “Then God has a bad sense of timing,” Henry had said, and even though Sally didn’t like it, she certainly recognized there was an element of truth to that. Henry then went on to point out that if man was made in God’s image and man was doing nothing to help him, then God would be doing nothing too. If God came down to walk about the earth, Henry said, and saw him sitting there outside the parking building, begging for change and food, then God would look right through him and just walk on by. The same way everybody else did.
zh_text: 她朝亨利微笑。自從在這裡停車開始，她每天都會見到他。剛開始幫他做三明治時（她絕不會給他錢——他一定會用錢去換取導致罪惡的物質），都是她在告訴他耶穌愛他。而他的回應向來都不正面。他從前總是說上帝和耶穌都痛恨他。上帝讓他失業。上帝讓他淪爲流浪漢。她說這一切很可能都是亨利自己造成的。他答道人們根本漠不關心，人類是以上帝的形象創造而來，而人們卻完全不願幫助他，那就表示上帝也不願意幫助他。如果上帝降臨人間，亨利說，看見他坐在停車場外乞討零錢和食物，那麼上帝也會視而不見，直接路過。就像其他所有人一樣。

en_text: Sally could almost see his point, but at the same time found it easy to dismiss, mainly because Sally never walked past Henry without helping him. After months of bringing him sandwiches, he ﬁnally allowed her to teach him more about God’s will. She knows it’s possible he only says these things to her so she will continue to bring him food, but she likes hearing it.
zh_text: 除了莎莉。莎莉絕不會對需要幫助的人視而不見。連續幾個月拿三明治給他吃之後，他終於允許她教導自己更多關於上帝的教誨。她知道他很有可能只是爲了讓她繼續帶三明治來才說這些話的。

en_text: “I’ll see you tomorrow, Henry. Take care now.”
zh_text: 明天見，亨利。好好照顧自己。

en_text: Henry sits back down and goes about taking care of himself the way she suggested, starting by reaching into the plastic bag. She walks inside and takes the elevator up to her car.
zh_text: 亨利坐回地上，開始依照她的建議好好照顧自己，從伸手到塑膠袋裡開始做起。她步入停車場，搭乘電梯前往停車的樓層。

en_text: A moment later her car is mingling with the town trafﬁc. It really is a beautiful city, she thinks. Voted friendliest in the world. It’s obvious why. So many good people. Caring people. She just wishes that sometimes they could show it a little more. By the time she climbs three ﬂights of stairs, she’s pufﬁng. She could take the elevator, but she’s been taking the elevator all day at work and this is her best chance for exercise. Lord knows she would be thankful to lose a pound or two. She reaches her car—a twenty-year-old sedan that doesn’t have much in the way of features but has plenty in the way of rust, but every day the engine keeps on ticking over and Lord knows she’s thankful for that too. The building exits on a different street from which she came in. Trafﬁc is thickening, and in an hour, some of these streets will almost grind to a halt. She smiles as she strikes a string of green trafﬁc lights. The sun is still out, there’s a warm breeze, and everywhere around her people are happy. She winds down the passenger window, but the one on her side doesn’t work, but that’s okay because enough of a breeze still makes it inside. She keeps smiling as she drives. There are so many ﬂower beds, so many trees, a river ﬂowing through the center of town—who would want to live anywhere else?
zh_text: 片刻過後，她的車子駛上馬路。這真是一個美好的城市，她心想。被票選爲世界上最友善的城市。原因十分明顯。太多好人了。關懷他人的好人。許多百年建築都維護得很好，爲這座城市扎好根基，許多重建的部分也盡可能做到和老建築一樣古色古香，這樣做需要龐大的經費，但卻能保持本城的傳統風味。這麼多花床、這麼多樹木、一條穿越市中心的河流：世界上還有其他她會想要居住的城市嗎？

en_text: The ﬁrst thing I notice is how stuffy the house is. It’s like the inside of a dryer. The summer heat has built up. I wish I could leave the door open. The second thing is that miracles do sometimes happen—no genitalia have been painted on the walls, there are no indications anything has been stolen. A quick ﬂick of a light switch shows even the power is still on.
zh_text: 我首先注意到的就是屋內有多凌亂。那種感覺就像身處烘乾機內一樣。聖誕節和新年的炎熱已經開始展現威力了。真希望我能把門打開。

en_text: Time for a casual stroll. I ﬁnd a few bottles of beer in the fridge. I also ﬁnd several foods that have gone past their expiration date, chunks of furry mold growing from wet-looking surfaces. It’s almost enough to put me off the beer—but only almost. It doesn’t have a twist-top cap, but there’s a bottle opener in one of the drawers. The beer is refreshing as I sit down and glance back through Daniela’s ﬁle. When I ﬁnish, I put the bottle in my briefcase, along with the cap and the bottle opener, and head upstairs.
zh_text: 該是四下閒晃的時候。我在冰箱裡找到一瓶未開封的啤酒。有何不可？我一邊喝著清涼提神的啤酒，一邊坐下來研究丹妮耶拉的檔案。喝完之後，我將酒瓶放入公事包，朝向樓上走去。

en_text: Up here it’s even hotter. It’s as if the heat from last summer and the one before that is being stored up here too. I take off my jacket and lay it on a small upstairs table, knocking the vase onto the ﬂoor to make room for it. It breaks. Oh well. The body was found in the master bedroom. Rather than wasting any more time, I head directly there.
zh_text: 樓上更熱。我脫掉外套，放上一張小桌子，推落上面的花瓶，騰出空間放它。花瓶摔碎了。喔，好吧。屍體是在主臥房發現的。我不想浪費更多時間，於是直接前往主臥。

en_text: The windows face west, and the lowering sun is coming right in. The bedroom is around the same size as any other I’ve broken into. The dark carpet looks both blue and green, but probably looks gray to anybody colorblind. Spread across the ﬂoor are more than a dozen plastic markers, each of them numbered. They’re bigger versions of ones some restaurants and cafés hand out to keep track of who ordered the salmon or the latte. In the ﬁle, the numbers represent things that were found on those points, things like hair, blood, and underwear. Spare evidence bags are littered here and there. No wonder the police can’t stick to a budget. Each time I kill somebody, that’s more money they have to come up with. Hopefully this doesn’t end up affecting my wages.
zh_text: 窗戶面西，低垂的陽光直接照入屋內。臥房跟我曾闖入過的臥房差不多大小。深色的地毯看起來像是藍色又像綠色。地板上擺了十來個塑膠牌，每一個上面都有標號。它們很像某些餐廳發給點了鮭魚或拿鐵的客人的號碼牌，不過比較大。在檔案裡，這些號碼表示在這些地方找到的物品，像是毛髮、血跡，以及內褲。地上隨處可見備用證物袋。難怪警方總是經費不足。我每殺一個人，他們就多一筆經費。希望此事到頭來不會影響我的薪水。

en_text: The walls are covered in red textured wallpaper that’s slightly too bright for this room, making it feel, if you can believe it, even hotter. The smell of death hasn’t left. It’s soaked into the carpet pile and will probably always be there. The windows take up most of the opposite wall, and beside me is a walk-in closet. A print of some foreign landscape that could be African or Australian hangs above the bed, and I think about taking it home for Mom. A bedside table has the usual ensemble of crap resting on it: a packet of painkillers; a small, smooth jar of night cream, whatever that is; an alarm clock; and a box of tissues. The alarm clock is still keeping accurate time. There’s a similar table on the other side of the bed. Scattered across the room, as it’s been scattered everywhere else in the house, is white ﬁngerprinting powder. It looks like Detective Schroder and his pals had a cocaine party.
zh_text: 牆壁上貼著對這個房間而言有點過亮的紅色花紋壁紙，感覺起來更加炎熱。死亡的氣息尚未完全消散。它滲入地毯之中，很可能永遠不會消失。對面的牆壁大部分都讓窗戶佔據，我身邊有座能讓人走進去的大衣櫥。床鋪上方掛著一幅可能是非洲或澳洲的風景畫，我考慮把它帶回家給媽。床頭桌上放著各式各樣常見的物品：一包止痛藥、一小瓶晚霜、一個鬧鐘、面紙。床的另一側還有一張差不多的桌子。到處都是白色的指紋粉，就像屋子裡其他地方一樣。那玩意兒看起來像是古柯鹼。

en_text: I take a look at the sketch map of the bedroom that was in the ﬁle. There’s also one of the entire ﬂoor. Can’t get lost in here. The purpose of the map is to show in an even perspective where everything was found. It tells me that on the far side of the bed is a door leading to a bathroom. I follow the map and see it speaks the truth.
zh_text: 我看了看檔案中的臥房素描地圖。另外還有一張這層樓的草圖。在這裡絕不會迷路。這些地圖是爲了更精確地標明所有物品的位置。它告訴我床的另外一邊有扇通往浴室的門。我跟隨地圖的指引，發現它所言不虛。

en_text: The body was found on the bed. There’s no tape or chalk outline of where her body was, because that’s only a TV thing. It’s a shame, because that would be a pretty sweet job to have. I can imagine the interview: Well, if you can trace an outline around this orange, the job is yours.
zh_text: 屍體是在床上發現的。標示出屍體輪廓的帶子還在原位。看起來像是小學生擺的。標示屍體一定是整個警界最簡單的工作。我可以想像面試的內容：「好吧，只要你能畫出這顆橘子的輪廓，工作就是你的了。」

en_text: I pick my way across the ﬂoor, stepping over the plastic numbers and evidence bags. I sit on the corner of the bed. The duvet sags and moves a little. So far, my effort has consisted of knocking over a vase and sitting on a comfortable bed, yet already I’m sweating. When I wipe my shirtsleeve across my forehead, it comes away wet. I roll up my sleeves and rest the briefcase on the bed. I open it so the gun is easily accessible. I see the empty bottle of beer and ﬁght the temptation to go back downstairs for a fresh one.
zh_text: 我穿越主臥，跨過塑膠號碼牌和證物袋，在床角坐下。墊子下陷，稍微移位。截至目前爲止，我唯一費力的事情就是打碎一只花瓶和坐上舒適的床鋪，光這樣我都會開始流汗。我伸出衣袖擦拭額頭，衣袖當場濕透。我捲起衣袖，將公事包放在床上。我打開公事包，方便隨時取用手槍。

en_text: I don’t know exactly what I’m looking for, so I decide to break my evening up into goals. Baby steps. My short-term goal has to be simple: ﬁnd something to work with, work with it, then turn it into a long-term goal. Set this guy up for the entire seven killings, and the eighth one too, if she ever gets found. I still have the ticket from the parking garage as evidence that I can plant. I close my eyes and imagine it all unfolding, then open them because I’m jumping ahead. I need to reach the short-term goal ﬁrst.
zh_text: 我不知道到底要找什麼，於是決定爲今晚設定幾個目標。一步一步來。我的短期目標必須簡單明瞭：找個東西來研究，好好研究，然後把它變成長期目標。將七件兇案通通嫁禍到這個傢伙身上，還外帶第八件，如果有人找到她的話。我手中依然握有可以拿來嫁禍的停車卡。不過我想太遠了。首先我得達成短期目標。

en_text: I begin looking around. Nice place. I could live here. A nice twentyinch ﬂatscreen TV in the corner that would look good in my place. It’s been turned off, though in the photographs it’s on. Maybe the killer watched TV while he was attacking her. Or maybe she watched. I wonder what was on at the time, if Walker was being raped to boring British theme music. The generic photographs of her family where they all fake smiles for the camera ﬁll the room. There are some on the bedside tables; others hang on the walls. If their eyes are looking at me, I don’t feel it here.
zh_text: 我開始四下搜尋。這房子不錯。我願意住在這裡。屋角有台很棒的二十吋電視。此刻它被關上了，不過照片上卻是打開的。或許兇手一邊強暴她，一邊看電視。又或許她原先在看電視。房間裡到處都是她的家人面對鏡頭假笑的照片。床頭桌上放了幾張；其他的則掛在牆上。如果他們正在看我，我可一點也感受不到。

en_text: A crossword-puzzle magazine sits on the second bedside table, along with a telephone. The phone is no good, though. It’s been torn from the wall. On the ﬂoor by the bedside table is the remote to the TV. It has white ﬁngerprinting powder on all the buttons. I put the crossword magazine in my briefcase, then check out the closet. Nice clothes. Hers aren’t my type. The husband’s are the wrong size. I rummage through a chest of drawers and ﬁnd nothing. Her underwear smells like fabric softener and feels soft against my face. I drop a pair of panties inside my briefcase.
zh_text: 一本塡字遊戲雜誌放在第二張床頭桌上，隔壁還有台電話。不過電話不能打了。它被人從牆上扯了下來。床頭桌旁的地板上躺著電視遙控器。所有按鍵上都有白色的指紋粉。我將塡字遊戲雜誌放入公事包，然後查看衣櫥。好衣服。她的衣服不適合我。丈夫的衣服尺寸又不對。我翻箱倒櫃，沒有任何發現。她的內衣帶有衣物柔軟精的味道，貼在臉上磨蹭也很柔軟。我拿了兩條內褲丟到公事包裡。

en_text: There is nothing of interest in the bathroom. The husband’s electric razor, sitting above the sink, looks nicer than mine. It’s one of many things the husband has left behind. Back in the bedroom, I sit down on the same corner of the bed and put the razor into my briefcase, ﬁrst wrapping it in the underwear to protect my knives. Red walls. Blue-green carpet. I’ve never known what fashion is in or out, so I’m not sure whether these colors are on their way in for the ﬁrst time or are already too old, or if they’re coming back in fashion. I’m not sure whether I should like them.
zh_text: 浴室裡沒有什麼有趣的東西。丈夫的電動刮鬍刀，擺在洗手台上，看起來比我的高級。這是丈夫所留下的衆多物品之一。回到臥室，我坐上剛剛的床角，將刮鬍刀放入公事包，拿內褲包起來，藉以保護我的刀。紅牆。藍綠地毯。我從來搞不清楚現在流行什麼，所以我不確定這種配色是即將開始流行，還是老舊到早已退流行，或它們又東山再起了。我不確定我喜不喜歡它們。

en_text: Concentrate. I think back to the autopsy report. Daniela was able to scratch her killer, and since there were marks on her wrists from being bound, she must have scratched him before he started to strangle her. Once my chest was scratched so badly I needed stitches, but because I couldn’t go to the doctor, I went to the supermarket and bought those Band-Aid stitches. Used half a dozen to close the wound. Healed up nicely. Except for the infection.
zh_text: 我回想驗屍報告。丹妮耶拉抓傷了兇手，由於手腕上有遭受綑綁的痕跡，她必定是在對方開始勒她之前抓傷他的。有一回我胸前的抓傷嚴重到必須縫合的地步，不過因為不能去看醫生，我只好去超市買那種創可貼縫合組。我用了半打針線組才縫好傷口。癒合得不錯。不過有感染。

en_text: The only blood found at the scene was hers. He didn’t stab her—just punched her in the face a few times. The drops of blood on the pillow from having her face pressed into it look like tears, as if a sad clown wept into it. More droplets have been sprinkled over the ﬂoor. On the handle to the front door, accompanying one of the latex smudges, is a smudge of her blood.
zh_text: 現場只有找到她的血跡。他沒有砍傷她——只有毆打她的臉部幾下。兇手將她的臉壓在枕頭上所留下的血滴像是紅眼淚。還有些血滴噴濺在地板上。門把除了乳膠污點外，還有一點她的血。

en_text: I read through the reports once more, then check the statements. Putting my money on the husband isn’t looking like a safe bet—he has an exceptionally good alibi. Her body was found with her arms folded across her chest, and a sheet was pulled up over her. Her eyes were open, but the smears on her eyelids suggest the killer closed them before he put his gloves on to clean up. If so, they opened by themselves. Again I think maybe he felt bad at what he had done. I spend a few seconds wondering what that would feel like—about feeling bad—but can’t get a feel for it. That doesn’t mean others don’t understand it. Maybe the guy who did this was deluded enough to think giving her some dignity in death made up for killing her. It looks like a classic domestic homicide, except for the alibi. Plus I saw the husband at the station the morning after the murder, and he looked genuinely messed up, as if he couldn’t believe anybody could do this to his wife.
zh_text: 我再度閱讀報告，然後查看證詞。我依然認爲是丈夫幹的，不過此刻看來可能性似乎不是那麼大了——他擁有很棒的不在場證明。她的屍體被發現時雙手於胸前交叉，身上蓋著一條床單。她的眼睛是睜開的，但是眼瞼上的污點顯示兇手在戴上手套開始清理前曾闔上她的雙眼。若真如此，那麼它們就是自行睜開的。我再度認爲他或許對自己的作爲感到內疚。或許他天真地以爲讓她死後有點尊嚴可以彌補殺害她的罪惡。一切看來都像是典型的家庭兇殺案，只不過他有不在場證明。而且兇案發生隔天，我在警局見過死者丈夫，他看起來一團糟，彷彿他無法相信有其他人會對他妻子做出這種事情。

en_text: I look back down at the report. It’s getting harder to read as it gets darker outside. Nothing has been reported stolen: no pieces of missing jewelry, no missing cash. In most cases the guilty husband would have tried to make it look like a burglary gone wrong. I never take anything when I kill, and since this person was trying to copy me, he never took anything either. How did he know that? Not through the media, that’s for sure. Is it just a coincidence?
zh_text: 我將報告往前翻。沒有任何東西失竊：沒有失竊的珠寶、沒有失竊的現金。大部分的案例中，犯案的丈夫都會想辦法讓現場看起來像是闖空門失控。我殺人的時候從不拿走任何東西，既然這個人想要模仿我，他也沒有拿東西。他怎麼會知道這一點？不是從媒體口中得知的，這點可以肯定。難道是巧合？

en_text: I don’t know. All I do know is that I’ve been here for nearly forty minutes and still don’t have any answers. I’m starting to think more and more of the beers downstairs. I should have opened a window. The air’s still stuffy, but the sun is no longer as strong. I loosen my grip on the thick ﬁle and the contents spill onto the bed. My ideas are starting to dissolve. Time keeps passing and I realize my mind has stagnated. I start running my eyes over the scene, imagining what happened here, putting myself in the killer’s mind. Getting inside is easy for a guy like me. So that’s what I do—I get inside his mind, I imagine her dying, and for a few minutes I can almost feel her beneath me.
zh_text: 我已經在這裡待了將近四十分鐘。我應該要開扇窗戶的。空氣依然悶熱，不過陽光已經沒之前那麼強烈。我鬆開厚厚的檔案夾，將一堆文件攤在床上。我的想法開始分崩離析。時間分秒過去，我發現自己的思緒停滯不前。我開始四下張望，想像當時的情況，讓自己融入兇手的內心。這麼做對我這樣的人來說並不困難。一時之間，我幾乎能夠感覺到她死前的模樣。

en_text: Still—no great insights, no ﬂashing sirens or ringing bells to signify a great breakthrough in the case. There are no breakthroughs, just one sloppy coincidence and a sweat-soaked shirt. I thought it would be easier. Hell, it should be easier. Only things never are. Not when it’s something you really want. I want to help this dead woman as much as I want to help myself, but does that matter? Does that make the answers any easier to ﬁnd? Of course not. The only thing I feel like doing is taking my free electric shaver and crossword puzzles out of here and never coming back. Go home, feed my ﬁsh, and take a nap. Put this episode behind me, like I have other episodes in my life, like I have with all of them. Move on. To what, I’m not sure.
zh_text: 然而我原先非常篤定能夠找到的答案卻不在這裡。沒有重大發現，沒有表示重大突破的響亮警笛或鈴聲。沒有任何突破，只有牽強的巧合和濕透的襯衫。我以爲查案很簡單。見鬼了，本來就應該很簡單才對。可惜世事向來沒有這麼簡單。特別是當你很想要辦成一件事情的時候。我就像想幫助自己一樣想要幫助這個死去的女人，但是這有差別嗎？這樣會比較容易找到答案嗎？當然不會。我唯一想做的事情就是帶著我的免費電動刮鬍刀和塡字遊戲雜誌離開這裡，永遠不要回來。回家，餵魚，睡個覺。把這件事情拋到腦後，好像我的生活裡還有其他事情可做一樣，好像我的人生十分充實。繼續走下去。走到哪裡，我不確定。

en_text:
I start stretching and yawning, ready to leave, ready to give up. The warm air is only helping to maintain this feeling of despondency. The yawning leads to blinking, quick, rapid-ﬁre blinking, and this in turn increases the blood ﬂow to my eyes. They begin to sharpen, the room taking focus again, the objects standing out like 3-D images. . . .
And there it is!
zh_text:
我開始伸懶腰，打呵欠，準備離開，準備放棄。悶熱的空氣助長了消沉的意志。呵欠導致我開始眨眼，迅速連續眨眼，而這種動作導致眼球充血。眼前的景象變得清晰，房間再度恢復焦點，物品如同3D影像般凸顯而出……
我看到了！

en_text: In an instant I’m overcome with several different thoughts and emotions. First of all I feel disgust. I’m ashamed with myself for being here so long and not seeing it until now. I’m excited that I’m suddenly looking at something—or not looking at something, to be exact—that may be crucial. And most of all, I’m relieved. I’m thankful I can move forward again, thankful I don’t have to give up the investigation—at least not yet, and relieved that Daniela may get the justice she deserves.
zh_text: 轉眼之間，我心中湧現數個不同的想法與情緒。首先，我覺得噁心。我對自己來此這麼久竟然沒有發現它感到十分可恥。我對自己突然看見了某樣或許非常重要的關鍵物品——或者明確來說，之前竟沒有看見該物品——感到十分興奮。最重要的是，我感到非常欣慰。謝天謝地，我又可以繼續下去，不需要放棄這次調查了——至少還不需要——我終於可以爲丹妮耶拉伸張正義了。

en_text: I start grinning. I almost can’t believe my luck. But of course it isn’t luck. Well, some of it is, I guess—because in an other ten minutes it would have been too dark to see anything unless I turned on the light. So sure, it’s luck, but it’s brilliance too. And insight. Yeah, it’s especially about insight.
zh_text: 我開始微笑。我幾乎難以相信自己的好運。不過當然這與運氣無關。實在是因為我太聰明了。還有敏銳的洞察力。沒錯，主要還是洞察力的關係。

en_text: I grab the photographs and begin ﬂicking through them until I ﬁnd one that shows the wall and the doorway to the hallway. I hold up the picture. Study it. Hold it away. Study the scene. The doorway is in each of them. Same walls. Same carpet. Same décor. A potted plant that looks lushly green in the picture is brown and disheveled in real life. In the photograph —lying against the base of the wall, next to the live plant—there is a fountain pen. In reality, lying next to the plant is a ballpoint pen. Sure, it’s only a pen, minor in the scheme of things, but what makes it interesting is the fact that it hasn’t been cataloged and taken away, meaning it was considered irrelevant.
zh_text: 我抓起照片，迅速瀏覽，找出顯示通往走廊的牆壁與門口的那張。我拿起照片。仔細研究。拿開照片。打量現場。照片與現場都能看到門口。同樣的牆壁。同樣的地毯。同樣令人質疑的時尚品味。照片中翠綠的盆栽在現實中枯萎凌亂，遭受所有人忽視，除了死神。在照片中，一支鋼筆躺在生氣盎然的盆栽旁的牆邊。現實裡，躺在盆栽旁的是支原子筆。沒錯，那只是一支筆，對整個案情而言並不重要，不過有趣的地方在於這支筆沒被造冊帶回，表示警方認為它與案情無關。

en_text: Well, it’s pretty relevant all right. Was the original pen a weapon? Was it mightier than the sword? I move over to the plant, crouch down, and peer at the wall. It’s hard to see the small mark embedded in it, but not impossible. I lean in closer. I can see a tiny dot of ink in the center. Was the original pen thrown against the wall? Where’s that pen now? Why the swap? Did Daniela cut him with it? Is that why it was thrown over here? If so, it has her attacker’s DNA on it. It’s a map to her killer. The pen is the sort of thing that would have its own individual photograph. Probably two or three. It would even have had its own individual report.
zh_text: 好了，這支筆一定與案情有關。原來的那支筆會是武器嗎？難道它比劍還要鋒利嗎？我走到盆栽前，蹲下去，查看牆壁。牆上的痕跡並不顯眼，但還不至於看不出來。我湊近一點。中間有個小墨點。原來那支筆是被人丟到牆上的嗎？那支筆現在在哪？爲什麼要掉包？難道丹妮耶拉用筆傷了兇手？筆就是因爲這樣才被丟到牆上的嗎？果眞如此，那支筆上就有兇手的DNA。那是通往兇手的地圖。這支筆是屬於會有特寫照片的那種東西。可能還有兩三張。它甚至應該有份獨立的報告。

en_text: I pick up the ballpoint pen in my gloved hand. It’s coated in a thin ﬁlm of white dust. It has been printed and put back down, but nothing of interest came from it. I line it up with the small indent in the wall but can’t ﬁnd anyway for it to ﬁt. The pens were switched at some point after the photograph was taken, and before the ﬁngerprinting took place. So who switched the pens?
zh_text: 我用戴手套的手撿起那支筆。它上面沾了一層薄薄的白粉。警方在上面採集指紋，然後又放了回去，不過沒有找到有趣的東西。這支筆在照片照好之後、蒐集指紋之前讓人掉包了。那麼是誰掉的包？

en_text: The answer is obvious. The killer. That’s who. And the only people in this room during that time frame were people who worked the scene. Her killer has to be a cop. That’s obvious too. Even more obvious, now that I think about what I’ve read, about their knowledge in police procedures. For a few seconds I close my eyes and visualize what happened. He came here.
zh_text: 兇手。就是他。而那段期間唯一待在這個房間裡的人只有在這裡工作的人！兇手絕對是個警察。

en_text: Attacked her. Hit her in the face. Then she stabbed him with the pen. Not seriously, but enough to anger him into throwing it against the wall. The nib chewed into it. He threw her onto the bed. He hadn’t planned on killing her, but he had to prevent her from identifying him. It was spontaneous. Unplanned. He had to use items in this house to bind her. He used her nail clippers to cut away any skin evidence from beneath her ﬁngernails. He used her comb to rake through her pubic hair. He didn’t bring any of this with him because it wasn’t part of the plan. When she was dead, he felt immediate guilt. He did what he could to hide any evidence he left behind, then he covered her body, closing her eyes ﬁrst. But he had to get out of here. Fast. Maybe he said a prayer for her. Maybe he didn’t. But what he did do was forget about the pen—until he came back to investigate her death. Then he saw the pen on the ﬂoor and remembered. The photographs had already been taken. He couldn’t just pick it up. But he didn’t have another fountain pen to switch it with. So he took the gamble that nobody would notice the difference and, for a while, nobody did. I’m nobody, and nobody’s perfect. It’s just a pen, a pen in the corner of the room next to a potted plant. In the center of the room was a dead body.
zh_text: 我閉上雙眼數秒鐘，想像案發當時的情況。他跑來這裡。攻擊她。打她的臉。接著她拿筆刺傷他。傷勢不重，不過足以激怒他將筆丟到牆上。筆尖插入牆中。他將她甩到床上。他沒計畫要殺她，不過必須防止她指證自己。一切都是臨時起意。沒有預謀。他必須拿這個房間裡的東西綑綁她。他用指甲剪剪掉她指甲中的皮膚證物。他用她的梳子清理她的陰毛。他沒帶這些東西來，因為這一切都不在計畫之中。她死的時候，他立刻感到罪惡。他盡可能湮滅自己留下的證據，然後闔上她的雙眼，遮蓋她的屍體。重點是他必須離開此地。而且要快。或許他有為她祈禱。或許沒有。不過他倒是留下了那支筆——直到他回來調查她的死因。接著他看到地上的筆，然後才想起它來。照片已經照了。他不能就這麼把筆撿起來。偏偏他又沒有鋼筆可以掉包。於是他賭沒有人會察覺異狀，一段時間過去，確實沒有人察覺。我是個普通人，人沒有完美的。那只是一支筆，一支掉在屋角盆栽旁邊的筆。屋子中央有具屍體。那具屍體後來變成誤導辦案的典型案例。看著一樣東西，忽視另外一樣。

en_text: The corpse ended up being a classic case of misdirection. Look at one thing and miss another. I open my eyes. That’s how I see it, but of course that may not be what happened. It feels right, though, and I’m sure some, if not most of it, will be. It doesn’t really matter how it happened, what matters is who made it happen. I’ve been here for an hour and already I know her killer is a policeman. What’s more, I know for sure I’m right. In all the books I’ve read, the serial killer is always the policeman. Or the coroner, or some forensic ofﬁcer. So why not now? Why should this be any different? Perhaps clichés in ﬁction come from clichés in real life? In some weird way it’s disappointing to ﬁnd that police work in the end is pretty simple. If the killer isn’t a husband or boyfriend, just get a witness to view a lineup of cops and pick one.
zh_text: 我張開雙眼。我來這裡超過一個小時，不過已經查出兇手是個警察。更有甚者，我很肯定我是對的。所有我看過的書裡，連續殺人魔都是警察。或是驗屍官、或是犯罪現場調查員。這回為什麼不能是他們呢？這件案子有什麼理由例外呢？就某種奇怪的角度而言，我很遺憾得知警方的工作畢竟還是這麼簡單。如果兇手不是丈夫或男朋友，只要抓個證人去排排站好的警察裡面挑一個出來就行了。

en_text: I leave the pen where it is since it can’t offer me any more help. I turn away and pack up my briefcase. I have an urge to shout, to sing, to dance, to hunt for those sirens and bells and whistles that ought to accompany a moment like this. By the time I reach the front door, via the kitchen and the fridge, it’s dark outside. I face the hallway and rooms as if to say goodbye to this house. I have no reason to return. No reason at all.
zh_text: 我將筆放回原地，因為它已經無法提供更多幫助。我轉過身去，收拾公事包。我有股想要吶喊、高歌、跳舞的衝動，去找些這種時候應該發聲的警笛、警鐘，和哨子。來到前門時，我轉過身去，彷彿想跟這棟房子道再見。我沒有回來的理由。我看著走廊以及旁邊的房間。完全沒有理由。

en_text: Unless . . .
zh_text: 除非……

en_text: Grinning, I put the beers and the bottle opener back and rush upstairs.
zh_text: 我咧嘴而笑，快步回到一樓。

en_text: When she gets home from work, Sally ﬁnds her mother upstairs, crying. At ﬁrst she pauses at the door, unsure whether to enter her parents’ bedroom. Her mother cried a lot after Martin died, and these days she’s crying a lot too.
zh_text: 下班回家後，她發現母親在樓上哭泣。一開始她在門口停下腳步，不確定該不該進入父母的臥房。馬丁死後，她母親常哭，而這些日子以來，她一樣很常哭。

en_text: “Sally?”
zh_text: 「莎莉？」

en_text: “Hi, Mom. Are you okay?” Sally asks, thinking that for her mom, okay ended a long time ago.
zh_text: 「嗨，媽。妳沒事吧？」莎莉問，心想對她媽來說，「沒事」已經是很久以前的事情了。「我還好。我也不知道我爲什麼這樣。」

en_text: “I’m ﬁne,” her mother says, offering a smile that she doesn’t quite get right, and of course Sally hasn’t seen one that has ﬁtted right and she knows it’s because her parents blame her for what happened to Martin. “I don’t really know why I’m like this.” When Sally puts an arm around her mother’s shoulders, she ﬂinches at ﬁrst, then relaxes. The room smells of incense and the warm air is slightly stale. She knows exactly why her mother gets like this, and her mother knows too. Martin’s birthday. She bought her dead brother a birthday card, ﬁlled it out, then buried it deep in her drawer beneath a pile of clothing. She isn’t sure if her parents do the same or similar things, and suspects it may not actually be that healthy if they do. Of course they never dare talk about it. To talk about it would allow their grief to take on more life, to continue to rise above them and push them down. In some ways she envies Joe. She wants to be as simple as him, not having to worry about the pain in the world, just moving along from A to B, keeping people happy, staying out of their way, making a life for herself that is good.
zh_text: 當莎莉伸手摟著母親肩膀時，她先是畏縮，然後才放鬆。房間瀰漫著焚香的氣味，溫暖的空氣有點混濁。她很清楚母親為什麼這個樣子，她媽也很清楚。今天是馬丁的生日。她為死去的弟弟帶了張生日卡片，寫完賀辭，然後將卡片塞在抽屜裡一堆衣服下。她不知道父母有沒有這麼做，或是做類似的事情，並且認爲如果他們有這麼做的話或許不太健康。當然他們從來不敢談論此事。談論這種事情會讓他們更加哀傷，一發不可收拾，直到將他們推向萬劫不復的深淵為止。就某方面而言，她很羨慕喬。她想要和他一樣單純，不需要擔心世界上的痛苦，每天只要從一個A地移動到B地，讓人們開心，不要打擾他們，自給自足就很好了。

en_text: “It’s okay, Mom,” she says, and there’s that word again. “I think Dad’s looking forward to his birthday.”
zh_text: 「沒事的，媽。」她又說了「沒事」。「我想爸很期待他的生日。」

en_text: Her mother nods, and they begin talking about how nice it’s going to be to go out for dinner. Her father’s birthday will be a challenge too. In the last year he has stepped outside the house for doctors’ appointments and graveyard visits and nothing else. Whether they make it to dinner on Thursday night is still something of a gamble.
zh_text: 她母親點頭，她們開始說起出門晚餐會多開心。他父親的生日也會是個挑戰。去年一整年，他除了去看醫生和到墳場探視馬丁外完全沒有出過門。禮拜四晚上能不能出門晚餐還是個未知數。

en_text: Sally opens the window. The air outside has cooled off. The warm air from the bedroom starts to waft out as fresh stuff replaces it. She wishes her dad’s disease could be swapped just as easily. She would happily take it into her own body to relieve him of it if she could. It would be the least she could do after what happened to Martin.
zh_text: 莎莉打開窗戶。室外的空氣已經轉涼。悶熱的空氣洩出窗外，新鮮空氣對流進來。她希望父親的疾病也能夠如此輕易地交換就好了。可以的話，她很樂意接收他的病，讓他遠離病魔。在馬丁的事情過後，這是她最起碼能爲父親做的。

en_text: “I’m sorry,” her mother says, looking up and releasing her grip on a damp handful of tissues. “I used to be stronger than this.” She starts rubbing the silver cruciﬁx hanging at her neck between her thumb and foreﬁnger.
zh_text: 「我很抱歉。」她媽說，抬起頭來，放開手中一把潮濕的面紙。「我從前比現在堅強。」她開始以食指與大拇指搓揉掛在脖子上的十字架。

en_text: “It will be okay, Mom,” Sally answers, staring at the cruciﬁx coming in and out of view, the okay word hanging in the room in the thick air. “You’ll see.” Of course her mother has said those same words many times since the day when Martin’s doctor gave them the news that led them to start thinking about where they wanted to bury their son. Strangely, it was Martin who suffered the least, because he didn’t understand he was dying. Even at the end he thought he was going to be getting better. Didn’t they all think that?
zh_text: 「會沒事的，媽。」莎莉回應道，凝望著十字架在眼前反覆出現，然後消失。「看著吧。」當然，打從醫生告訴他們那個讓他們開始考慮該將馬丁葬在何處的消息之後，她媽已經說過同樣的話很多次了。奇怪的是，他們家受苦最少的反而是馬丁，因為他並不知道自己快死了。即使到最後，他還以爲自己會好起來。他們可不是全都如此以爲嗎？

en_text: Yes. Life was always going to get better.
zh_text: 是啊。人生總是會好起來的。

en_text: All they have to do is remember that. All they have to do is have faith. Her mind slowly turns toward Joe. She wonders if he believes in God, and assumes that he does—he’s too good-natured not to. Still, she decides to ﬁnd out, because God may be the one thing they have in common.
zh_text: 他們只需要牢記這一點就好了。他們只需要保持信心就好了。她的思緒緩緩轉移到喬的身上。不知道他相不相信上帝，假設他相信——他本性太好，不可能不信。儘管如此，她還是決定要問問他，因為上帝或許就是他們唯一的交集。

en_text: I’m not actually sure where ideas come from, whether they’re just ﬂoating around out there in some dimension close to but not quite of this world, where our minds can reach out and pluck them, whether a series of ﬁring synapses in our mind weigh up cold data into cold possibilities, or whether it comes down to a simple train of thought riding through Lucksville. Ideas come at any time, often when you’re not expecting them. I’ve had them in the bathroom, cleaning ﬂoors. I’ve had them when dreading the walk from the sidewalk to my mother’s front door. The spontaneous ideas are often the best. Sometimes they shock you into making a decision. Only hindsight tells you whether it was good or not.
