zh_text: 我不能肯定點子這種東西是打哪兒來的，或許它們就飄在某個不屬於這世界的鄰近空間裡，等待我們的內心跑去信手拈來，又或許我們腦中某兩個神經突觸會將冰冷的資訊換算爲冰冷的可能性，又或許它們只是單純地搭乘思想列車穿越幸運谷而來。點子隨時都會出現，通常是在你想不到的時候。我在浴室裡掃地的時候會靈光一現，在戰戰兢兢踏上通往我媽前門的小徑時也會突然想到什麼。突如其來的點子通常都是最好的。有時候它們能夠衝擊你做出決定。只有等到事後你才能得知那是個好點子還是壞點子。

en_text: The only light coming into the room now is from the streetlights outside. I turn the duvet over to hide the splashes of blood. I pick up the plastic markers and throw them into the closet along with the evidence bags, next to a shoe rack and a pile of old clothes. The room no longer looks like a crime scene, but something out of Poor Housekeeping. I wipe away the ﬁngerprint dust with the husband’s shirt, then I close the curtains knowing that when I come back I’m going to have to turn on the lights. I make my way downstairs in the dark and do the same thing. By the time I ﬁnish up and get outside it’s after nine o’clock.
zh_text: 我在床上鋪了一張床單，遮起屍體輪廓和血跡。我撿起塑膠號碼牌，全部丟到衣櫥中的鞋架及一堆舊衣服中間。我把備用證物袋也通通塞到裡面去。臥房看起來不再像是犯罪現場，只是不擅長打理家務者的凌亂房間。我用丈夫的襯衫拍掉指紋粉，然後到樓下去做同樣的事情。我一直弄到九點多才完工離開。太陽已經下山，不過天色還沒全黑。這個狀況還會維持二十分鐘。

en_text: I walk down the sidewalk to the Honda and climb inside, tossing my briefcase onto the passenger seat. From the moment I ﬁrst saw this car, I’ve been wearing latex gloves. My ﬁngers are sweating beneath them, but it’s better than leaving ﬁngerprints. I pull them away from my hands. They’re like an extra layer of skin. I don’t put on a replacement pair and make a mental note to remember to wipe down every surface I touch. I drive toward town. I have a job to do, but I don’t want a particularly late night. Rather than looking for an innocent victim, I decide to look for somebody who will gladly be one for a price.
zh_text: 我沿著步道走回本田汽車，上車，將公事包丟到乘客座上。打從看見這輛車開始，我就已經戴上乳膠手套。我的手指在手套內流汗，不過總比留下指紋好。我脫下手套。它們就像第二層皮膚。我擦乾雙手，又戴上備用手套。好多了。我開往城內。我有工作要做，但又不想弄得太晚。於是我決定不找無辜的受害者，直接找個願意爲錢而擔任受害者的人。

en_text: I ﬁnd her standing on a Manchester Street corner in town. A skirt so short it’s more of a thick belt than anything else. Low-cut top. Fishnet stockings. Costume jewelry on her ﬁngers. A small tattoo on her neck and another at the top of her left breast. Other hookers are hanging around trying to attract business, women who look like they’ve been dragged out of a trailer park by their teased hair. If her pimp is nearby he may or may not note down the registration plate of my stolen car, but in this city I can’t imagine pimps caring enough. It doesn’t matter either way.
zh_text: 我在城裡曼徹斯特街的街角找到她。她的裙子短到像條厚皮帶。低胸上衣。魚網襪。手指上戴著人工珠寶，脖子上有個小刺青，左胸上也有一個。附近還有其他妓女在招攬生意，全都是一些看起來像是被人抓住蓬鬆的頭髮從拖車區拖出來的。如果她的皮條客在附近，他可能會也可能不會記下我偷來的車的車牌號碼。不管記不記都無所謂。

en_text: Before the car comes to a complete stop, she opens the passenger door and offers up today’s specials as if reading from a menu. I accommodate her by clearing the seat. She tells me what I can get for twenty dollars, sixty dollars, and even a hundred. I ask her if there’s a cash discount and she gives me a confused look until I tell her I’m just joking. She doesn’t laugh. Then I ask her what I can get for ﬁve hundred. “Is that you still being funny?” she asks. I reach into my pocket and pull out my wallet. I show her what ﬁve hundred dollars looks like.
zh_text: 我開到她旁邊，還沒開口說話，她就已經拉開乘客座的門。我清理座位讓她坐。她直接開始推銷，好像唸菜單一樣說出她所提供的特殊服務。她告訴我二十塊錢、六十塊錢，甚至一百塊錢可以做些什麼事情。我問她五百塊可以怎樣。

en_text: “You can have whatever you want, baby,” she says, and I’ll certainly hold her to that.
zh_text: 她說你想怎樣就怎樣，寶貝。

en_text: She closes the door and the interior light blinks out, but not before I end up taking a longer look at her than I would like. She’s in her late twenties, though that’s really just a guess. She’s underweight, which isn’t a guess, and looks like an ad for starving children in Third World countries. She has blond hair with black roots and so much hair spray the strong nor’westers we’ve been getting wouldn’t budge it. Her brown eyes reveal nothing, as though her mind is somewhere else, maybe in a world where she doesn’t have to wrap her thighs or lips around men for money. When she smiles at me, her swollen lips glisten with either moisture, or her last client.
zh_text: 她關上車門，車內燈隨即熄滅，不過我還是有時間看清楚她的長相。她大概快要三十歲。體重不足。看起來像第三世界國家的飢餓兒童廣告。她滿頭金髮，看得見黑色的髮根，而且髮膠多到就連此刻的西北強風都吹不動它。她的棕眼沒有神采，彷彿她的心思放在別處，或許放在一個她不需要爲錢而用大腿或嘴巴去夾男人的世界。當她對我微笑時，她腫脹的嘴唇散發潮濕的光澤。

en_text: I head back to Daniela’s house. We make small talk on the way, mostly about the weather. I’m sure she’s heard the news and knows what’s been happening to all sorts of women in the city, but she doesn’t look nervous sitting in a car with a man she’s known all of two minutes. She can’t afford to be nervous. I have no interest in what she does outside working hours. She doesn’t care who I am. Then we start setting the mood. She tells me I have a nice car. I tell her she has a great body. She tells me she’ll be an awesome fuck. I tell her for ﬁve hundred dollars she ought to be. We reach the house and I don’t bother driving around the block, but opt to park up the driveway. If anybody is around they won’t be able to get a good look at me. Even if they do take a peek, they’ll think it’s the husband returning home to quench his sexual thirst.

But she put the chain going up and down, not side to side, so all any intruder needs to do to unhook it is put his ﬁnger inside and lift. She closes the door, removes the chain, and opens it back up. I take a step inside, bracing myself, because I know it’s coming.
zh_text: 安全鏈阻擋屋門繼續開啓。我媽——上帝保佑她——於四年前「鄰居小孩」偷了她的錢後加裝這道安全鏈。不過她把鎖鏈上下直著裝，而不是橫著裝，所以任何入侵者想要打開此鏈，只需要伸根手指進來往上挑就行了。她關上門，移開安全鏈，然後向後拉開屋門。我跨入屋內一步，屏息以待，因為我知道接下來會發生什麼事情。

en_text: She clips me around the ear. “Let that be a lesson to you, Joe.”
zh_text: 她擰了擰我的耳朵。「給你一點教訓，喬。」

en_text: “I’m sorry, Mom.”
zh_text: 「我很抱歉，媽。」

en_text: “You never come and see me anymore. It’s been a week since you were last here.”
zh_text: 「你現在都不來看我。你上次來已經是一個禮拜前了。」

en_text: “I was here last night, Mom,” I say, and I’ve had conversations like this with her before, and will have more of them until the day she dies.
zh_text: 「我昨晚才來過，媽。」

en_text: “You were here last Monday.”
zh_text: 你是上禮拜一來的。

en_text: “And it’s Tuesday now.”
zh_text: 「是這禮拜一。」

en_text: “No, it’s Monday. You were here last Monday.”
zh_text: 「不，是禮拜一。你是上禮拜一來的。」

en_text: She clips me around the ear. “Don’t talk back to your mother.”
zh_text: 她又擰一下我的耳朵。「別跟你媽頂嘴。」

en_text: “I’m not talking back, Mom, I’m just telling you what day it is.”
zh_text: 「我又不是在頂嘴，媽。」

en_text: She raises her hand and I quickly apologize, and she ﬁnally seems appeased by the gesture. “I cooked meatloaf, Joe,” she tells me, lowering her hand. “Meatloaf. That’s your favorite.”
zh_text: 她揚起手掌，我立刻道歉。「我做了烤肉餅，喬。烤肉餅。你的最愛。」

en_text: “You don’t need to remind me.”
zh_text: 「妳不需要提醒我。」

en_text: “What do you mean?”
zh_text: 「這麼說什麼意思？」

en_text: “Nothing.” I open up the supplies I brought with me, and pull out a bunch of ﬂowers. I hand them to her. No thorns this time. “They’re beautiful, Joe,” she says, her face beaming with excitement.
zh_text: 「沒事。」我打開剛買來的東西，拿出一束花。我交給她。這回沒有刺。「這花真美，喬。」她說，臉上綻放興奮的光芒。

en_text: She leads me through to the kitchen. I set my briefcase down on the table, open it up, and look at the knives inside. Look at the gun too. My hand rests on the handle of the Glock, and I try to take some strength from it. Mom puts the ﬂowers into a vase, but doesn’t put in any water. The rose from yesterday is gone. Perhaps she thought it was a week old. She reaches up into a cupboard and grabs hold of a packet of aspirin, and drops one into the vase. “It keeps them alive longer,” she says, turning and winking at me, as if she’s letting me in on a family secret. “I saw it today on a TV show.” “You still have to add water,” I point out.
zh_text: 她帶著我來到廚房。我將公事包放在桌上，打開來，看著裡面的刀具。還看了看槍。她將花插入花瓶，不過沒有裝水。或許她希望它們枯死。昨天的玫瑰已經不在了。或許她以爲那朵花已經插一個禮拜了。

en_text: “I brought something else for you, Mom.”
zh_text: 「我還幫妳帶了點別的，媽。」

en_text: She looks over at me. “Oh?”
zh_text: 她看了看我。「喔？」

en_text: I pull out a box of chocolates and hand it to her.
zh_text: 我拿出一盒巧克力给她。

en_text: “You trying to poison me, Joe? Are you trying to put sugar into my cholesterol?”
zh_text: 你想毒死我嗎，喬？你想要在我的膽固醇裡放糖嗎？

en_text: Oh, Christ. “I’m just trying to be nice, Mom.”
zh_text: 喔，老天啊。「我只是想要對妳好，媽。」

en_text: “Well, be nice by not buying me chocolates,” she says, looking really annoyed at me.
zh_text: 「好啊，不買巧克力給我就是對我好了。」

en_text: “But Coke has sugar in it, Mom.” “Are you being smart?”
zh_text: 「但是可樂裡面也有糖，媽。」你在耍嘴皮子嗎？

en_text: “Of course not.”
zh_text: 「當然不是。」

en_text: She throws the box at me and the corner bounces off my forehead. I see stars for a few seconds. I rub my head where it hit. The box has left a small impression, but no blood.
zh_text: 她將巧克力丟向我，盒角撞到我的額頭。我眼前出現了幾秒星星。我揉了揉被打到的地方。巧克力盒在上面留了點印子，不過沒有流血。

en_text: “Your dinner’s cold, Joe. I’ve had mine.”
zh_text: 「你的晚餐冷了，喬。我吃過了。」

en_text: I put the chocolates back into my briefcase as she dishes my dinner. She doesn’t offer to heat it for me, and I’m too frightened to ask. I head over to the microwave to do it myself.
zh_text: 我趁她幫我裝晚餐的時候將巧克力放回公事包。她沒說要幫我熱，我也不敢請她熱。我走到微波爐前自己動手。

en_text: “Your dinner’s cold, Joe, because you let it get cold. Don’t think you’re going to use my electricity to warm it up.”
zh_text: 「你的晚餐冷了，喬，因為你讓它變冷的。別想用我的電去加熱。」

en_text: We walk into the living room and we use her electricity to get the TV working and we sit in front of it. There’s some show on—I’ve seen it before, but don’t know what it’s called. They’re all the same. Bunch of white guys and girls living in an inner-city complex, laughing at everything that goes wrong for them, and there’s a lot that goes wrong. I wouldn’t be laughing if those things happened to me. I wonder if there’s a complex like that in this city, or even in real life. If so, I wouldn’t mind ﬁnding it. According to the TV the women in those complexes are damn sexy. I seem to recognize this episode but can’t be sure it’s a repeat since they do the same thing every week.
zh_text: 我們走到客廳，坐在電視前面。正在播某個影集——我以前看過，不過忘了叫什麼。影集都一樣。一堆白種男人和女人住在市中心的建築裡，嘲笑生活中出錯的每一件事，而他們生活中有很多事情都在出錯。如果那些事情發生在我身上，我一定笑不出來。我懷疑這座城市裡有沒有那種地方，甚至真實世界裡都未必有。要是有的話，我倒想去找找看。根據這個節目，那個地方的女人都性感得不像話。我似乎有看過這一集，不過不確定是不是重播，因為他們每集做的事情都差不多。

en_text: Mom doesn’t talk to me while I eat. This is a surprise, because I generally can’t shut her up. She always has something to complain about. Normally it’s the price of something. I’m grateful for the silence, so much so that I consider maybe I should be late more often. The downside is her disappointment hangs over the room. I’m so used to it it’s almost part of the furniture. As soon as I throw the last cold scoop of meatloaf into my mouth she uses the remote to kill the TV, then turns toward me. Her mouth sags open, she bares her teeth, and I can see the start of a sentence forming. “If your father knew you treated me like this, Joe, he’d be rolling in his grave.”
zh_text: 我吃飯的時候，媽沒有跟我說話。這倒令我有點驚訝，因為通常我都沒有辦法讓她閉嘴。她隨時都有東西可以抱怨。一般而言是某樣東西的價格。她的失望之情瀰漫在整個屋子裡；我早已習以為常到把它當作家具的一部分了。我剛把最後一片肉餅塞入嘴裡，她立刻拿遙控器關上電祝，然後轉身面對我。她張開嘴巴，露出牙齒，我可以看見句子在她口裡成型。「如果你爸知道你這樣對我，喬，他在墳墓裡也睡不安穩。」

en_text: “He was cremated, Mom.”
zh_text: 「他是火葬的，媽。」

en_text: She stands up and I shrink back, expecting her to tell me off, but instead she puts her hand out for my plate. “I may as well clean up for you.”
zh_text: 她站起身，我向後縮。「我乾脆幫你洗盤子吧。」

en_text: “I’ll do it.”
zh_text: 「我來就好了。」

en_text: “Don’t bother.” She grabs my plate and I follow her into the kitchen.
zh_text: 「不用麻煩。」她抓起我的盤子，我跟著她去廚房。

en_text: “Do you want me to make you a drink, Mom?”
zh_text: 「要我幫妳弄杯飲料嗎，媽？」

en_text: “What, so I’ll be up all night running back and forth to the toilet?”
zh_text: 「幹嘛，好讓我一整個晚上都睡不著覺跑廁所？」

en_text: I open up the fridge. “Anything in here you want?”
zh_text: 我打開冰箱。冰箱裡有什麼想拿的嗎？

en_text: “I’ve had dinner, Joe.”
zh_text: 「我吃過晚飯了，喬。」

en_text: I need to cheer her up, so I turn the subject toward something in her element. “I was at the supermarket, Mom, and I saw they have orange juice on sale.”
zh_text: 我必須逗她開心，所以我轉移到她感興趣的話題上。「我剛剛去過超級市場，媽，我看到柳橙汁在特價。」

en_text: She turns toward me, still scrubbing at my plate, the ﬂesh around her mouth moving aside for her beaming smile. “Really? What brand?” “The brand you drink.”
zh_text: 她轉向我，手裡還在刷我的盤子，嘴角移向兩旁，露出笑容。「真的嗎？什麼牌子？」「你渴的那個牌子。」

en_text: “Are you sure?”
zh_text: 「你確定？」

en_text: “Positive.”
zh_text: 「非常確定。」

en_text: “In the half gallon?”
zh_text: 「三公升裝的？」

en_text: “Yeah.”
zh_text: 「是啊。」

en_text: “How much?”
zh_text: 「多少錢？」

en_text: I can’t just say three dollars. I have to be accurate. “Two ninety-nine.”
zh_text: 我不能約略說個三塊錢。我得要講精確一點才行。「兩塊九毛九。」

en_text: I can see her thinking about it, but I don’t interrupt with the answer. “That’s two forty-four off. Quite a savings. Have you seen my latest jigsaw puzzle?”
zh_text: 我看得出來她在計算這個價錢，不過我沒有打擾她。「便宜兩塊四毛四。省不少錢呀。你看過我的新拼圖嗎？」

en_text: It’s actually two forty-six off, but I say nothing. “Not yet.”
zh_text: 其實是便宜兩塊四毛六，不過我沒說什麼。「沒看過。」「你覺得怎樣？」

en_text: “Go and take a look. It’s by the TV.” I look at the jigsaw puzzle. I mean, really look at it because I know she’ll quiz me on it. A cottage. Trees. Flowers. Sky. Jigsaw puzzles are like sitcoms, I guess—they’re all the fucking same. I head back into the kitchen. She’s drying my plate. “What did you think?” she asks, using a tone that suggests my answer is important to her, but only as long as it’s the right answer.
zh_text: 我看了看拼圖。我是說，仔細研究了一下，因為我知道她會來問我問題。一座農舍。有樹。有花，有天空。拼圖就像情境喜劇，我猜——它們全都他媽的一模一樣。我走回廚房。她在擦乾我的盤子。

en_text: “Nice.”
zh_text: 「很棒。」

en_text: “Did you like the cottage?”
zh_text: 「喜歡那座農舍嗎？」

en_text: “Yeah.”
zh_text: 「喜歡。」

en_text: “What about the ﬂowers?”
zh_text: 「那些花呢？」

en_text: “Colorful.”
zh_text: 「七彩繽紛。」

en_text: “Which ones did you like the best?”
zh_text: 「你最喜歡哪些花？」

en_text: “The red ones. In the corner.”
zh_text: 「紅花。角落那些。」

en_text: “The left or right corner?”
zh_text: 「左邊還是右邊角落？」

en_text: “You’ve only done the left corner, Mom.”
zh_text: 「妳只拼了左半邊，媽。」

en_text: Satisﬁed I’m telling the truth, she puts the dishes away. Back in the lounge we sit down and continue talking. About what, I have no idea. All I can think about is what it would be like if she lost her voice.
zh_text: 確定我沒敷衍她後，她收起盤子。回到客廳，我們坐下來繼續聊天。聊什麼，完全不知道。我腦子只想著如果她變啞巴了會怎麼樣。

en_text: “I’m just going to get myself a drink, Mom. Are you sure you don’t want one?”
zh_text: 「我要去弄點東西喝，媽。妳確定妳不喝嗎？」

en_text: “If it will shut you up, I will. Make it a coffee, and make it strong.”
zh_text: 如果能讓你閉嘴的話，我就喝。弄杯咖啡好了，濃一點。

en_text: I head into the kitchen. Put the kettle on. Scoop some coffee into two cups. I grab the bag of rat poison that was also on sale at the supermarket, but not quite as good a savings as the orange juice I didn’t buy, but Mom would still be proud of the savings nonetheless. I scoop a generous amount into her coffee. Mom needs her coffee strong because her taste buds are failing her. When the kettle has boiled, I stir the stuff for two minutes until it dissolves.
zh_text: 我走向廚房。燒開水。舀了點咖啡到兩個杯子裡。我拿起同樣在超級市場裡特價的老鼠藥，不過它不像我沒買的柳橙汁便宜那麼多。我舀了一大瓢放到她的杯子裡。媽要咖啡濃一點是因為她的味蕾已經不行了。水開了後，我整整攪拌了兩分鐘，直到裡面的粉末通通溶化。

en_text: Back in the living room she has the TV going again but starts talking to me anyway. I hand over her drink. She adjusts the volume on the TV so she can still hear the voices while talking to me. The white guys are doing something oddly funny. I wonder how funny they would be if they lived in an apartment complex like mine. Mom hunches over and slowly drinks her drink, holding the cup defensively as if she’s expecting somebody to make a grab for it. When she ﬁnishes, I offer to wash her cup. She refuses, does it herself, then complains. Since she is complaining anyway, I make a deliberate show of looking at my watch, scrunch my face up in surprise at how late it is, and tell her I really need to be going.
zh_text: 回到客廳，她又打開電視，不過還是開口跟我聊天。我把咖啡遞給她。她調整電視的音量，讓她能一邊跟我講話，一邊聽到電視裡的聲音。那些白人又做了一些非常好笑的事情。我在想如果住在我那種公寓的話，他們是能好笑到哪裡去。媽弓身緩緩喝著咖啡，緊緊握著杯子，一副有人要搶她的模樣。喝完之後，我說要幫她洗杯子。她拒絕，自己去洗，然後抱怨。反正她已經在抱怨了，我乾脆故意看了看手錶，裝出一副驚覺時間已經這麼晚了的樣子，然後告訴她我真的該走了。

en_text: I have to go through the whole scenario of kissing her good-bye on the doorstep. She thanks me for the ﬂowers and makes me promise to stay in touch, as if I’m heading to another country rather than the other side of the city. I promise I will, and she looks at me as though I’m going to ignore her for the rest of her life. It’s her guilt look, and I’m familiar with it. Nonetheless, it makes me feel bad. I was already feeling bad. Bad that she is alone. Bad that I am a bad son. Sad that one day something may happen to her, God forbid.
zh_text: 我必須走完在門口親吻她的完整流程。她謝過我的鮮花，讓我保證要常常聯絡，彷彿我是要出國，而不是要回家。我保證會聯絡，而她以一副我這輩子都不會管她的神情看著我。那是她專門讓我感到罪惡的神情，我早就看習慣了。無論如何，這個神情還是讓我罪惡。我本來就覺得很罪惡了。爲了讓她一個人住感到罪惡。爲了我是個壞兒子感到罪惡。爲了某天她可能會出什麼事而感到哀傷，但願不要。

en_text: I wave from the sidewalk but she is already gone. Where would I be without Mom? I don’t know and I never want to ﬁnd out.
zh_text: 我在門前走道上揮手道別，不過她已經回去了。要是沒有媽的話，我現在會流落何方？我不知道，而我從不想知道。

en_text: The bus comes along and it’s not the same old guy from last night, and I’m pretty sure I know why that is. This is some young guy in his midtwenties. He calls me man, grins at me, and because I’m the only person on the bus, he feels obliged to make conversation. I stare out the window and nod and say yeah when he expects it, which is far more often than I’d like. There isn’t much in the way of life beyond the bus windows; the occasional taxi, the occasional person out late walking a dog, those occasions become more regular the closer we get to town, then less regular once we pass through it. I am more than three-quarters of the way home when I see it. It’s just lying there on the side of the road, still moving. Kind of.
zh_text: 公車來了，司機不是昨天晚上那個老頭。搞不好他已經死了。今天的司機是個二十來歲的年輕小夥子。他叫我「老兄」，朝我咧齒微笑，由於我是車上唯一的乘客，他覺得有義務跟我聊天。我凝望窗外，在該有反應的時候點頭稱是。

en_text: “You said . . .”
“Just stop it, okay?”
zh_text: 「停車，好嗎？」

en_text: “You’re the boss, buddy.”
zh_text: 「你說了算，老兄。」

en_text: He stops the bus, and if I really was his buddy he would give me a quarter of my fare back. The swish of the doors as they close behind me, the purring of the motor, the shuddering of heavy metal, and the bus leaves me behind. We’re about halfway between town and my apartment. It’s a suburb where people who have made poor choices in life live. I rush over the road and crouch next to it. It’s mostly white, with a few streaks of ginger through it. Its mouth is slightly open. It’s not moving: maybe I made a mistake when I ﬁrst saw it. When I put my hand on its side, it’s still warm. Its eyes open and look at me. It tries to meow but can’t. One of its legs sticks out in that same awkward way as Candy’s arm.
zh_text: 他停車，真要跟我稱兄道弟，他就更應該退我四分之一的車錢。我聽見車門在我身後關閉的聲音、引擎呼嘯聲、沉重金屬震動的聲音、接著公車揚長而去。我快步衝到路旁，蹲在牠的旁邊。牠毛色幾乎純白，微帶幾絲薑黃色的斑紋。牠的嘴角微張，沒有在動；或許剛剛是我看錯了。我伸手觸摸牠的身側，還有體溫。牠張開雙眼，看著我。牠想叫，但是叫不出聲。牠其中一條腿折成像是坎蒂手臂那種奇特角度。

en_text: Funny what fate does to us. Two nights ago it wasn’t my place in this crazy, mixed-up world to question the fact that animals are used as tools. They’re used every single day. Chemicals are tested on them so we can have higher-quality health care, higher-quality shampoos, matching eyeliners, warmer clothes. Others are killed for food. And here’s my opportunity to balance the scales for what I did to poor Fluffy.
zh_text: 命運真有趣。兩天前，我一點也不質疑在這個瘋狂混亂的世界中拿動物當作工具的事情。牠們每天都被當成工具。人們拿牠們實驗化學藥劑，好讓我們享有品質更好的醫療、品質更好的洗髮精、對稱的眼線、溫暖的衣服。其他動物則被當作食物。而此刻就是我彌補殺害可憐小貓的機會。

en_text: I pick the cat up, careful to keep my hands away from its broken leg. It meows loudly and tries to struggle, but doesn’t have the energy to struggle hard. The long graze down the side of its body looks bloody and raw. Its fur is matted. Strange sounds are coming from it. Rather than holding it against my body, I remove the plastic bag that the groceries came in from my briefcase and rest the cat inside. I begin to walk home.
zh_text: 我撿起那隻貓，小心不去觸碰牠的斷腳。牠喵喵大叫，試圖掙扎，但是沒有體力用力掙扎。牠身側長長的一道擦傷看來血肉模糊。牠的毛蓬亂糾結。牠不斷發出奇怪的聲音。我不想把牠抱在身上，於是自公事包中拿出購物袋，將貓放入其中。我開始走路回家。

en_text: After less than half a mile I come across a phone booth. I ﬁnd the number for an all-night vet and tell them I’m on my way. Then I call a taxi. It takes ﬁve minutes to arrive. The driver is foreign and speaks the same amount of English as the cat. I’ve torn the page from the phone book and I hand it to him. He reads the address and starts driving. The cat is no longer meowing, but it’s still alive. I let it out of the bag before stepping through the vet doors.
zh_text: 走不到半公里，我路過一座電話亭。我找出一間半夜有開的獸醫診所，告訴他們我要過去。接著我打電話叫計程車。車子於五分鐘後抵達。司機是個外國人，會說的英文不比那隻貓多。我把剛剛自電話簿中撕下的頁面拿給他看。他記下地址，開始開車。貓不叫了，不過還活著。我在踏入診所大門前將貓取出購物袋。

en_text: Inside a woman about my age waits behind a counter. She has long red hair tied in a ponytail. She wears little makeup and doesn’t need it—she’s a natural beauty with soft brown eyes and full lips. She’s wearing a white medical jacket unbuttoned halfway down, as if she’s about to step onto the set of a porn movie. Beneath it is a blue T-shirt. A great set of breasts pushes its way forward. She smiles at me for less than a second before her concern turns to the cat.
zh_text: 裡面有個跟我年紀相仿的女人等在櫃檯後。她將一頭紅髮綁成一條馬尾。她有上薄妝，不過沒有必要——她是個天生的美人，有著淡棕色的眼眸和豐厚的嘴唇。她身穿白色的醫療外套，上半身沒扣釦子，彷彿正要踏入色情片的拍攝現場一樣。外套下是件藍汗衫。高聳的雙峰向前隆起。她對我微笑了不到一秒，注意力隨即轉移到貓的身上。

en_text: “You’re the man who just called?”
zh_text: 「你是剛打電話來的人？」

en_text: “Yeah.”

“You ran the cat over?” she asks in a soft voice, without managing to sound accusing. “I found him,” I say. “I don’t have a car, that’s why I had to catch a taxi here,” I say, and for some reason it’s important to me that she believes that.
zh_text: 「你壓過這隻貓？」她輕聲詢問，沒有指責的意味「我發現牠。」我說。「所以我才搭計程車過來。」

en_text: She takes the cat from me without comment then disappears. I’m left standing by myself. I take a quick look around the clinic. Not much to see. Two walls are dedicated to products like leashes, collars, ﬂea powder, bowls, cages, and food. Another wall has a thousand brochures and pamphlets that don’t concern me since none of them is about getting away with murder. I take a seat. I should have been in bed by now. Should have been asleep. I stare at a display of bags of cat litter. I know from experience it’s twice the price here than at the supermarket.
zh_text: 她不加評論，自我手中接過貓咪，然後離開。我被獨自留在那裡，不明白我為什麼會想解釋真實的情況。我迅速打量診所。沒什麼好看的。兩面牆上展示著鏈條、項圈、除蚤粉、碗、籠子以及食物。另外一面牆上擺滿一千張我沒興趣的傳單跟小冊子，因為沒有一張在教人如何擺脫殺人罪嫌。我找個位子坐下。現在我應該已經上床了才對。應該已經睡著了才對。我望著一包貓沙。根據我的經驗，這玩意兒在這種地方的售價比超級市場貴一倍。

en_text: I sit patiently. Five minutes turn into ten, then into twenty. I pick up a pamphlet on ﬂea control. On the cover is an artist’s impression of what a magniﬁed ﬂea would look like if it were wearing sunglasses and a leather jacket and hosting a party in the fur of a cat. On the next page is an actual photograph of a ﬂea, magniﬁed several hundred times. It seems the artist had it completely wrong. I’m halfway through the brochure, thinking about how scary the world would be if ﬂeas were actually several hundred times bigger, when the redhead comes back out. I put the pamphlet down and hold my breath and stand up.
zh_text: 我耐心等候。五分鐘、十分鐘、二十分鐘。我拿起一份防治跳蚤的小冊子。封面上畫了一隻藝術家眼中的跳蚤——如果牠正戴著太陽眼鏡、穿著皮夾克、在貓的毛皮上開派對的話。下一頁有張放大幾百倍的跳蚤照片。看來藝術家完全畫錯了。看到一半的時候，紅髮女子走了出來。我起身。

en_text: “The cat’s going to be okay,” she says, breaking into a smile.
zh_text: 「貓會好起來。」她說，面露微笑。

en_text: “What a relief,” I say, almost too tired to mean it.
zh_text: 「太好了。」我說，疲憊到語氣聽來不太誠懇。

en_text: “Do you know who he belongs to?”
zh_text: 「你知道他的主人是谁嗎？」

en_text: “We’re going to need to keep him here for a few days.”
zh_text: 「我們需要留牠在這裡幾天。」

en_text: “Sure, sure, that sounds good,” I say, thankful for her help. I realize I’m nodding like an idiot. “Umm, what happens if you can’t ﬁnd the owner? I mean, it won’t get put down, will it?”
zh_text: 「當然，當然，聽起來很好。」我說，感激她的幫助。「呃，如果找不到主人怎麼辦？我是說，你們不會把他安樂死吧？」

en_text: She shrugs, like she doesn’t know, but I think she does. I give her my name and phone number, then pay for the medical attention the cat will need using the money Candy no longer needs. She doesn’t try to stop my generosity, but she does point it out. She says I’m an incredibly nice man. I see no need to argue. She tells me she will call to let me know of the cat’s progress.
zh_text: 她聳肩，好像她不知道，但是我認爲她知道。我留下我的姓名和電話，然後支付那隻貓需要的醫療費用。她沒有阻止我付那麼多錢，不過她有告知我付太多了。她說我是個難得一見的大好人。我看不出來有爭辯這一點的必要。她說她會打電話讓我知道之後的發展。

en_text: I ask her if she can call me a taxi, but she says she’s about to leave, and offers me a lift home.
zh_text: 我請她幫我叫計程車，不過她說她要下班了，可以載我回家。

en_text: I glance at my watch. It would be fun to get a ride with her, but where would I dump her body? “I don’t want to put you out. A taxi’s ﬁne.”
zh_text: 我看了我的錶一眼。坐她的車會很愉快，不過我要在哪裡棄置她的屍體？「我不想太麻煩妳。計程車就好了。」

en_text: She seems disappointed, but doesn’t strengthen her offer. The taxi driver is a large man whose stomach rests on the steering wheel and toots the horn every time we go over a bump. He drops me off outside my apartment, the potholes in my street making him wake up the neighbors in the process. The trash outside my apartment has been added to by more trash, and I have to bat away a few ﬂies as I make my way inside. I’m struggling to stay awake as I climb my way up to my door. Inside I ignore my ﬁsh, making me not quite the nice guy the vet receptionist thought I was, opting to spend some quality time with my bed instead. I lie down and close my eyes and pretty much fall right asleep.
zh_text: 計程車司機是個胖子，肚子頂在方向盤上，車身每次震動都會壓到喇叭。他在我家門口放我下來。我沒管我的魚，直接爬上床，轉眼沉沉睡去。

en_text: Seven thirty my eyes open. Right on time. I don’t have to worry about shaking away any dregs of a dream, because I never dream. I guess I don’t because half the shit people dream about I actually do. If I did, I suppose it would be of being married to some plumpish woman with poor taste in everything from fashion to sexual positions. I’d be living inside a house with a mortgage that would take a lifetime to pay off, getting nagged by two unﬁt kids every single day. I’d be taking out trash and mowing lawns. Each Sunday morning as I pulled out of the driveway in my station wagon on my way to church, I’d have to avoid running over the dog. A Goddamn nightmare.
zh_text: 我雙眼於七點半睜開。很準時。我不需要用開任何夢中殘餘的片段，因為我從不做夢。我想之所以不做夢是因為我真的會去做半數人們在夢裡會做的事情。萬一真的做夢，我想我會夢到跟個從時尙感到性愛姿勢通通品味不佳的胖女人結婚。我會住在一間貸款交到死都交不完的房子裡，每天都讓兩個討人厭的孩子煩得要死。我得要倒垃圾，還得給草皮除草。每個禮拜天，當我駕駛休旅車前往教堂時，我都必須小心不要壓到狗。真他媽的惡夢。

en_text: I share my morning routing with a feeling I can’t quite shake, like there’s bad news I haven’t been given yet. It becomes so strong that I have to take a few minutes to sit down on the sofa and take some deep breaths. My eyes blur with tears, and even playing with Pickle and Jehovah can’t cheer me up. I think of the cat I saved last night. That can’t cheer me up either. Something bad has happened. I think of Mom and hope she’s okay.
zh_text: 換衣服的時候，一股不祥的預感突然來襲。那感覺像是一個我還沒收到的壞消息。我不確定是怎麼回事，不過在進行上班前的例行公事期間一直有這種感覺。我的雙眼泛淚，就連跟泡菜還有耶和華玩都沒辦法讓我好過一點。我想著昨晚救的那隻貓。一樣沒能讓我好一點。有壞事發生了。我想到媽，希望她沒事。

en_text: I make myself a quick breakfast before going to work. No need to walk around hungry just because of bad premonitions. I’m running late so have to run for the bus. Mr. Stanley sees me coming and waits. “Almost missed you this morning, Joe,” he says, and this time he punches my ticket— perhaps as punishment for putting him thirty seconds off schedule. Despite that, I still like him. He’s an okay guy.
zh_text: 我匆匆吃了早餐，然後去上班。沒必要爲了不祥預感就餓肚子。公車上，史丹利先生剪了我的票，照例跟我嘘寒問暖。我喜歡史丹利先生。他人不錯。

en_text: Now, Mr. Stanley lives my nightmare. He’s married with two kids, one of them in a wheelchair. I know all this because I followed him home one day. Not as a potential victim (though everybody has potential, so I learned in school), but just out of curiosity. It’s amazing that a guy with a useless kid and an ugly wife and a crappy job can be so friendly every day. Perhaps more suspicious than amazing. I want to ask him what his secret is.
zh_text: 好吧，史丹利先生就是活在我的惡夢裡。他結婚了，有兩個小孩，其中之一必須坐輪椅。我知道這些是因為我跟蹤他回家過一次。不是把他當作有潛力的目標（雖然根據我在學校所學，每個人都有潛力），只是爲了滿足我的好奇。我很難想像有個廢物小孩、醜老婆以及爛工作的男人每天怎麼還能如此和善。

en_text: I walk down the aisle. Find a seat behind a couple of businessmen. The two of them are talking loudly about money, mergers, and acquisitions. I wonder who they are trying to impress on this bus. Maybe each other.
zh_text: 我沿著走道走去，坐在兩個生意人後方。他們兩個大聲談論著金錢、併購及獲利之類的事情。我不知道在這輛公車上他們是在講給誰聽。或許是彼此。

en_text: Mr. Stanley stops the bus directly outside work for me. The doors open. I climb out. It’s another hot summer day. It will get somewhere around eighty-ﬁve or ninety degrees, I’m guessing. I lower the zip on my overalls from my neck down to my waist, revealing my white T-shirt, and I roll up my sleeves. There haven’t been any scratches on my arms for nearly two months.
zh_text: 史丹利先生爲我將公車直接停在警局外面。車門開啓。我下車。又是一個炎熱的夏天。今天最高溫會高達三十二或三十三度，我猜。我拉下工作服的拉鍊，捲起我的衣袖。我的手臂已經將近兩個月沒有被人抓傷了。

en_text: The air shimmers. The day is still. It’s classic global warming weather. I wait for two cars to run the red light before I cross the road. Outside the police station the drunks from the night’s holding tanks are being let out, their faces scrunched up in the bright autumn sun.
zh_text: 空氣微微閃爍。四周一片沉悶。我等待兩輛汽車闖紅燈，然後才穿越馬路。警局外，昨晚拘留的酒鬼都被放了出來，他們的臉在耀眼陽光下揪成一團。

en_text: The air in the police station is cool. Sally is waiting outside the elevator. She spots me before I can make a dash for the stairs, so I have to head over. I push the button, then keep pushing it because it’s what’s expected of somebody with no clue how things in this world work.
zh_text: 警局裡的空氣十分清涼。莎莉等在電梯外。她在我有機會衝到樓梯口前發現了我，所以我只好走過去。我按下按鈕，然後繼續按，因為像我這種對世界運作方式毫無概念的人就是應該做出這種行為。

en_text: “Morning, Joe,” she says in the carefully structured, drawn-out way of a woman struggling with the concept of speech. I have to offer my own version of it, because retarded or not, everybody around here expects me to talk like an imbecile.
zh_text: 「早安，喬。」她以一種咬字清晰又拉得很長的語調說話，像個搞不清楚該怎麼講話的女人。我也得裝出這種語調，因為不管是不是白痴，這裡的人都期待我像個低能兒般講話。

en_text: “Hi morning, Sally,” I say, and then I smile the big-kid smile with all the teeth, the one that suggests I’m proud to have strung three words together to make a sentence, even if I did fuck it up.
zh_text: 「嗨早安，莎莉。」我說，像個大男孩般露齒而笑，一副我對自己能夠說出由三個單字組成的句子十分驕傲的模樣，雖然這句話說得怪怪的。

en_text: “What a beautiful day. Do you like this weather, Joe?”
zh_text: 「真是美好的一天。你喜歡這種天氣嗎，喬？」

en_text: Actually it’s a bit hot for my taste. “I like the warm sun. I like summer.” I’m talking like an idiot so Slow Sally can understand me. “I like Christmas even more.”
zh_text: 事實上，我覺得有點熱。「我喜歡溫暖的陽光。我喜歡夏天。」我像白痴般講話，好讓智障莎莉聽懂我在講什麼。

en_text: “You should join me for lunch by the river,” she says, hitting on me and almost making me gag. I can just imagine how much fun that’d be. How much fun I’d have as the other people walk by looking at one person pretending to be retarded while the other pretends to be normal. We could throw bread at the ducks and tell each other which clouds look like pirate ships and which look like the bloated corpses of drowning victims. Damn, does Sally even know she isn’t normal? Do their kind know that about themselves?
zh_text: 今天跟我去河邊午餐吧。」她說，主動搭訕，讓我差點嗆到。我能夠想像那景象有多有趣。看著路過的人欣賞一個假裝白痴的正常人和一個假裝正常的白痴一起吃飯的模樣會多有趣。我們可以丟麵包給鴨子吃，告訴對方哪片雲看起來像海盜船，哪片看起來像浮屍或是溺斃的被害人。可惡，莎莉究竟知不知道自己不正常？她們那種人知道自己與衆不同嗎？

en_text: The elevator arrives. I’m confused as to whether I should do the gentlemanly thing and let her step in ﬁrst, or do the retarded thing and push ahead of her? I do the gentlemanly thing, because the retarded thing means I’d have to scream as the elevator goes up a few stories and then pretend to be in awe at how the scenery has changed when the doors open.
zh_text: 電梯到了。我不知道該像個紳士般讓她先進去，還是像個智障般搶先進去？我決定當紳士，因為當智障就表示我得要在電梯上升幾樓後開始尖叫，然後在發現電梯門後景觀不同時做出驚訝的反應。

en_text: “Fourth ﬂoor, Joe?”
zh_text: 「三樓嗎，喬？」

en_text: “Sure.”
zh_text: 「當然。』

en_text: The doors close.
zh_text: 門關了。

en_text: “So?”
zh_text: 「那麼？」

en_text: “So what’ll it be? You want to join me for lunch?”
zh_text: 「那麼你覺得呢？你要跟我共進午餐嗎？」

en_text: “I like my ofﬁce, Sally. I like sitting there and looking out the window.” “I know you do, Joe. But outside is good for you.”
zh_text: 「我喜歡我的辦公室，莎莉。我喜歡坐在裡面，看著窗外。」「我知道，喬。但是出去走走對你比較好。」

en_text: “Not always.”
zh_text: 「不是一直都這樣。」

en_text: “Thanks.” “Do you enjoy catching the bus home?”
zh_text: 「你喜歡坐公車回家嗎？」

en_text: “I can give you a lift sometimes, if you’d like.”
zh_text: 「喜歡的話，我可以載你回家。」

en_text: “I like the bus.”
zh_text: 「我喜歡公車。」

en_text: She shrugs, gives up on our conversation. “I’ll drop off those sandwiches for you soon.”
zh_text: 她聳肩，放棄交談。「我過一會兒送三明治給你。」

en_text: “Thanks, Sally. That’ll be nice.”
zh_text: 「謝謝，莎莉。那樣好。」

en_text: And it would be nice. Sally may be a dimwit, she may have a crush on me, but she’s always been good to me. Always friendly. Nobody else has ever offered me food, or offered me a lift home (though surely she can’t drive—she must mean a lift with her mom or something), and I could do a lot worse. Even though I don’t like her, I don’t not like her as much as I don’t like everybody else. In a way that makes her the closest thing I have to a friend. Outside of my goldﬁsh.
zh_text: 那樣確實不錯。莎莉或許是個傻瓜，她或許喜歡我，不過她總是對我很好。總是非常親切。沒有別人帶東西給我吃，或是說要送我回家（不過她當然不會開車——她一定是指讓她媽或是誰來載我們一起回家），而我可能會遇上更糟糕的人。儘管我不喜歡她，但是我不喜歡她的程度還沒有到我不喜歡別人那種地步。從某方面而言，她是最接近朋友定義的人。除了我的金魚之外。

en_text: The doors close, and the smile I offer Sally as they do isn’t forced, it’s natural, and I realize this too late to change it to my big-boy grin. She stares at me with a blank look on her face, then the doors close and Sally is gone, and a moment later she is gone from my thoughts. I head straight to the conference room.
zh_text: 電梯門關閉時，我向莎莉露出的笑容並不是勉強擠出來的，而是很自然的，當我發現這一點時已經太遲，沒機會換回那個大男孩微笑了。電梯門關了，莎莉離開了，片刻過後，她也遠離我的腦海。我直接走向會議室。

en_text: “Hi there, Joe.”
“Morning, Detective Schroder.”
zh_text: 「早安，施羅德警探。」

en_text: I start looking at him as a suspect, trying to picture him killing Walker. It’s easy to do. Of course it’s easy to picture any of these people killing her, from the photographer to the pathologist. The ﬁrst thing I need to do is get a list of these people, then begin eliminating them. As suspects, that is.
zh_text: 我開始把他當成嫌犯般打量，試圖想像他殺害沃克的模樣。施羅德身材壯碩，看起來像是由一團批著皮膚的肌肉組成。如果我會被抓的話，我會盡量不讓他抓到。現在我要將所有偵辦此案的人員當成嫌犯，從攝影師到法醫。我要做的第一件事就是弄一份這些人員的名單，然後開始排除他們。排除嫌犯的可能，我是指。

en_text: “How’s the in . . . inv . . . invest . . .” I stop. Just long enough for him to think I’m in that small percentile of the population with an extra chromosome. “How’s the case going, Detective Schroder? Found the killer yet?”
zh_text: 「那件……那件……」我說到一半停下。剛好久到讓他以爲我就是那百分之零點五多出來一條染色體的人。「那件案子怎麼樣了，施羅德警探？找到兇手沒？」

en_text: He shakes his head slowly, as if he’s trying to line up a few thoughts in there, but not too hard in case some of them get broken. “Not yet, Joe. Getting there.”
zh_text: 他緩緩搖頭，彷彿試圖在裡面排列一些思緒，但又沒有很用力在排，因為怕弄破它們。「還沒，喬。快找到了。」

en_text: “Any suspects, Detective Schroder?”
zh_text: 「有嫌犯嗎，施羅德警探？」

en_text: “A few. And Joe, you can call me Carl.”
zh_text: 「有幾個。還有喬，你可以叫我卡爾。」

en_text: I’m not going to call him Carl. He’s asked me before. Anyway, I’ve already shortened detective inspector to just detective. And as for there being a few suspects—he’s lying.
zh_text: 我才不要叫他卡爾。他以前就這樣說過了。反正我已經把偵緝督察簡化爲警探了。

en_text: He stares at the photographs, grimacing, like he does every morning now. Almost as though he’s expecting to come in and ﬁnd one of the victims has reached out from her portrait and written an answer up there for him. In reality he has nothing. He knows it. I know it. Everybody knows it. Especially the media.
zh_text: 他盯著照片，眉頭深鎖，就跟每天早上一樣。那感覺就像是他期待能夠一到警局就發現有個被害人從照片裡跑出來爲他寫下答案一樣。在現實裡，他毫無線索。他知道。我知道。所有人都知道。特別是媒體。

en_text: “Are you sure they’ve all been killed by the same person, Detective Schroder?” He turns and stares at me, and I regret my question. “Why’s that, Joe? Have you been listening in on our conversations?”
zh_text: 「你確定他們都是同一個人殺的嗎，施羅德警探？」

en_text: I look down. “Umm . . . I was just, you know, curious.”
zh_text: 我低頭。「呃……沒有，施羅德警探。我只是，你知道，好奇。」

en_text: “Life is curious, Joe, and to answer your question, all of these murders all related.”
zh_text: 「人生總是非常奇妙，喬，還有沒錯，這些案子全都有關聯。」

en_text: I lift my head up fast and look over at him, widening my eyes in what hopefully looks like surprise. “They’re all sisters, Detective Schroder?”
zh_text: 我迅速抬頭，看向他的身後，瞪大雙眼，故作驚訝貌。「她們都是姊妹，施羅德警探？」

en_text: I ought to get a Goddamn Emmy for this performance.
zh_text: 我的演技應該得艾美獎。

en_text: “Not related that way, Joe,” he sighs, and after a pause of a few seconds he carries on. “I mean they were all killed by the same person.” “Oh. But that’s good, right? Better to have one killer out there than seven?”
zh_text: 「不是那種關聯，喬。」他嘆氣，停了將近十秒。「我是說她們都是同一名兇手所殺。」

en_text: He nods. “It doesn’t make any difference to them,” he says, pointing at the photographs. “But in this case,” he says, then pauses, “you’re not going to repeat any of this to anybody, are you, Joe? You don’t have friends in the media?”
zh_text: 「喔。你確定嗎？」「不會把我的話轉述給別人，是吧，喬？你沒有媒體界的朋友吧？」

en_text: I shake my head, trying to keep a similar pace to Schroder’s shake a few minutes ago. He thinks I have no friends. He doesn’t know about Pickle and Jehovah. “You guys are the only friends I have, Detective Schroder.”
zh_text: 我搖頭，試圖模仿幾分鐘前施羅德警探搖頭的步調。他以爲我沒有朋友。他不知道泡菜和耶和華的事情。「你們就是我唯一的朋友，施羅德警探。」

en_text: “Have you ever heard of a copycat killer, Joe?”
zh_text: 你有聽說過模仿殺人犯嗎，喬？

en_text: I stop shaking my head before whiplash sets in. “Why would somebody kill cats?” There’s another long sigh from Schroder, and I realize I might be laying it on a bit thick.
zh_text: 我搖頭搖到快要扭傷脖子才停。「怎麼會有人殺貓？」施羅德警探再度長嘆，我發現我裝得或許太過火了。

en_text: “Not quite, Joe. A copycat killer is somebody who kills to imitate a serial killer.”
zh_text: 不是殺貓，喬。模仿殺人犯是模仿連續殺人犯殺人的人。「他們爲什麼要這麼做？」

en_text: “Why would they do that?” “Because they can. Because they want to. Because they’re insane.”
zh_text: 「因為他們能這麼做。因為他們想這麼做。因為他們瘋了。』

en_text: “Oh. Then why are these people out there, Detective Schroder? Why don’t they get put in jail?”
zh_text: 「喔。那這種人爲什麼能逍遙法外，施羅德警探？爲什麼不把他們抓起來關？』

en_text: “That’s a good question,” he says, and I smile at his praise. “And it comes with a simple answer. The world is screwed up. You know when you turn on the news and some bastard has gone and shot his family and a few of his neighbors?”
zh_text: 「這是個好問題。」他說，我假裝在他讚揚的語氣下微笑。「答案很簡單。世界亂了。你知道那種打開電視就看到有人槍殺自己家人和鄰居的新聞的感覺？」

en_text: I start nodding. Stab thy neighbor. I’m familiar with it.
zh_text: 我開始點頭。刺死你的鄰居。我很熟悉那種感覺。

en_text: “The family, the other neighbors, they all say what a quiet guy he was. He had a collection of gun magazines and problems. Then we use hindsight as a preventative, even though it’s too late by then. There’s nothing to prevent, because everybody’s already dead. . . . I’m sorry, Joe,” he says, sighing. “I’m rambling on a bit. And venting. I shouldn’t be burdening you with any of this.” “I don’t mind.”
zh_text: 「家人、其他朋友，他們全都宣稱兇手是個安靜的人。他有很多槍械雜誌和問題。我們總是事後才恍然大悟，但是一切都太遲了。我們沒有辦法預防這種事情，因為所有人都已經死了……我很抱歉，喬。」他嘆氣說道。「我在胡言亂語。我不該說這些話給你聽的。「我不介意。」

en_text: “I just wish we could do more. I mean, we see these guys every day, but can we do anything about it? No. Because they have rights. Just like the rest of us. And until they ﬁnally kill somebody—and they often try to— those rights make them untouchable. Do you know what I mean, Joe?”
zh_text: 「我只希望有更多我們能做的事情。我是說，我們每天都看到這些人，但是我們能夠做任何事情來預防這種情況嗎？不行。因為他們都有人權。就像我們其他人一樣。除非他們終於動手殺人——而他們通常都會嘗試動手——他們都受到人權保護。你知道我的意思嗎，喬？」

en_text: “Kind of, Detective Schroder.”
zh_text: 「大概吧，施羅德警探。」

en_text: He waves his hand at the wall. “A hundred to one we’ve spoken to this guy at some point in the past. We know he’s got either a drug or a mental problem, but we could never do anything about it. Right now he’s watching us, mocking us, laughing at us. I guarantee we’ve wanted to lock this guy up before, but weren’t allowed. I guarantee we’ve had this guy in this building before.”
zh_text: 他向牆面揮手。「我敢打賭一賠一百，我們已經跟兇手會過面了。我們知道他要嘛就是有毒癮，不然就是心理有問題，但是我們什麼都不能做。此刻他正在監視我們，愚弄我們，嘲笑我們。我敢說我們絕對曾想要把這傢伙關起來過，只是上面不允許。我敢說我們曾把這傢伙抓進警局過。」

en_text: He’s right and wrong, but I can’t point this out to him. Can’t take a bet on his odds. With all his sermonizing I quickly lose faith in Schroder as an appropriate suspect. “I understand, Detective Schroder.”
zh_text: 他說得對也不對，但是我不能爲他指出這一點。我不能跟他對賭一賠一百。這段長篇大論讓我迅速將他排除在嫌犯名單外。「我了解，施羅德警探。」

en_text: “You’d be one of the few if you do, Joe. You want to know something funny?” “Sure.”
zh_text: 你是少數能夠了解的人，如果你真的了解的話，喬。想聽件可笑的事情嗎？當然。

en_text: “Serial killers like to stay ahead of the game, and you know how they do that?”
zh_text: 「連續殺人犯喜歡領先警方，你知道他們會怎麼做嗎？」

en_text: Fact is, I do know. They hang around the edges of the investigation. They might come into the station and say they saw something going on. They come in and try to get a feel for the investigation. Some even hang around in cop bars, listening to idle chitchat, even participating in conversation. Or hang out with reporters looking for an inside scoop.
zh_text: 事實上，我還眞的知道。他們會在調查人員旁徘徊。他們可能會跑來警局，宣稱他們見過某些事發經過。他們跑來打探調查的進度。有些人甚至會跑去警察酒吧混，聽他們說長論短，甚至參與討論。或是混在記者之間，試圖探聽內幕。

en_text: “No. How?”
zh_text: 「不知道。怎麼做？」

en_text: He shrugs again. “Sorry, Joe, I shouldn’t be chewing your ear off like this.”
zh_text: 他再度聳肩。「抱歉，喬，我不該這樣煩你。」

en_text: “So what about the cat killer?” I ask.
zh_text: 「那貓咪殺手怎麼樣？」

en_text: “Some other time,” he sighs, and he says it in a way to indicate the conversation is over. I leave him staring silently at the wall of the dead.
zh_text: 「改天再說吧。」他嘆氣，我留他一個人繼續去盯著死者牆壁看。

en_text: I reach up and run my ﬁnger across the nameplate on my ofﬁce door. To the sides of it are four small screw holes. There never used to be anything on it until Sally showed up one day with a small sign with my name on it. Inside I swap my thoughts for a mop and bucket, and then go about cleaning the toilets. Before lunch I carry the vacuum cleaner into Detective Superintendent Stevens’s ofﬁce just as he is leaving. Stevens is the guy everybody answers to, even though he doesn’t do any of the footwork, groundwork, or thought work that goes into solving this case. Stevens has been ﬂown down from Wellington, and is one of the highestranking detectives in the country, though I can’t see why. All he does is sit in his appointed ofﬁce, ordering people about while demanding answers.
zh_text: 我伸手觸摸我辦公室門上的名牌。邊邊有四個小螺絲孔。從前這塊牌子上寫著維修室，直到有一天莎莉拿了一塊刻有我名字的小名牌過來。我進去拿了抹布和水桶，然後開始打掃廁所。午餐前，我在史帝文斯偵緝督察長出門的同時帶著吸塵器進入他的辦公室。所有人都要向他回報，即使他完全沒有參與此案跑腿、偵辦或是腦力激盪等工作。史帝文斯是從威靈頓空降來的，是全國階級最高的警探之一，不過我看不出他有何能耐。他每天就是坐在上面指定給他的辦公室裡，下達命令，要求答案。偶爾他會走來走去，抓起一疊文件或是文件夾，裝出一副好像他有事要忙或有地方要去的模樣。大部分的時間他都是個脾氣暴躁的傢伙。我不喜歡他，不過束手無策。偵緝督察長遭人殺害會讓這個部門成爲目光焦點，甚至讓人懷疑到我頭上來。

en_text: Occasionally he walks back and forth, grabbing a pile of papers or a folder, just trying to look as though he has something to do or someplace to be. Most of the time he’s a pretty pissed-off guy. I don’t like him, but can’t do anything about it. Murdering a police superintendent would be like playing with ﬁre. Stevens is in his late ﬁfties, has thinning black hair, and looks like the sort of policeman you wouldn’t approach for help. He is just over six feet and solidly built, but has these black eyes that any author would associate with crazed serial killers. He has a long face with wrinkles that run its entire length, like shallow knife wounds. His tanned skin is pitted with old acne scars around his neck. When he talks, he has a deep voice and an accent that sounds Caribbean, but that’s probably because of the cigars he’s always smoking. He’s one of those useless bastards who wear sports jackets with elbow patches sewn into them.
zh_text: 年近六十的史帝文斯有著一頭稀疏的黑髮，看起來就像那種你不會考慮找他幫忙的警察。他身高六呎出頭，體格十分結實，不過眼旁的黑眼圈會讓任何作家聯想到連續殺人魔。他長臉之上皺紋滿布，看來很像淺淺的刀傷。頸部的深色皮膚上密密麻麻都是年代久遠的粉刺疤痕。開口說話時聲音低沉，帶有一股加勒比腔調，不過那很可能是因為隨時不離手的雪茄菸的關係。他就是那種身穿手肘處縫有補綴的運動外套的大廢物。

en_text: I wonder if the ballpoint pen that was left behind was his. I look into his black eyes, searching for the evil that ﬁction suggests should be there, but I can’t see any of it.
zh_text: 我懷疑留在現場的原子筆是不是他的。我凝望他的黑眼珠，尋找小說裡描述的那種邪惡目光，不過看不出來。

en_text: He tells me to do a good job, says he’ll be back after lunch. That gives me plenty of time. So it’s just me in his ofﬁce, me and Mr. Vacuum Cleaner. I sweep it around the carpet like it makes a difference, looking left and right for any information that will help. Like the conference room, Stevens’s ofﬁce looks out onto the fourth ﬂoor, meaning people can look in if the blinds are open, as they are. Ten minutes of sucking the same piece of carpet go by, and it’s not getting any cleaner. I drop a rag behind his desk, bend down, and use the chance to peek into his desk drawers. I rummage through them, ﬁnding a roster of everybody involved in the case in the third drawer I check. I slip it into my overalls. Then I start coughing. Yep, Joe the retard needs a drink. I head to the water cooler. On the way back I pass the photocopying room. It’s empty, so I step inside and photocopy the roster. Walk back to the ofﬁce. Place the document back into the folder.
zh_text: 他叫我好好打掃，說他吃完午飯就會回來。這表示我時間充裕。只有我在他的辦公室裡，我和吸塵器先生。我在地毯上吸來吸去，好像當眞吸得乾淨一樣，左顧右盼地尋找可能會有用處的線索。跟會議室一樣，史帝文斯的辦公室能夠看見三樓內的景象，也就是說如果百葉窗拉起來的話，外面的人就會看見裡面，而現在百葉窗就是拉起來的。同一塊地毯吸了十分鐘，一點都沒有比較乾淨。我丟了塊抹布到他辦公桌後方，彎下腰去撿，趁機偷看他的抽屜。我拿起最上面的文件夾，打開它。裡面是所有參與此案人員的名冊。我將檔案夾塞入工作服。然後開始咳嗽。沒錯，智障喬需要喝點東西。我走向飲水器。回程時我路過影印室。裡面沒人，於是我走進去影印了一份名冊。走回辦公室。將文件放回文件夾。及時吸完地毯，回去吃午飯。

en_text: Finish vacuuming in time for lunch. The sun is shining through my ofﬁce window, so I sit in front of it and pretend I’m getting a tan. I’d have to pretend really hard for other people to see it. Sally knocks on my door, then steps in and hands me a small parcel of food. I give her a small thank you in return. She asks me again if I want to join her outside, and I make the mistake of saying maybe next time. She positively beams at this before she leaves. I stare out the window on the chance I might see her out there, but my view doesn’t overlook the river so the only people I see are strangers. On the horizon I see something I haven’t seen in weeks—rain clouds. They’re too far away to tell which direction they’re moving.
zh_text: 陽光自我的辦公室窗口灑落，於是我坐在窗前，假裝曬太陽。我必須努力假裝給其他人看。莎莉敲了敲門，然後走進來，給我一小袋食物。我輕聲道謝。她又問我要不要跟她出去吃，我不小心說了或許改天吧。她帶著愉快的微笑離開。我凝望窗外，看看能不能看到她。不過我的窗口看不見河岸，所以我只看到一群陌生人。

en_text: I eat my sandwiches while looking at the list. With over ninety names on it, ninety-four to be exact, it’s pretty big. I don’t know what I expected —maybe half a dozen or so—but ninety-four suggests a lot of people running around not knowing what’s going on. Dozens more ofﬁcers took statements, but it’s only the detectives who work the scene. Only the detectives who see the body.
zh_text: 我邊看名冊，邊吃三明治。名冊上有超過九十個名字，精確來說是九十四個，很長的名單。我不知道原先期待看到多少——或許半打左右——不過九十四個就表示有一大票搞不清楚狀況的人在現場附近出沒。有數十名警員在外面蒐集鄰居證詞，不過只有警探才會處理犯罪現場。只有警探才會看到屍體。

en_text:
I begin to panic: this could take me forever. The feeling that this is going to be a big waste of time is creeping deep into my thoughts. But not all of the people on this list would have been to each of the crime scenes, right? Maybe half of them at each one, maybe not even that. The trick is to ﬁgure out which of these ninety-four people went to Daniela Walker’s house.
Call sheets.
zh_text:
我開始慌了：這件事情可能要搞很久。我心裡產生一股很可能會白忙一場的恐懼。不過並非所有這份名單上的人都曾到過所有犯罪現場，是吧？或許只有半數，甚至可能不到。竅門在於弄清楚這九十四個人裡有多少人到過丹妮耶拉·沃克家。
排班表。

en_text: Daniela was discovered late on a Friday night. Therefore, several phone calls had to have been made to the people who are on this list. None of the detectives would have been working that late. They were off eating with their wives or girlfriends and were interrupted with the news that dinner was over. Only one of them already knew, because one of them had built up an appetite by strangling Daniela and throwing her pen across the wall.
zh_text: 丹妮耶拉的屍體是在禮拜五晚間發現的。這表示這份名冊上有幾個人接到了通知電話。警探不會工作到那麼晚。他們都跑去跟老婆或是女朋友共進晚餐，然後被這件讓晚餐提早結束的消息打斷。只有其中一人早就得知此事，因為他爲了勒死丹妮耶拉和把她的筆丟到牆上而累得食慾大增。

en_text: Lunch isn’t over yet, but I’m too excited to keep eating. I head into the records room and give it a good spring cleaning. I take extra time near the hard copy of the phone records, giving the area around it an extremely thorough polishing.
zh_text: 午餐還沒吃完，不過我已經興奮到吃不下飯了。我前往紀錄室，好好來個大掃除。我在電話紀錄區多花了一點時間，把那附近擦得特別乾淨。

en_text: On the night Daniela Walker was killed, ﬁfteen phone calls out of twenty were successfully made. These are the people who showed up. Fifteen people, plus however many ofﬁcers showed up on the scene to report it.
zh_text: 丹妮耶拉·沃克遇害當晚，二十通電話中有十五通成功接通。這些就是有前往現場的人。十五個人，加上天知道多少進入現場回報的警員。

en_text: The original phone call made from the victim’s husband to police dispatch is here too. I start reading, but ﬁnd it has little interest.
zh_text: 被害人丈夫報警的電話紀錄也在這裡。我開始閱讀，不過沒什麼好看的。

en_text: Dispatch sent the nearest car to the scene to begin controlling things before the cavalry arrived. Two ofﬁcers. Their names are on my list. I circle them. I also circle the ﬁfteen called that night—including the pathologist, the photographer, and Detective Superintendent Stevens with the jetblack eyes.
zh_text: 勤務中心派遣最近的警車前往現場，在大隊人馬抵達前控制狀況。兩名警員。他們的名字在我的名單上。我把他們圈出來。我同時也圈出了當晚十五通電話通知的人——包括法醫、攝影師，以及雙眼漆黑的史帝文斯偵緝督察長。

en_text: This means I’ve just cut nearly eighty people off my suspect list. The fear I have of this being a waste of time creeps away. I’m down to seventeen people. I doubt the two ofﬁcers who ﬁrst responded to the husband’s call have anything to do with her death. First of all, they were together for the previous six hours on their shift, and the body was discovered only an hour after she was killed. Second, what are the chances that the person who killed her was the very ofﬁcer called to the scene? Pretty low, that’s what. I cross their names off the list.
zh_text: 這表示我自名單中排除了將近八十個人。深怕白忙一場的恐懼緩緩消失了。嫌犯剩下十七個。我懷疑率先抵達現場的兩名警員會跟此案有關。第一，之前六個小時他們都在一起值班。第二，殺害她的兇手剛好就是被派遣到現場的警員的機會有多高？很低，非常低。我將他們的名字劃掉。

en_text: Fifteen people.
zh_text: 十五個人。

en_text: I think about the pathologist. He found several differences between this body and the others. Because he works alone, he could have easily manufactured evidence to make the residues and ﬁbers on this victim identical to the others, but he didn’t. Who was going to check his work? Nobody. That’s who. If he had killed her, the results would be identical to the others. But they’re not.
zh_text: 我考慮法醫。他在這具屍體上發現了好幾處跟其他屍體不同之處。由於獨自工作，他可以輕易竄改證據，讓殘留組織和纖維物質吻合其他屍體，但是他沒這麼做。有誰會去檢查他的報告？沒有人。沒人會檢查。如果兇手是他，驗屍結果就會跟其他屍體一樣。但是結果不同。

en_text: So it isn’t him.
zh_text: 所以不是他。

en_text: Fourteen people.
zh_text: 十四個人。

en_text: Could this be any easier?
zh_text: 有沒有這麼容易？

en_text: I glance at my watch. It is nearly four o’clock. I have been in here all afternoon, cleaning the room for most of that. The smell of furniture polish is close to making me gag, and I’m getting concerned about how my lungs are looking after breathing in a couple of cans. I head back to my ofﬁce, grabbing a coffee on the way and pausing in the conference room to switch audiotapes.
zh_text: 我看了看錶。將近四點。我一整個下午都待在這裡，大部分都在打掃這個房間。清潔劑的味道幾乎令我窒息，我已經開始擔心吸入幾罐清潔劑後我的肺會變成什麼德行。我朝向我的辦公室走去，順道泡了一杯咖啡，在會議室停留片刻，更換錄音帶。

en_text: Back in my ofﬁce the sun is no longer streaming in, instead one of the rain clouds is covering it, but the cloud is still holding onto its payload. I can’t remember the last time I saw rain. When I sit and look at the list again, I see something obvious I missed while in the records room. Of the fourteen left, four are women. I cross them off the list. I could have narrowed down the original ninety-four the same way, but it doesn’t matter now. Ten people. I write their names onto a fresh piece of paper, then sit there staring at them until four thirty comes along and says hello. I say good-bye to everybody who crosses my path on the way out of the building. Sally isn’t among them. On the way to the bus stop I remember the feeling I had this morning that something was wrong with my mother, and I chide myself for being foolish. If something had happened I would have got the bad news by now.
zh_text: 回到辦公室，再度坐下來研究名單時，我發現了在紀錄室裡忽略掉的一個明顯的線索。剩下的十四個人裡，有四個是女人。我劃掉她們的名字。我可以用同樣的方式排除原先的九十四人，不過那已經不重要了。十個人。我將他們的名字寫在一張白紙上，然後坐下來瞪著它們，直到四點半跑來跟我打招呼爲止。我在離開警局的路上跟所有路過的人招呼。沒有遇上莎莉。前往公車站途中，我想起今天早上那種我媽出事了的感覺，隨即責罵自己太愚蠢了。如果出了什麼事，我早就應該收到消息了。

en_text: I catch the bus home. The trash outside my house has been collected. I lie down on my bed. Stare at the ceiling. I’ve narrowed down the suspects to ten people. The police have narrowed theirs down to about ten phone directories. I glance at my watch. I can’t lie down on the bed forever. Ceiling isn’t interesting enough for that. I get to my feet and grab my briefcase. There’s still plenty of work to do.
zh_text: 我搭公車回家。躺在我的床上。凝視天花板。我將嫌犯排除到十個人。警方的嫌犯卻多達將近十本電話簿。我看了看錶。我不能一直躺在床上。天花板沒有那麼好看。我站起身來，拿起公事包。還有很多工作要做。

en_text: The smile has been with her all day. From the moment the elevator doors closed on Joe’s smile, she’s been able to think of little else. She’s always thought his big, expressionistic smiles were so natural, so pure, because they were the same as Martin’s. But this morning’s smile was something different. Pure? She thinks so. Joe has a pure soul, but there is something about it, something she is struggling to recognize. In those few seconds Joe was more of a man than a boy, more sophisticated than clumsy. There was a spark there that suggested Joe is more of everything else than she had thought.
zh_text: 她一整天都在微笑。打從電梯門在喬的笑容中關閉開始，她腦中就一直容不下其他事情。她一直認爲他那真情流露的大微笑非常自然、非常純真，因為看起來就跟馬丁一模一樣。不過今天早上的微笑不同。純真？她想是。喬擁有純真的靈魂，但是那道笑容中還隱藏了其他東西，她努力想要認出的東西。在那短短數秒之間，喬看起來像個男人，而不像男孩，較爲世故，而不笨拙。他眼中閃耀著一道火花，超越他所給人的印象。

en_text: But what, exactly?
zh_text: 但到底是什麼樣的火花呢？

en_text: She likes to think that it means Joe likes her, that their friendship is moving along the way she wants. Of course, it might have been a ﬂuke. Joe might have been staring off into space as he is apt to do when she is around him.
zh_text: 她希望這表示喬喜歡她，表示兩人的友誼正朝著自己期望的方向發展。當然，那也可能只是碰巧而已。喬或許只是跟以往在她身邊的時候一樣眼神放空而已。

en_text: Yet there is no denying that it didn’t only make him look grown-up, it made him more . . . more . . . attractive? Sadly, the answer is yes. Joe is attractive, and she had never noticed it before. She doesn’t want to think about it now, either, because she ﬁnds it confusing.
zh_text: 難以否認的是，這個笑容不但讓他有種長大的感覺，同時還讓他……更加……迷人？不幸的是，答案是肯定的。喬很迷人，而她之前都沒注意到這一點。

en_text: She spends the day at work ﬁxing a section of faulty air-conditioning. It’s a job that has taken the last few weeks of her time. It breaks down every year or two, and the government isn’t prepared to budget more money for police, let alone make their surroundings slightly more comfortable. So she does what she can—stopgap measures that will keep it working until the day those measures fall short.
zh_text: 她一整天都在修理部分區域的空調。過去幾個禮拜她都在跟空調系統奮戰。空調每隔一兩年就會壞一次，但政府並不打算爲警方編列更多預算，更別提讓他們的工作環境更加舒適。於是她盡力而爲——運用權宜之計維持空調運作，直到所有權宜之計通通失效爲止。

en_text: Yet her mind keeps returning to Joe. She’s sure he doesn’t know that he’s not the only cleaner employed here. After six o’clock every night, well after Joe has gone home, a team of cleaners come through and do their thing. They vacuum, wipe, dust, sanitize the bathrooms, reﬁll the paper towel dispensers, clean and put away the dishes in the coffee rooms, replace dirty towels with clean ones, and empty the trash cans. Some of these things Joe will do once a week, or once every few weeks, but he doesn’t know other people are taking care of them every single day. Joe is here during the day to keep things tidy and, she suspects, to keep people happy. Special people like Joe can struggle to ﬁnd work, and in a world where they must contribute, where they must fend for themselves, sometimes the government must step in and create positions for them. She knows nobody has told Joe he’s not alone in his profession here because it might shatter the image he has of his importance. Sweet, sweet Joe.
zh_text: 想起喬就讓她忍不住微笑。她很肯定他不知道他不是警局中唯一的清潔工。每天晚上六點過後，早已過了喬回家的時間，一組清潔隊員就會打掃整棟大樓。他們吸塵、擦拭、除灰、消毒廁所、補充紙巾機、清理並收拾咖啡間、以乾淨的毛巾更換髒的、並且清空垃圾桶。有些事情喬一個禮拜會做一次，或是隔幾個禮拜會做一次，但是他不知道有其他人每天都在處理它們。喬白天待在這裡是爲了維持環境整潔以及，她懷疑，爲了讓大家高興。像喬這種特殊人士要找工作不容易，而在這個他們必須付出、必須自給自足的世界裡，有時候政府必須出面幫他們製造一些工作機會。她知道沒有人告訴喬這個工作還有其他人在做，因爲這樣可能會粉碎他看待自己的價值。甜蜜、甜蜜的喬。

en_text: She doesn’t see Joe when she leaves work. Only a few people ﬁnish at four thirty, and because of her father’s illness, she’s one of them. She heads down Cashel Mall, a shopping street that runs through the center of town that’s a few blocks from the Christchurch Cathedral, the city’s most iconic church that’s made of stone and was built well over a hundred years ago. She tried once to go inside and sit in the silence, only there wasn’t any— too many tourists for that. She doesn’t make it as far as the church today, instead she pauses outside shop windows and occasionally goes inside, searching, hunting, trying to ﬁnd a gift for her dad that he will appreciate. She needs a card too. Something funny. Something that for the briefest of moments will take his mind off his failing body and her late brother. Just what do you buy for the parent who’s losing everything?
zh_text: 她下班時沒看到喬。只有少數人能在四點半下班，而由於父親生病的緣故，她是其中之一。她走向凱歇爾購物中心，在櫥窗前佇足，偶爾走入店內，尋找、搜索、試圖買樣她爸會喜歡的禮物。她也需要買張卡片。有趣的卡片。一張可以短暫讓他忘卻越來越差的身體和她死去弟弟的卡片。失去一切的父親到底會喜歡什麼禮物？

en_text: The answer is a DVD player. With the salesman’s advice, she ﬁnds the simplest-to-use player in her price range, and she chooses four classic westerns she’s conﬁdent her father will love. All have Clint Eastwood in them. Could there be anything better?
zh_text: 答案是一台DVD播放器。在店員的建議下，她找到預算範圍內最容易使用的播放器，並且挑了四部肯定她爸會喜歡的經典西部片。每一片都有克林·伊斯威特。還有更好的禮物嗎？

en_text: She carries her purchases back to her car, pausing only to give Henry another small bag of sandwiches. She wonders if a guy like Henry ever tries to save for anything. How hard it must be to have goals in life when you have nothing. It’s not like the poor guy can buy a suit and go to a job interview. It’s not like he can show up to one dressed the way he is. She thinks she ought to try and help him out there.
zh_text: 她將購買的禮物搬到車上，中途只有停下來交給亨利另外一袋三明治。在一無所有的情況下保持人生目標一定是件很難的事情。

en_text: “Jesus loves you,” he reminds her, opening the bag. “Remember that, Sally, and everything will be okay.” By the time she reaches her car, she feels like crying. Not even thinking about Joe’s smile can cheer her back up.
zh_text: 「耶穌愛妳。」他提醒她，打開袋子。「記住這點，莎莉，一切都會沒事的。」抵達車旁時，她覺得好想哭。就連回想喬的微笑都沒辦法讓她恢復之前的心情。

en_text: I pull out the latest cassette tape from the conference room and listen to the private words falling from the small speaker of my recorder as I pace back and forth. Not just hear, but really listen. I’ve heard all of the other tapes over the months, but I was only ever listening to see how the investigation was going. Now I have something new to listen for.
zh_text: 我拿出最新的會議室錄音帶，一邊來回踱步，一邊聽著小錄音機喇叭裡傳來的機密交談。不光只是聽，而是用心聽。幾個月來每一卷帶子我都聽過，不過都只是在聽警方有沒有線索而已。如今我有其他東西要聽。

en_text: Detective Taylor is for the theory that they’re looking for more than one killer.
zh_text: 泰勒警探認爲理論上兇手不止一人

en_text: So is Detective McCoy, who suspects the killers are working together.
zh_text: 麥考伊警探也是如此認爲，他懷疑兇手在合作犯案。

en_text: Detective Hutton is still of the opinion that it’s one person.
zh_text: 胡頓警探仍然認爲是一人所爲。

en_text: Other theories. Mixed theories. Confused theories.
zh_text: 還有其他理論。雜亂的理論。迷惘的理論。

en_text: A confused investigation is a messy investigation. Nobody can agree. Nothing gets done. This makes people hard to catch. Makes things good for me.
zh_text: 一場迷惘的調查就是亂七八糟的調查。沒有人能取得共識。什麼事都辦不成。這會讓他們難以掌握大局。情況對我有利。

en_text: I make some dinner. Nothing exciting. Instant pasta that cooks quickly in the microwave, and some coffee. Then I change into something more casual—jeans and a shirt. I’m looking pretty good, better than good. I put on a dark jacket. Even better.
zh_text: 我做了點晚餐。不算豐盛。微波完就可以吃的義大利麵，搭配一杯咖啡。接著我換上一套輕便的衣服——牛仔褲和襯衫。我看起來很帥，帥斃了。我穿上一件深色外套。更帥了。

en_text: I’m just about to go out when the phone rings. My ﬁrst thought is that it’s Mom, and then I remember the bad feeling I had this morning, so my next thought is it may not be Mom, but somebody calling about Mom. I have no idea where it comes from, but an image of making funeral arrangements and sausage rolls for the after-funeral party ﬂashes through my mind. I sit to prepare for the shock that will put both my investigation and my life on hold. My heart races as I put my hand out to the receiver. Please, God, don’t let it be so. Don’t let anything bad happen to my mother.
zh_text: 正當我打算出門時，電話響了。我直覺認爲是媽打來的，接著想起早上那股不祥的預感，我又覺得或許不是媽，而是爲了媽的事情打來的人。我的心中浮現一幅幫媽安排葬禮以及準備儀式後聚餐食物的畫面。我坐下來，準備迎接將會打斷我的調查和人生的震撼消息。我心跳加速，伸手去拿聽筒。拜託，上帝，不要出這種事。不要讓壞事發生在我媽身上。

en_text: I pick it up and do my best to sound calm. “Hello?”
zh_text: 我拿起話筒，盡可能表現冷靜。「哈囉？」

en_text: “Joe? Is that you?”
zh_text: 「喬？是你嗎？」

en_text: “Mom, boy, am I glad to hear from you,” I say, the words coming out in one long clump. “It’s your mother. I’ve been trying to ring you all day.”
zh_text: 「媽，天啊，我真高興聽到妳的聲音。」我說，聲音有點含糊不清「我是你媽。我一整天都在打電話找你。」

en_text: I look at my answering machine. The little light isn’t ﬂashing. “You didn’t leave any messages.”
zh_text: 我看向答錄機。留言燈沒閃。「妳沒有留言。」

en_text: “You know I don’t like talking to a machine.” This, of course, is a fallacy.
zh_text: 你知道我不喜歡跟機器說話。

en_text: Mom will talk to anything if the opportunity is there. “Are you coming to see me tonight, Joe?”
zh_text: 這當然是睜著眼睛說瞎話。只要有機會，媽會跟任何東西說話。「你今天要來找我嗎，喬？」

en_text: “It’s Wednesday.”
zh_text: 「今天禮拜三。」

en_text: “I know what day it is, Joe. You don’t need to tell me what day it is. I just thought you might want to come around and visit your mother.”
zh_text: 「我知道今天禮拜幾，喬。你不需要告訴我今天禮拜幾。我只是認爲你或許會想過來看看你老媽。」

en_text: “I can’t. I’ve got plans.”
zh_text: 不行。我今天有事。

en_text: “A girlfriend?”
zh_text: 「女朋友？」

en_text: “No.”
zh_text: 「不是。」

en_text: “Oh. I see. Well, I wish you weren’t—” “I’m not gay, Mom.”
zh_text: 「喔，我知道了。好了，這種事情是不……」「我不是同性戀，媽。」

en_text: “You’re not? I thought that maybe—” “What do you want, Mom?”
zh_text: 「你不是？我以爲或許……」「妳想幹嘛，媽？」

en_text: “I thought you might want to come and see me after I was sick all night.” “Sick?”
zh_text: 我想在我不舒服一整晚後，你或許會想來看看我。

en_text: “More than sick, Joe. I’ve been up all night sitting on the toilet,” she says, and already that’s more information than I needed. Before I can stop her or shoot myself she carries on. “I had stomach pains. I’ve never experienced anything like it. I was squirting water.” I look around my room for a security blanket, something to keep me in reality, to stop me from fainting. To kill the imagery. Luckily I’m sitting down. Luckily I was expecting a shock. “The diarrhea was so bad, Joe, I spent an hour running back and forth soiling my nightgown before deciding to spend the whole night in there. I ended up taking a blanket because it was cold, and I took my jigsaw puzzle in with me to stop the boredom. I actually got the other corner done. It’s looking good. You should come around and see it.”
zh_text: 「很不舒服，喬。我一整晚都坐在馬桶上。我胃痛。我從來沒有那麼痛過。大便都是用噴的。」我環顧四周，尋找提供安全感的東西，讓我能夠保持清醒，不要昏過去的東西。能夠抹除那個畫面的東西。幸好我是坐著。幸好我本來就準備迎接震撼的消息。「拉肚子拉得太厲害了，喬，我在廁所和臥室間來來回回跑了一個小時，睡衣都弄髒了，最後才決定乾脆待在廁所。我拿了條毛毯裹著，因為很冷，然後我拿了拼圖遊戲進去打發時間。我把另外一個角落拼好了。看起來很棒。你該過來看看。」

en_text: “Good thinking,” I hear myself say.
zh_text: 「妳眞厲害。」我聽見自己說道。

en_text: “Uh huh. Uh huh.” To me my words sound like they’re coming from a mile away.
zh_text: 「嗯哼。嗯哼。」我覺得我的聲音彷彿發自一里之外。

en_text: “I felt so sick.”
zh_text: 「我好難過。」

en_text: “I’m sorry, Mom, I’ll come over one night soon and help, okay?”
zh_text: 「抱歉，媽，我改天晚上去找妳，好嗎？」

en_text: “Okay, Joe, but—” “I’ve really got to go, Mom. Taxi’s waiting. Love you.”
zh_text: 「好，喬，但是……」「我真的要出門了，媽。計程車在等。愛妳。」

en_text: “Well, okay, Joe, I love—” “Bye, Mom.” I hang up.
zh_text: 「呃，好吧，喬，我愛……」「再見，媽。」我掛斷。

en_text: I go to the sink. Gulp down a glass of water. Rinse out my mouth and pour a second glass thinking I need something stronger, then remembering the beers I transferred from the Walker fridge. I grab one and pop it open with the Walker bottle opener. Pictures of my mother sitting on the toilet with a thousand-piece jigsaw puzzle on a board on a stool in front of her and soiled underwear around her ankles are hard to shake. Cottage . . . blue sky . . . ﬂowers . . . trees. I walk over to the sofa and sit down with my ﬁsh. I feed them, and a second later, the phone rings. What does she want now? To tell me how many sheets of toilet paper she used? I let the machine get it.
zh_text: 我走到水槽前。倒了一杯水。漱了個口。然後又倒了一杯。我媽坐在馬桶上，面前擺個放有一千片拼圖的板凳，腳踝附近的衣角沾滿大便的畫面實在太難擺脫了。農舍……藍天……鲜花……樹木。我走向沙發，坐在我的魚旁邊。我餵他們，片刻過後，電話響了。這下她又想幹嘛了？告訴我她用了多少張衛生紙？我讓答錄機接聽。

en_text: It’s the woman from the veterinary clinic. She identiﬁes herself as Jennifer, and tells me the cat is doing ﬁne. She tells me they’ve had no luck in ﬁnding the cat’s owner. She asks me to call her, and adds that she’ll be at work until two in the morning.
zh_text: 是獸醫診所的女人。她自稱珍妮佛，告訴我那隻貓的狀況良好。她說他們找不到飼主。她請我回電，並說她會上班到凌晨兩點。

en_text: I ﬁnish the beer and say good-bye to my ﬁsh and am just heading out the door when I suddenly remember I have done nothing about Candy— haven’t made the anonymous call I was supposed to make. I’ll wait now until I narrow down my list. It will be easier to watch for Daniela’s killer when there are only a few names left.
zh_text: 我跟魚說再見，走出家門，接著才突然想起我忘了處理坎蒂的事情——還沒撥打計劃中那通匿名線報。現在我打算等到進一步縮小嫌犯名單之後再說。只剩下幾名嫌犯比較容易觀察丹妮耶拉兇手的反應。

en_text: Because the police have no leads, I have no time limit for solving my own case. I can take days or weeks. However, I have this competitive streak inside me. Right now it’s ordering me around, telling me to keep focused and sort out this investigation. I want to prove to myself I can do this, and do it well. I want to prove I’m better than the police, not just at eluding them, but at solving their own case. What sort of man doesn’t try to better himself? What sort of man doesn’t test himself?
zh_text: 由於警方沒有線索，我可以在沒有時間壓力的情況下調查此案。要花數天或數週的時間都無所謂。然而我天性愛好競爭。而此刻這股天性正在左右我的行爲，要求我集中精神，完成這個調查。我想要向自己證明我辦得到，而且能夠處理得很好。我想要證明我比警察還強，不光是能逃避法律制裁，還能偵破他們自己的案子。什麼樣的男人不會努力超越自己？什麼樣的男人不會測試自己？

en_text: Another part of me, the more recreational side, is suggesting why not make it harder for the police? Throw in another victim to investigate? When investigations deal with only one victim, the police can take statements from two or three hundred people, even a thousand. They crossreference these statements in an attempt to draw a map of the person’s activities that day. Toss in another victim, and the number of statements doubles, and so does the workload. They spend less time with the people from the previous killing, and close to none with the people before that. One trail is fresh while the others get cold. Soon they stop focusing on the evidence, and wait for the next victim, hoping that will be where they catch a break in their case. They become increasingly understaffed and overworked. A stressed detective is a sloppy detective. Kill two people in a row, and all previous statements are tossed into a pile beneath a conference room table in a large box.
zh_text: 另一部分的我，玩世不恭的我，建議何不增加警方辦案的難度？多丟一具屍體去給他們調查？當一件案子裡只有一名死者時，警方需要蒐集兩三百人的證詞、甚至可能超過千人。他們會相互參照這些證詞，試圖拼湊出案發當日死者的活動。多丟一名死者，證詞的數量就會加倍，工作量也一樣。他們不會花那麼多時間在前一件案子的證人身上，而再前一件案子的證人幾乎就會被遺忘。他們會跟緊一件案子，放棄其他案子。沒過多久他們就會忽略證據，等待下一名被害人出現，希望案情能夠有所突破。他們逐漸開始人手不足，工作過量。壓力大的警探就會變得懶散。連續殺害兩人，之前所有的證詞都會被丟到會議室桌下的一個大箱子裡。

en_text: I vacuum around them every couple of days or so.
zh_text: 我每隔兩天就會在那個箱子旁邊吸塵。

en_text: I catch the bus into town. Getting into a police station is easy when you work there and have a swipe card to open one of the side doors. I do just that, and step into a rear stairwell. I know a record is taken each time an ID card is swiped, but there is no reason for the records to ever be checked. If they are, and I get asked, I’ll simply say I got confused about the time, or that I came to get my lunchbox. I make my way to the fourth ﬂoor, taking the stairs. Less risky this way. I encounter nobody. Detectives, unlike beat patrol ofﬁcers, work gentlemen’s hours. Unless a homicide is reported, or one is in the process of being solved, the detectives work from nine o’clock until ﬁve thirty. After that they go home, and the cubicles, the conference room, and the ofﬁces are close to empty.
zh_text: 我搭乘公車，進入市區。當你在警局工作並且擁有側門磁卡的時候，想要混進警局就很容易。我執行以上動作，進入後方的樓梯間。我知道每次刷身分磁卡都會留下紀錄，但是沒人會去檢查。如果有人檢查，跑來問我，我只要說我弄錯時間或是回來拿我的午餐盒就好了。我爬樓梯前往三樓。這樣風險比較低。我一個人也沒碰到。警探跟巡邏警員不同，可以正常上下班。除非有人回報兇殺案，或是有件案子快要偵破，警探都是從早上九點上到晚上五點半。五點半過後，他們就會回家，到時候辦公隔間、會議室、辦公室就會幾乎空無一人。

en_text: I take another look at the conference room wall. The prostitute I killed last night is still to be discovered. Same with the woman I stuffed into the trunk at the long-term parking garage. Not wanting to hang around, I quickly swap the cassette tapes and leave. The microcassette recorder I use has a voice-activated system. This allows the unit to be left on standby mode, where it won’t actually start recording until it hears sound. When the sound stops, it stops, so I can leave it on and there will be no wasted tape. I also replace the batteries.
zh_text: 我又去看看會議室的牆壁。還沒有人發現昨晚被我殺害的妓女。塞在長期停車場後車廂裡的女人也一樣。由於不想待在會議室裡，我迅速更換錄音帶，然後離開。我使用的微型錄音機具有聲音啓動功能。這讓機器處於一種待命模式，沒聽見聲音就不會錄音。聲音停止，它就停止，所以我可以一直開著，不必擔心浪費錄音帶的問題。我同時也更換了電池。

en_text: Of the ten names on my list, only a few work on this ﬂoor. Some of the others don’t even work in this building, but have come here from other cities to help with the investigation. The chances are high that it’s going to be one of these men—taking the opportunity of killing while away from the wife and family is pretty hard to turn down.
zh_text: 我名單上的十個名字裡，只有幾個在這一層樓工作。有些人甚至不在這棟大樓裡工作，而是從其他城市調來協助偵辦此案的。真兇是那些人的機率很高——在遠離妻子與家人的時候趁機殺人可是很難抗拒的誘惑。

en_text: I decide to begin with the ﬁrst name on my list.
zh_text: 我決定從名單中第一個人查起。

en_text: Detective Wilson Hutton has been a detective far, far longer than I’ve been cleaning, and he has been overeating far, far longer than he’s been a detective. He, like the others, likes me. I move down the aisle, glancing at the cubicles to my left and right, double-checking that I’m alone. Most of the ceiling lights have been turned off. Only every ﬁfth one is going, so it’s pretty dim, like being outside under a quarter moon. This gives the place a slight look of life, while also saving power. It also enables staff to come here and not knock themselves out on furniture. I can hear the slight humming of the lights. The ticking of the air-conditioning. But I can’t hear a single person. The ﬂoor has the feeling of an empty house. Like a tomb. No glowing desk lamps, no squeaking ofﬁce chairs, no shifting of weight, or a cough, or a yawn. Things look tidier in this light. Cleaner. That’s because an hour and a half after I leave, a team of cleaners comes in and spends two hours doing all the things they think I’m too stupid to manage. Nobody has ever mentioned it to me. Maybe they think I think a team of magic trash fairies comes in and makes things sparkly and clean.
zh_text: 威爾森·胡頓警探擔任警探的時間遠比我擔任清潔工的時間要長多了，而他暴飲暴食的時間又遠比他擔任警探的時間要長多了。他就像其他人一樣喜歡我。我走過走道，瞄向左右的辦公隔間，確認辦公室裡沒有其他人。大部分天花板上的燈都被關掉了。每隔五盞燈只開一盞，所以光線十分昏暗，感覺就像在弦月時分身處戶外一樣。這種燈光使這地方保有一點生氣，同時又能節約用電。它同時還能讓員工來此加班，偏偏又不會在椅子上睡著。我聽得見燈管發出的細微嗡嗡聲和空調的滴答聲。不過一點人聲都聽不見。這一整層都散發一股空屋的感覺。像是一座陵寢。沒有發亮的桌燈、沒有吱吱作響的辦公椅、沒有人在改變坐姿、咳嗽或打呵欠。在這種燈光下，一切看來井然有序。比較整潔。這是因為我下班一個半小時後，一組清潔人員會跑來花兩個小時去做那些他們認爲我蠢到不會做的工作。沒有人跟我提過此事。也許他們認爲我會以爲是一群魔法仙子跑來讓一切乾乾淨淨、閃閃發光。

en_text: I ﬁnd Hutton’s cubicle and sit down. He’s a big guy, and the ass groove in his reinforced ofﬁce chair reﬂects this as I try to get comfortable. At forty-eight years old, he’s a candidate for a heart attack, and it wouldn’t surprise me if he has already had several minor ones. The only exercise I’ve ever seen him do is chew junk food. I feel nauseous just sitting in his chair. I also feel like I’m putting on weight.
zh_text: 我找到胡頓的辦公隔間，在裡面坐了下來。他是個大胖子，強化辦公椅上的屁股印完全反映出這個事實。以一個四十八歲的男人來說，他絕對是心臟病的候選人，就算已經輕微發作過幾次也不會讓我驚訝。我唯一看他做過的運動就是咀嚼垃圾食物。光是坐在他的椅子上就讓我感到一陣作嘔。同時我也覺得自己變胖了。

en_text: I turn on his lamp. Staring at me is a name plaque sitting on his desk, probably a gift from his wife. It says Detective Inspector Wilson Q. Hutton. I don’t know what the Q stands for. Probably queer. I look at the photographs of his family that he’s pinned to the inside wall. His wife has similar weight issues, but her problems don’t end there. The hair on her arms and legs, and the small splashes on her face, look like wool. The couple looks happy together. I cross his name off the list and ﬂick off the lamp. Mr. Doughnut didn’t do this. It isn’t possible. He would have come close to dying just chasing the victim up those stairs, and I doubt his ability to gain an erection—something the killer repeatedly used. Though he must have used one at least twice: there are two overweight children in the photographs.
zh_text: 我打開他的桌燈。面前有塊名牌擺在桌上，或許是他老婆送的禮物。名牌上印著「威爾森·Q·胡頓督察。」我不知道這個Q代表什麼。或許是古怪（Queer）的意思。我看著他釘在隔板上的家庭照片。他老婆也有差不多的體重問題，不過她的問題不只如此。手腳上的毛還有臉上的斑點就像羊毛般濃密。這對夫妻看起來十分幸福。我劃掉他的名字，關上他的桌燈。甜甜圈先生不是兇手。不可能是他。他光是追被害人上樓多半就要心臟病發了，而且我也懷疑他有沒有能力勃起——兇手可是有反覆使用那個地方。儘管他肯定起碼用過兩次：照片裡還有兩個過重小孩。

en_text: Nine people left.
zh_text: 剩下九個人。

en_text: I push the chair back into the position it had been in, which isn’t hard to ﬁnd. The carpet is nearly worn through where the casters normally sit. So is the ﬂoor beneath it. I move into the opposite cubicle.
zh_text: 我將椅子推回原位，原位並不難找。輪子所在處的地毯幾乎都已經磨破了。其下的地板也樣。我走到對面的辦公隔間。

en_text: Detective Anthony Watts has been with the police department for twenty-ﬁve years, a detective for the last twelve. I’m considering him as my next suspect as I sit down and ﬂick on his lamp. There’s a photograph here. Watts and his wife sharing a happy moment together. Jesus, these people get happy and some prick has to take a picture as proof.
zh_text: 安東尼·華茲警探任職警局已經二十五年，晉升警探也已十二年。我將他視爲下一個嫌犯，坐下去打開他的桌燈。他桌上也有張照片。華茲和他太太共度美好時光。老天呀，這些人一高興就要照張相來以資證明。

en_text: Once again I begin to see things for what they are. Watts has that wrinkled look that comes with being sixty. He has gray hair, but not a lot of it left. I’m trying to imagine him having the strength to ﬁght Daniela, let alone strangle her, but I can’t do it. So I try to imagine him raping her in the way she’d been raped. Can’t see him doing that either. Watts just doesn’t have it in him. Daniela didn’t have him in her.
zh_text: 再一次，我開始觀察小細節。華茲臉上布滿六十歲老人該有的皺紋。他一頭灰髮，不過也沒剩多少。我試圖想像他有力氣攻擊丹妮耶拉，並且將她勒斃，但是辦不到。跟著我又試圖想像他以她被法醫證實的攻擊方式強暴她——我也無法想像他能辦到。華茲根本沒有能力這麼做。丹妮耶拉沒有被他插入過。

en_text: I cross him off the list. Turn off his lamp. Push his chair back into place.
zh_text: 我刪掉他的名字。關上他的桌燈。將他的椅子推回原位。

en_text: Eight suspects. I’m beginning to enjoy myself.
zh_text: 八名嫌犯。我開始享受這種感覺了。

en_text: The center aisle, once it reaches the end of this ﬂoor, branches into a T formation. I go left, directly to Detective Shane O’Connell’s cubicle.
zh_text: 中央走道的盡頭是個T型路口。我轉而向左，直接前往蕭恩·歐康納警探的辦公隔間。

en_text: Here I don’t even bother sitting down. O’Connell, a forty-one-year-old detective with the ability to solve cases that involve signed confessions and not much more, broke his arm three weeks before the murder. His arm had been in a cast when Walker was killed. Even if he did have the strength to do this, there were no suggestions of plaster ﬁbers found on the body or on the bed.
zh_text: 這回我連坐都沒坐下。歐康納是個有能力讓人認罪破案的四十一歲警探，不過在六個禮拜前弄斷了手臂。儘管他的手臂現在已經沒裹石膏了，但是在處理案發現場的時候有。就算他有力氣犯案，屍體和床上也沒有發現任何石膏殘跡。

en_text: Seven suspects.
zh_text: 七名嫌犯。

en_text: The next stop and two cubicles along for me is Detective Brian Travers. I slip in and ﬂick on his desk lamp. No photographs of family here—all I’m seeing are swimsuit calendars. This year’s, last year’s, and the year’s before that. I can well understand his hesitancy in throwing away the old calendars.
zh_text: 下一站是位於兩個辦公隔間外的布萊恩·崔佛斯警探。我溜進去，打開他的桌燈。沒有家庭照片——我只看到泳裝月曆。今年的、去年的，還有前年的。我看得出來他捨不得丟舊月曆的原因。

en_text: I ﬂick back through last year’s calendar. Look at the date Walker was murdered. He hasn’t marked anything on it. I ﬂick through an old desk calendar and see the same thing. There isn’t any note saying “Kill bitch tonight. Buy milk.”
zh_text: 我翻閱去年的月曆。看看沃克遇害當天那一格。沒有記載任何行程。我翻閱舊的桌上月曆，結果一樣。沒有像是「幹掉那個婊子。買牛奶。」之類的待辦事項。

en_text: I open the desk drawers and rummage around. Look through ﬁles, folders, any scrap piece of paper, but there is nothing here relevant to the case. I ﬁnd nothing to suggest his guilt. Or his innocence. I listen to his phone messages with the volume turned down low. I tip back the trash can under his desk, but it’s empty.
zh_text: 我打開辦公桌抽屜，在裡面翻來翻去。翻閱檔案、文件夾、任何小紙張。我沒有找到他有涉案的證據。也沒有東西顯示他是無辜的。我調低音量，聽取他的電話錄音。我拉出他桌下的垃圾桶，空的。

en_text: Travers is in his midthirties. He has a lean and strong body. Just under six feet, he has the type of casual good looks that easily attract women and could get him off on a rape charge with the He’s so clean cut he could have any woman he wanted defense, which juries still fall for. He doesn’t have a wife, and if he has a girlfriend, unless she’s Miss January, he hasn’t put up any pictures of her. I put a question mark next to his name.
zh_text: 崔佛斯三十五歲左右。體格精壯。身高將近六呎，擁有一張俊俏的面孔，能夠輕易吸引女人，並且以「他英俊瀟灑到能夠追到任何想追的女人」那種說詞來洗脫強暴罪嫌——陪審團到現在還是很吃這一套。他沒有老婆，至於女朋友，除非她是一月小姐，不然他沒有擺出任何照片。我在他的名字旁邊畫了個問號。

en_text: Still seven suspects.
zh_text: 還是七名嫌犯。

en_text: I continue on my merry way and sit down behind the desk of Detective Lance McCoy. I start out with the same procedure I used in Travers’s cubicle. McCoy is in his early forties, married, with two kids. The photograph telling me all this sits in a small frame on his desk, center stage. Other pictures hang on the walls of his cubicle. His wife looks ten years younger than him. His daughter is quite attractive, but his son looks like a moron. McCoy is a dedicated family man, I can tell just by sitting here in his extremely tidy cubicle. Small mottoes are pasted around the place, on coffee cups and notepads and plaques: Work to live not live to work, and Sloppiness leads to a path of depression. I look for but can’t ﬁnd one that says The only good bitch is a dead bitch, so I can’t have him as my lead suspect. I can’t ﬁnd any notes that he’s made on the case. I put a small question mark next to his name.
zh_text: 我繼續愉快的行程，坐在蘭斯·麥考伊警探的辦公桌後。我從崔佛斯辦公隔間裡那一套開始。麥考伊今年四十出頭，已婚，有兩個小孩。告訴我這一切的照片位於桌上的小相框中，最顯眼的地方。隔板上還掛了其他照片。他老婆看起來比他年輕十歲。他女兒相貌迷人，不過兒子看起來像個白痴。麥考伊是個將一生奉獻給家庭的男人，我光是坐在這個超級擁擠的辦公隔間裡就可以看出這一點。到處都是處世格言，咖啡杯上、筆記本上，還有白板上：「爲了生活工作，不要爲了工作生活。」以及「懶散會通往沮喪之路」。我找了一找，不過沒看到「唯一的好婊子就是死婊子」，所以我沒辦法把他列爲頭號嫌疑犯。我在他的名字旁邊畫了個小問號。

en_text: Seven suspects. Isn’t this supposed to be getting easier? I check my watch. It’s nine thirty-ﬁve, but my internal clock tells me it is only eight thirty, so something must be out of whack. When I enter Detective Bill Landry’s ofﬁce—yes, an ofﬁce, not a cubicle—I conﬁrm that my watch spoke the truth. Like Schroder and many of the other detectives, Landry is involved with trying to solve other crimes and ﬁnding other killers. A few months ago bodies were found in a lake in a cemetery, making me not the only serial killer in town—which, I have to say, is actually pretty annoying.
zh_text: 七名嫌犯。這種事不是應該越來越簡單嗎？我看看手錶。九點三十五分，不過我的生理時鐘宣稱現在才八點半，所以一定有什麼不對勁的地方。進入艾力克斯·漢森的辦公室時——沒錯，一間辦公室，不是辦公隔間——我確認手錶的時間沒錯。除了施羅德外，漢森也是本案的主導人員。兩年前他曾參與偵辦全國第一宗連續殺人魔案件。

en_text: It would have been great to have been the only one, just as it would have been great to have been the ﬁrst. Before recently, the country had only ever seen one serial killer, and that was a guy who had a thing for killing prostitutes, and that was twenty years ago, a guy by the name of Jack Hunter who the media called “Jack the Hunter,” a cute allusion to Jack the Ripper.
zh_text: 截至目前爲止，我已經注意到大部分的警探都用電腦，除了胡頓和華茲。胡頓太胖了。就算他有辦法拿鍵盤打出連貫的句子，按鍵中間的縫隙多半也會被他嘴角落下的食物碎屑給填滿。華茲純粹是因爲年紀太大。我翻找漢森的檔案，不過沒有什麼值得懷疑的。他認爲這些案子有兩個獨立犯案的兇手。

en_text: Landry has been helpful by making a list of notes that point out how different the Walker scene is from the others. He wouldn’t do that if he were the killer. In fact his notes have the word copycat at the top of the ﬁrst page, with a ring around it and a question mark next to it.
zh_text: 我將漢森自名單中劃掉。他不太可能是兇手，在經歷兩年前那些事情之後不太可能，而且如果是他，他的筆記就應該認定只有一個兇手。

en_text: I cross Landry off my list. Then I head back up the center aisle and directly to Detective Superintendent Dominic Stevens’s ofﬁce. Fumble with the lock. Eight seconds. I close the blinds and use the small ﬂashlight I’ve brought along with me. Sneaking around in Stevens’s ofﬁce is far more obvious than sneaking around the cubicles. There’s a copy of a report he has written for his superiors on his desk. It explains in detail where the investigation is, which, in simple terms, is nowhere.
